articles.title: 2027 budget bicam proceedings transcripts to be released, will help track realignments - Lacson
articles.summary: The Senate will release transcripts of the discussions during the bicameral conference committee deliberations on the P7.2-trillion national budget for fiscal year 2027, Senator Panfilo Lacson said…

blocks.text: Published November 8, 2026 2:55pm

The Senate will release transcripts of the discussions during the bicameral conference committee deliberations on the P7.2-trillion national budget for fiscal year 202, Senator Panfilo Lacson said Sunday.
In a statement, Lacson said the transcript would help lawmakers and the public track who pushed for realignment of specific items in the budget.
“Kailangan may minutes ‘yan para maliwanag sino nag-initiate ng amendment at sino nagtulak ng realignment,” Lacson said.
(There should be a transcript containing the minutes so it will be clear who initiated amendments and who pushed for realignments.)
He added that the Senate is also pushing for continued livestreaming of the bicam conference committee discussions.

Aside from continuing transparency measures from the 2026 budget, Lacson said the Senate also plans to identify senators who proposed amendments to the budget bill and posting the proceedings on the Senate’s website.
For the 2027 budget, Lacson said the Senate plans to invite budget advocacy groups like the People’s Budget Coalition to the bicameral proceedings to better ensure transparency.
“Panawagan ko nga vigilance is not enough. Panawagan ko sa kanila baka pwede na sila mag-resort sa shaming para pwedeng tablan ng hiya ang iba,” he said.
(I told the groups that vigilance is not enough and that they should resort to shaming against lawmakers who sneak in questionable realignments.)
Senate finance committee chairperson JV Ejercito has committed to inviting civil society organizations (CSOs) to observe the bicameral conference committee deliberations on the proposed budget.

Ejercito also confirmed that the bicameral deliberations which would reconcile the Senate and the House of Representatives’ differing versions of the budget bill, would also be livestreamed to allow the public to watch the proceedings in real time.
Lacson also raised concerns over the questionable coordinates in the proposed 2027 national budget flagged by budget advocacy groups.

“Akala ko malayo na ‘yung Leyte, hanggang sa marinig ko yung People’s Budget Coalition, umabot pa ng Celebes Sea. So hindi ito typo error kasi naka-geotag, dapat pinpointed talaga. Yun ang gamit nga ng geotagging, na kung saan madaling hanapin yung project at madaling ma-inspect para pag yung quality control nila, madaling malaman kung talaga nagawa yung proyekto,” the senator said.

(I thought Leyte was already far enough, until the People’s Budget Coalition flagged a project whose coordinates pointed to the Celebes Sea. So this is not a mere typo error because the projects are geotagged and should be pinpointed. That’s what geotagging is for– to make it easy to locate and inspect a project so its quality can be checked and verified.)

Meanwhile, Lacson said senators would relay Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) Secretary Giovanni Lopez’s requirements for project funding, including program of works, feasibility studies, and geotagging.
The senator also said the Unified Account Code Structure (UACS) throughout the process to ensure smooth tracking of project implementation.

Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian had said the Senate would remove infrastructure projects worth P8.836 billion from the proposed 2027 national budget because of missing documentation from the DPWH. —Mariel Celine Serquiña/RF, GMA News

articles.title: Pope Leo accepts resignation Bangued bishop
articles.summary: The Pontiff accepted Jaucian’s resignation on Sunday, November 8, according to the Vatican Press Office.

blocks.text: November 8, 2026 | 2:49pm
Bangued, Abra Bishop Leopoldo Jaucian
Diocese of Cubao
MANILA, Philippines — Pope Leo XIV has accepted the resignation of the Diocese of Bangued, Abra, Bishop Leopoldo Jaucian.
The Pontiff accepted Jaucian’s resignation on Sunday, November 8, according to the Vatican Press Office.
Jaucian, 66, is a priest from the Society of Divine Word (SVD), has served as the bishop of Bangued since 2007, upon the appointment of Pope Benedict XVI.
He replaced the former Bishop Artemio Lomboy Rillera, who was also from the SVD.
Catholic Bishops are required to submit their resignation upon reaching the age of 75, according to church law.

According to CBCP News, the Pontiff accepted his resignation under Paragraph 2 of Canon 401 of the Code of Canon Law, which provides for bishops who are unable to fulfill their duties because of ill health or another grave reason.
Jaucian was ordained to the priesthood in 1988 at the Divine Word College Chapel in Urdaneta City.
With Jaucian’s resignation, the CBCP News said the number of vacant ecclesiastical jurisdictions in the Philippines has risen to seven.
These include the dioceses of Bangued, Parañaque, Masbate, Kabankalan, Ilagan and Borongan, as well as the Apostolic Vicariate of Jolo.
With Jaucian's resignation, an apostolic administrator is expected to be appointed within eight days the prelate's resignation.

articles.title: EXPLAINER: Who are qualified to get DepEd's new laptops for teachers?
articles.summary: The Department of Education released the guidelines on who are eligible to receive the brand new laptops it procured for public school teachers.

blocks.text: Published November 8, 2026 2:31pm
The Department of Education (DepEd) released the guidelines on who are eligible to receive the brand new laptops it procured for public school teachers.
The DepEd earlier secured over 172,000 units of Apple's MacBook Neo laptops, which the tech giant reportedly acknowledged as its "biggest education deal ever" for its MacBook line.

"Dahil limitado pa ang available units na kayang mabili sa allocated national budget, hindi pa lahat ng guro ay mabibigyan sa round na ito. Sisikapin nating matiyak ang patas at maayos na pamamahagi ng mga laptop," said DepEd.
Who are eligible for the budget MacBook laptops?
DepEd said that it would prioritize schools and teachers who have yet to receive any laptop.
It would also prioritize those personnel holding EdTech leadership roles or those actively helping in teaching with technology.
The beneficiaries should be active employees in the listed school during the selection, it added.
Teachers who still have a working government/school laptop issued last January 2023 to November 6, 2026 are not eligible to receive the brand new units.
However, DepEd said that those who bought their own laptops are not disqualified from receiving MacBook Neo units.

Further, the department said that former laptop recipients can still receive the MacBook Neo units by providing official records declaring that their laptops are unserviceable and decommissioned; lost or damaged because of calamity; or lost due to theft or robbery.
The department said that eligible teachers should have an active DepEd email account and the two-factor authentication must be on.
How will the recipients be chosen?
According to DepEd, there will be a draw if the allotted units are not enough for the priority groups.

Moreover, DepEd reminded that the brand new laptops are government properties. Hence, they cannot be sold or transferred to new owners without the proper authorization by the school head and property custodian.
If a teacher will be transferred to another school, the department said the laptop accountability shall be transferred as well to the new school.
Once a teacher decides to retire or resign, the laptop shall be returned to the supply officer or property custodian.
Each MacBook Neo unit was procured at P43,000, which is P6,900 below the current suggested retail price in the Philippines for the base model.
The DepEd said this included a five-year warranty, which is a first for the agency's laptop procurement, instead of the typical one-year warranty. —Vince Angelo Ferreras/KG, GMA News

articles.title: Hot fridges, a fake nuclear alert and a $6bn heist: are we in the foothills of a hacking epidemic?
articles.summary:
As AI exposes flaws in IT systems and geopolitics plays out on the cyber frontline, some experts say the events of recent weeks could soon be a common occurence

Alex Pearce was doing the…

blocks.text: Alex Pearce was doing the morning rounds at his fruit and vegetable wholesale business in London on Monday last week when he noticed something odd.
The defrost light on refrigeration unit 2 was on, and the panel reading was 150C. Unit 4 was the same.
As he approached his biggest unit, its defrost light also blinked on.
It was at this point that Pearce thought: is this a cyber-attack? He walked over to the box connecting the units to the internet and yanked out the cable.
He was right.

blocks.caption: Alex Pearce unplugged the internet at his wholesale fruit and vegetable business after seeing the temperature of the refrigeration units shoot up.  Photograph: Martin Godwin/The Guardian

blocks.text: On the same day, retailers in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Finland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden reported similar problems, with refrigerators and freezers in some shops soaring to as high as 50C (122F).
“If it had happened on a Saturday morning, when I don’t tend to be here, it could ultimately have led to a fire,” Pearce said.
But it is not just Pearce and a disparate group of retailers, as well as French blood banks, that have been suffering.

The hacking attack was one of three over a number of days. On 30 October, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, Binance, was robbed of $6.3bn (£4.7bn) in a record heist and on 1 November hackers targeted Ukraine’s emergency alert app, sending people in Kyiv a fake nuclear strike alert.

blocks.caption: Hackers targeted Ukraine’s emergency alert app this month to send warnings to people in Kyiv.  Photograph: Roman Pilipey/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The official message after the fridge attacks is: expect more disruption. We are in the “foothills” of a new hacking landscape, the head of the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre said this week.

Referring to flaws in IT systems that are being exposed by AI technology, the NCSC boss, Richard Horne, said: “There are so many vulnerabilities out there that … you could say are waiting to be exploited.”

He added: “The most serious risk we face in the short term is just a huge rise in the volume of incidents … and I think you could probably point to the last few months and say we’ve started to see that.”

Websites around the world were temporarily taken out of service as a precaution last month when AI technology from the ChatGPT developer OpenAI helped discover a flaw in PHP, a computer language used to build much of the world wide web. French supermarket fridges were also attacked last month in what could have been a trial run for the more expansive foray this week.

blocks.caption: Boxes of perished goods outside an Intermarché in Paris last month after a cyber-attack that could have been a trial run for this week’s foray.  Photograph: Lucien Libert/Reuters

blocks.text: To Azeem Azhar, a tech entrepreneur and commentator, the way AI models were discovering flaws that assailants could harness recalled China’s Covid ground zero. This was, he said, a “Wuhan moment”.

Azar’s assertion headlined a Substack post that also quoted the cybersecurity executive Matthew Prince, who said last month: “We’re going to have a couple of years where every single week it’s going to feel like the sky is falling.”
Not long afterwards, Pearce’s defrost lights went on.

There are two factors underpinning the NCSC warnings: geopolitics and AI. At least one expert has said the fridge attacks bear Russian hallmarks, while the Binance hack has been attributed to the North Korean state, and Russia is naturally a suspect in the Ukraine incident.

The NCSC said last week that AI-powered malicious software was “highly likely” to be used in hacking attacks against the UK’s power stations, airports and hospitals by 2028. AI would help attackers with tasks such as scouting targets, locating weaknesses in IT networks and writing malicious code, the organisation said.

But there are caveats. The NCSC’s director of operations, Paul Chichester, said the cold storage hackers “really didn’t need” to use AI to discover the fridge flaws because they were already out there, including default access passwords that were published in one fridge operating company’s manuals.

Sophos, a leading cybersecurity firm, said it had not seen any major incidents among its clients related to the PHP glitch, although – like others in the industry – it had seen a significant number of attempts to take advantage of the vulnerability.

And one expert said we had been here before. Ciaran Martin, the founding chief executive of NCSC, played down the “Wuhan moment” comparison. This was not the first time the world had faced a concerted threat, he said, pointing to the NotPetya and WannaCry cyber-attacks in 2017, which have been blamed on Russia and North Korea respectively, and a surge in ransomware attacks in 2021. North Korea, hobbled by sanctions and starved of cash, has a well-established reputation as a crypto hacker.

blocks.caption: Ciaran Martin, the founding chief executive of the NCSC, has played down the gravity of the moment.  Photograph: Wolfgang Rattay/Reuters

blocks.text: “It’s a bad run, but it’s not unprecedented,” Martin said. “The idea that we are having a Wuhan moment is not true. We are having one of those waves of incidents that happen every few years.”

Nonetheless, AI is exposing vulnerabilities. This is the term for a flaw in an IT system that a hacker can exploit, a door that is ajar and unnoticed or ignored by its owner. Since April, when the AI startup Anthropic released its Mythos model, which has a startling ability to flag IT flaws, the amount of vulnerabilities found by leading tech companies has soared eight-fold.

Attacks have not increased by the same volume, however. The cybersecurity expert Tal Be’ery has speculated that criminal hackers are struggling to make money from these flaws, as shown by a recent decline in revenues from ransomware attacks.
“It seems that currently the surge in vulns [vulnerabilities] does not translate to a surge in breaches,” Be’ery wrote last month.

The fridge targeting is carried out by attacking the companies that provide operating systems for commercial refrigeration units. These systems are connected to the internet, giving the hackers a remote access route to the ultimate victims. The Danish firm Danfoss, one of the affected system providers, said most of the affected equipment was old and no longer received security updates. It said it had “long recommended” customers install updates or replace obsolete software.

The NCSC, part of the GCHQ spy agency, said the hacks were a reminder of the vulnerability of everyday objects with internet access, from smart speakers to broadband routers. Ollie Whitehouse, NCSC’s chief technology officer, said this week it was “quite clear” that such devices could be “susceptible” to hackers. Manufacturers need to invest more in making their products secure and consumers need to be willing to pay more for the most robust products – and to keep updating them.
A key flaw targeted by hackers, including in the fridge attacks, is “end of life” versions of products that are no longer being produced by companies or receiving glitch-eradicating software updates.
Referring to the prospect of more attacks on internet-connected domestic devices, Whitehouse said: “To be worried, I think, is [too] strong. But we need to be more mindful, definitely.”

blocks.caption: The hacks are a reminder of the vulnerability of everday objects with internet access, experts say.  Photograph: Fred Tanneau/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Pearce said he now realised his fridge monitoring system, by the US firm Copeland, which was installed in 2018, would need updating.
“Have we learned a lesson? Yes,” he said. “There is a vulnerability we probably should have been aware of, but luckily the ramifications for us were not severe.”

The need for mindfulness is heightened by the nation state threat. Criminal gangs carry out ransomware attacks, where a victim’s computer files are encrypted and assailants demand a cryptocurrency “ransom” to unlock them. But there is a cyber frontline where nation states operate too. Geopolitics, exemplified by Russia’s hybrid warfare campaign against Europe, have made this conflict grey zone a particular source of concern.

blocks.caption: Alex Pearce says he now realises his fridge monitoring system will need updating.  Photograph: Martin Godwin/The Guardian

blocks.text: Last month, the UK government launched the Be Ready campaign, urging people to stock up on three days’ worth of food and up to nine litres of bottled water in case of a weather, cyber or other serious emergency. Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, said the country needed to prepare for the threat of “state-sponsored terrorism” targeting everyday infrastructure.

One expert said he believed the fridge attacks, for all the simplicity of the weaknesses they exploited, showed Russian traits. Xavier Bellekens, the chief executive of the cybersecurity firm Lupovis, said his startup set up “honeypot” traps involving the same fridge controllers targeted by the Europe attackers. The techniques used by the lured hackers included using internet service providers that were particularly tolerant of malicious activity – a tactic linked with previous malicious activity carried out by Russians.
“Are we certain they are Russian groups? We are not. But elements of this point in that direction,” he said.

blocks.caption: Geopolitics, exemplified by Russia’s hybrid warfare campaign against Europe, have made the cyber frontline a particular source of concern.  Photograph: AP

blocks.text: On the frontline of the grey war, there is no shock at recent events. Experts and officials in Finland said the fridge attacks were not a surprise, but part of a pattern they had seen growing for years.

Finland shares a 1,340km (832 mile) border with Russia. Since the 2022 Ukraine invasion, cyber-attacks of all kinds have escalated. Last year, the country’s national cybersecurity centre recorded nearly 21,000 incidents – targeting a population of fewer than 6 million people. In 2022 it was about 13,000 incidents.
This year, hackers managed to compromise up to 50,000 Finnish government mobile phones; last year, they took down the website of the country’s ministry of defence.

blocks.caption: Freezers at a supermarket in Sweden are emptied after temperatures reached 50C.  Photograph: Johan Nilsson/TT/Shutterstock

blocks.text: It is a trend across Europe and Nato countries but is especially pronounced in nations that border Russia.

However, Russia was not the only reason cyber threats were increasing, said Samuli Bergström, the vice-president of WithSecure, a Helsinki-based cybersecurity company. AI was boosting attacks as well and he echoed the warnings about internet-connected appliances.

“These attackers are mostly opportunistic,” Bergström explained. “When they see something that is facing the internet, they will probably attack it. [If you have a device] connected to the internet, you have to assume that it will be attacked, sooner or later.”
Bergström and others also emphasised that Russian state actors were not the only culprits – or even, necessarily, the most sophisticated ones.

There is a vast, unseen economy of hackers in the world. Some are activists. Some are mercenaries, in it for money. A good number of them have links to states, such as Russia and Iran. But this affiliation could be loose, which makes it difficult for officials to concretely attribute a motive to a given attack.

What does this mean for Europe? The world’s cyberthreat actors are growing more sophisticated and more resourced – better able to spot vulnerabilities, more capable of exploiting them. These advances invite doomsday speculation: could an entire nation’s power grid flicker out in -mid-winter, or could commerce grind to a halt?
Finland – and most European nations – have plans in place for disrupted payment systems, or an attack on the grid. But cyberthreats are not the same as kinetic war.

Bombing a power station could take out an electricity grid for months, or even longer, given the years-long wait to buy transformers. Cyber-attacks won’t necessarily have the same effect. Software is more quickly patched; it is usually possible to disconnect a device from the internet.

blocks.caption: The fridge control panel at Alex Pearce’s London warehouse. He has not reattached the internet cable but said his business is otherwise unaffected.  Photograph: Martin Godwin/The Guardian

blocks.text: The goal – at least for state actors – in mounting these cyber-attacks could be more psychological than anything, some officials said. Turning fridges into ovens, or compromising a blood bank, is dramatic; it sears itself into the memory. But those vulnerabilities are likely to now be patched. There is no guarantee that a criminal group might be able to mount that exact attack again.
Still, there are many vulnerabilities, and legacy systems, left for malevolent actors to exploit. These attacks “are more frequent, and they continue to happen”, said Bergström.

Pearce has not reattached the internet cable but said his Langridge Organic business was otherwise unaffected. He said even after the French fridge attacks last month, he did not expect his company to be next.
“Hacking for the sake of being disruptive is a strange concept to most people.”

articles.title: Environmentalists criticise choice of Earthshot prize venue owned by fossil fuel firm
articles.summary:
Mumbai facility is part of Reliance Industries, owner of world’s biggest oil refinery and funder of controversial mega-zoo

The Prince of Wales’s
articles.byline: Rebecca Ratcliffe, Gloria Dickie and Elisângela Mendonça

blocks.text: The Prince of Wales’s Earthshot prize will host its forthcoming annual awards ceremony at a venue owned by the billionaire Ambani family conglomerate, drawing criticism from conservationists over their fossil fuel businesses and their foundation’s controversial mega-zoo.

A spokesperson for the Earthshot prize, which awards £1m to five winners every year to invest in conservation work, confirmed to the Guardian and the news outlet Mongabay that this year’s ceremony will be held at the Jio World Convention Centre in Mumbai on 17 November.

The venue is part of Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries, which also owns Jamnagar, the world’s biggest oil refinery in Gujarat on India’s western coast. The group’s philanthropic arm funds the 400-hectare (3,500-acre) private zoo Vantara, which was founded by Mukesh’s son Anant Ambani and inaugurated by the Indian prime minister, Narendra Modi, last year. The zoo is embroiled in a long-running controversy over its vast collection of more than 150,000 animals, which reportedly includes some of the world’s most endangered species – from the radiated tortoise, native to Madagascar, to the Spix’s macaw, endemic to north-eastern Brazil but now considered extinct in the wild.

Megan Carr, of the Wildlife Animal Protection Forum South Africa (WAPFSA), warned that using a venue owned by Reliance “could lend an unearned environmental prestige to a corporate group currently under question by the global conservation community”.

Conservation groups, including WAPFSA, have raised concerns about the speed with which Vantara has amassed so many animals, and about how they were sourced. The site, near the family’s oil refinery, houses more than 2,000 species of animals.

This week, the 32-member committee that governs Cites, the UN-administered body that regulates trade in endangered species, requested that India submit another report on the steps it is taking to address concerns relating to its imports of protected species.
The committee also requested the Cites secretariat review 11 cases where there are unresolved questions over how animals were sent to Vantara.

Joanna Swift, the executive director of communications at the Earthshot prize, said it had not sought a philanthropic partnership for its award ceremony venue and that it was paying the standard commercial rate to rent the space.

“The [Jio World Convention Centre] was selected because it allowed us to host the event in Mumbai while meeting the practical requirements of an event of this size. It offers world-class facilities, technical infrastructure and experience of hosting major international events, including environmental ones,” Swift said. “In February this year, JWCC hosted the first ever Mumbai climate week.”
Vantara, Kensington Palace and JWCC have been approached for comment.

Vantara has previously denied allegations of wildlife trafficking and says its purpose is “to rescue wild animals in distress, provide treatment along with lifelong care, and rehabilitate those fit for the wild”.

“With regulatory approval, we also breed select endangered or extinct-in-the-wild species, serving as a modern Noah’s Ark to ensure their survival under human care and restore wild populations through reintroduction,” Vantara says on its website.
Last year, India’s supreme court cleared the zoo of allegations that animals had been acquired illegally or mistreated.

A later Cites fact-finding mission raised concerns about India’s compliance with international rules on animal imports in 2025. It recommended temporary restrictions on India, although the recommendation was later withdrawn.
after newsletter promotion

Susan Cheyne, the vice-chair of the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s small apes section, said that Vantara’s model has not yet been shown to support conservation and “may be driving demand for wild animals in trade”.

“For gibbons and other primates, this matters a great deal. Moving animals out of their range countries into a private facility does nothing for wild populations unless there is a transparent, credible plan for those animals: for welfare, for any conservation breeding with clear goals, and for return to range states where that is possible. Real rescue and sanctuary work for primates is done by underfunded centres in range countries,” Cheyne said.

Daniela Freyer, co-founder of the German NGO Pro Wildlife, added: “Our planet is increasingly threatened by the overexploitation of wildlife and by climate change driven by fossil fuels. This week, the Cites Standing Committee, which oversees international wildlife trade, decided to keep India under its compliance procedure, as questions remain about the origin of some of the world’s rarest animals imported to Vantara. A prize whose goals include protecting nature and fixing our climate should be careful not to lend its reputation to these questions.”

Vantara had sought to lobby the UK, the chair of this week’s Cites meetings, attempting to persuade officials to take a more sympathetic view of India’s handling of imports to Vantara, the Guardian and Mongabay reported earlier this month. Ministers were advised not to engage formally with Vantara, internal documents revealed.

The Earthshot prize, founded by Prince William in 2020, is billed as the most prestigious environmental award. William appeared on the BBC’s Graham Norton show last month to promote the prize, saying it was designed to “talk about urgency and optimism together”.
Swift said that it was vital to host an edition of the Earthshot prize in India.

“Mumbai is the sixth largest city on earth. It is home to exceptional environmental solutions and the people behind them, with an impact felt in India and around the world. Spotlighting progress like this, to the largest possible audience, is why the Earthshot prize exists,” Swift said.

articles.title: Does Andy Burnham’s pivot from press to social media put scrutiny at risk?
articles.summary:
A lifestyle podcast or brief TV clip is less taxing than a full press conference – but No 10 insists the PM is not ducking accountability

In an interview this week Andy Burnham said he…

blocks.text: In an interview this week Andy Burnham said he believed the traditional media was less relevant and the world was “not like that any more”. But some people are now asking: does this change in approach mean less scrutiny?

The question was in part prompted by Burnham’s decision to travel to the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm) without the usual accompanying pack of reporters, instead bringing just one TV crew and a news agency journalist.

Across three days of the event, which featured discussions of an apology for slavery and possible reparations, and during which significant global events occurred, including the US midterm elections, Burnham faced just seven-and-a-half minutes of media questions, via two brief BBC chats.
Downing Street officials say Chogm is unique in offering very limited access to journalists, and that the prime minister had done other interviews and media events beforehand.

But it was nonetheless a change. At the last Commonwealth summit in 2024, Keir Starmer took along a full press contingent, submitting himself to both a press conference and a “huddle” – an off-camera but on-record Q&A on the government plane on the way over, in which each travelling journalist gets a question.

When it comes to communications, Burnham and his team are unapologetic about doing things differently. As well as talking to influencers and podcasters, the prime minister is an adept social media performer himself, with an output that ranges from more traditional pieces to camera to a YouTube video where he and the chancellor, John Healey, ranked pub snacks.

blocks.caption: In a video on Andy Burnham’s TikTok account, he went for a run with Mo Farah.  Photograph: Andy Burnham/TikTok

blocks.text: Asked about the pub snack video in an interview with ITV that was broadcast this week, Burnham said he hoped such content “connects with people, particularly younger people who may have felt quite distanced from politics”.

Asked whether his focus on that sort of output was a sign he cared less about rightwing newspapers such as the Sun and the Daily Mail said about him, Burnham replied: “Definitely. I left Westminster for a reason. I got fed up with commentators deciding things down there, and the whole world is meant to believe what they believe. Well, sorry, the world’s not like that any more.”

While no one in politics disagrees with the need for leaders to keep up with the fast-changing ways in which people consume news, it is undeniable that an interview on a lifestyle podcast, or a brief TV clip in which the reporter has to cover all the news of the day, is less taxing than a full press conference with specialist journalists.

No 10 is insistent that Burnham does not dodge scrutiny, pointing to recent longer-form interviews, as well as a grilling last month on ITV’s Good Morning Britain, where the comfy sofas generally come with robust questioning.

blocks.caption: Andy Burnham being interviewed during the UN general assembly in New York. Photograph: Simon Dawson/No 10 Downing Street

blocks.text: Some observers nonetheless detect what they see as efforts by his team to make Burnham’s mix of media engagements slightly less onerous than it might be.

“When the going is good, he can probably get away with it,” said one former media adviser who worked with several Conservative prime ministers. “But if things get worse and it feels like the press is getting shut out, or not being given the chance to properly scrutinise policies, then in my experience the media are pretty good at working as a pack, and will come down quite hard.”
after newsletter promotion

There is a particular incentive for a prime minister to dodge the traditional on-plane media huddle en route to a summit, which can often involve more than a dozen questions, ranging from global events to relative trivia.

The repercussions can be significant, usually more so for prime ministers already under pressure. In a passing remark on a flight to China in 2018, Theresa May said she planned to fight the next election, galvanising critics on her own backbenches.
“Misadventures have a way of happening when prime ministers go out on the road,” said Paul Harrison, who was May’s press secretary.

“A huddle with the travelling press pack is about as unpredictable a high-wire act as there is for a PM – potentially 15 journalists each asking blind questions on absolutely anything they like. And a bad answer delivered en route to a summit can still be making headlines long after you’ve got home.”

Liz Jarvis, a Liberal Democrat MP who is a former journalist and sits on the culture, media and sport select committee, said while it was undeniable that politicians needed to communicate differently, it felt as though Burnham was being shielded at times.

She said: “He is a very skilled orator, but when you break down his PMQs answers, for example, there sometimes isn’t much substance to it. When the honeymoon period ends he will be held to account, so he can’t avoid media scrutiny for ever.”

articles.title: Niño Alcantara, the ‘kuya’ of Philippine tennis, still enjoys the grind
articles.summary: Filipino tennis veteran Niño Alcantara reflects on two decades of sacrifice, a historic junior Grand Slam triumph, and the life-changing perspective of fatherhood

blocks.text: Three days after becoming a father, Francis Casey “Niño” Alcantara had to leave his newborn son behind.
His wife, Meanne, gave birth on a Tuesday, and by Friday, Alcantara was already leaving for the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan.
Though his wife approved of the trip, leaving was still difficult.
“I didn’t want to leave the baby,” Alcantara said, “But at the same time, I wanted to go play in the Asian Games.”
Yet, fatherhood ignited a fresh spark within him.
“I was playing for him every match,” Alcantara said. “It was all dedicated to my baby and my wife.”

blocks.caption: Baby, Newborn, Person

blocks.text: In Japan, his mixed-doubles run with Shaira Hope Rivera ultimately ended in the round of 16. Despite winning no medal, representing the country meant everything to him.
“It feels different playing for the flag,” the 34-year-old Alcantara said.
As the only veteran male athlete alongside four women in the Philippine tennis delegation, he also naturally embraced the role of a kuya (big brother).
“I am the kuya/bodyguard,” he said, laughing.

blocks.caption: The Philippine tennis delegation at the 2026 Asian Games.

blocks.text: Long before the international rankings, the grueling travel schedules, and the responsibilities of fatherhood, Alcantara’s young life revolved around a wide variety of sports.
He was only four or five years old when he first picked up a tennis racket in Cagayan de Oro, but basketball, badminton, table tennis, and billiards were also among the regular sports he played.
“I was very athletic so I played most sports,” he said.

Alcantara even earned basketball MVP honors and maintained school honors from first to fifth grade. His father, however, saw a different path forward — seeing tennis as his son’s ultimate ticket to securing scholarships in Manila.

blocks.caption: Alcantara, holding a ball, with the Xavier-Ateneo basketball team.

blocks.text: Tragedy struck when his father passed away when Alcantara was just in elementary.
“It was tough at first,” he recalled. “Like you know, not having a dad from 10 years old.”
Yet, the blueprint his father left behind kept him moving forward.
“I think overall if he was still alive, he’ll be very happy and proud of us,” he said.

blocks.caption: Alcantara’s dad hands his medal
Alcantara’s baby photos with his parents.

blocks.text: By his early teens, Alcantara left regular schooling behind for homeschooling through Xavier University-Ateneo de Cagayan so he could train full-time in Manila.
“I really had to sacrifice time, family, and friends,” he said. “So, that’s what I did. And yeah, I think it really paid off.”

Those sacrifices bore historic fruit in 2009 when Alcantara captured the Australian Open junior boys’ doubles title alongside Taiwanese partner Hsieh Cheng-peng, with his mother proudly watching from the stands.

“Uy, first Filipino ka pala na nanalo and all (Hey, so you’re the first Filipino to win and all that),” Alcantara recalled people telling him. “It was a special moment. I didn’t know it was that big at first.”

blocks.caption: Alcantara (right) and Hsieh Cheng-peng with their 2009 Australian Open juniors trophy.

blocks.text: The historic Grand Slam triumph skyrocketed him to No. 14 in the world junior rankings and opened the doors to numerous US college scholarship offers.

“Instead of begging the coaches, I had to pick a school na lang kung saan ako pupunta (I just had to pick a school to go to),” shared Alcantara, who went on to see action in the US NCAA, playing for Fresno State University (2011-2012) before transferring to Pepperdine University (2012-2014).
However, transitioning to the professional circuit in 2016 proved to be an entirely different beast.
“Tennis is super tough,” he said. “And it’s very hard to transition from juniors to pros.”

blocks.caption: Alcantara poses with Alex Eala and her bronze medal during the 2026 Asian Games.

blocks.text: Alcantara had to grind through low-level tournaments just to qualify for bigger brackets. Yet, over a decade of relentless effort, he kept pushing — learning from every victory and setback alike.

Whether battling on the pro circuit or proudly representing the Philippines in international play — where he has won a mixed doubles bronze in the 2022 Asian Games and all medal colors in six Southeast Asian Games editions — his passion never wavered.
“I’m still here. I’m still grinding, I’m still ready to compete,” he said.
Now a veteran of the sport, Alcantara estimates he has two or three years left in his competitive career, depending on how his body holds up.
Retirement, when it eventually comes, will mean less traveling and more time to consider what comes next.
For now, he is taking a well-deserved five- to six-week break to enjoy fatherhood before gearing up for a heavy 2027 schedule of 25 to 30 tournament weeks.
While leaving his newborn son again may be difficult, it gave Alcantara a new perspective on why he continues to compete.
“The fire and the love of the game is still there,” said Alcantara. “It’s still the same.” – Rappler.com
Jade Tan is a Rappler intern studying AB Journalism at University of Santo Tomas, Manila.

articles.title: As COP31 Antalya kicks off, can world move beyond big promises?
articles.summary: Droughts, floods and extreme heat are upping the pressure on delegates at the UN climate talks in Antalya, Turkey. Can countries move beyond pledges to concrete action?

image.caption: Finding a path away from polluting fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas will once again be on the agenda at COP this yearImage: Goksel Yapar/AFP

blocks.text: With its pulsing music, flashy images and barrage of special effects, the key message in Antalya's marketing video is clear: Turkey, the host of the 31st edition of the UN climate talks, is cool, stylish, modern — and eco-conscious.

Both President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and his wife, Emine, make an appearance, with Turkey's first lady calling climate change "one of the most visible manifestations of the burden human activity has placed on our planet."

From November 9-20, delegates from nearly every country in the world are coming together in the Mediterranean city of Antalya to chart a way out of the climate crisis. Turkey is the official host, and Australia will lead the negotiations. But the issues they'll confront during those 12 days are far more serious than the showy marketing campaign make them out to be.
Severe drought, extreme heat, wildfires and record-low water levels in Europe's main waterways — summer across the continent was dominated by climate emergencies.

And in late August, a series of flash floods triggered by a rock-ice avalanche in Nepal and Tibet washed away entire villages, killing more than 1,400 people and leaving thousands missing. Climate experts have linked the disaster to melting ice and a warming climate.
Can shipping adapt as Germany's busiest river runs dry?

Globally, carbon emissions are still rising: the UN has concluded that it is no longer possible to keep global temperature rise to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial levels, the goal agreed at COP21 in 2015.

The global transition away from polluting fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas will be at the center of attention in Antalya — once again. To date, there's been no consensus on whether and how to transition rapidly away from this main source of global warming.
Climate talks not enough to save
Despite the setbacks, the world has made some progress thanks to the 2015 Paris Agreement.
David Victor, a climate expert at the University of California San Diego, pointed out that before then, the planet was hurtling toward an average temperature rise of between 3-3.5 C.

If current climate commitments are fully implemented, the latest UN projections show a rise of up to 2.6 C. It's a significant step forward, even though warming of that magnitude will still have worldwide consequences.
"There's no question that we could be doing more," said Victor, though he cautioned against pinning too much on this year's summit.

All agreements at COP need to be unanimous, meaning individual states can quash any sweeping resolutions. Added to that challenge are the ongoing wars, trade conflicts and other economic problems swirling around this year's negotiations.

"It's like a giant Christmas tree in which everybody's hung their different ornaments, and the tree is groaning and more ornaments are being put on it," said Victor. "We have to look at it for what it is: It's a place where people talk about stuff."
Climate 'clubs' banding together to enact change

Instead of waiting for all COP member states to come to an agreement, Victor sees a better chance for change in what he called "clubs" — smaller alliances of governments and companies working together to advance actual solutions, whether it be in aviation, shipping or electromobility.
"The Paris process is important. It has to go forward," he told DW. "But all the work is going to be done in clubs."
Small states push fossil fuel treaty amid Iran energy crisis
An example of this approach was last April's first ever International Conference on Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels in Santa Marta, Colombia.

Colombia and the Netherlands invited representatives from 57 countries and key sectors to discuss ways to move the world away from coal, oil and gas, after an agreement on a similar plan failed at the 2025 climate summit due to opposition from several oil-producing states.
Spark new momentum on decarbonization

With an eye to the ongoing trade conflicts and energy crisis, hosts Turkey and Australia have included green industrialization and the clean energy transition among their aims. One goal is to increase the share of electricity in global energy consumption to 35% by 2035, up from around 20% today.
EU to weaken combustion engine ban amid industry pressure

A recent analysis by the International Energy Agency found accelerating electrification could cut fuel-importing countries' energy bills by more than $400 billion (€357 billion) by 2035, compared to 2025 levels. The idea could appeal to regions dependent on fossil fuel imports — among them Germany and the European Union.
Ahead of COP31, German Environment Minister Carsten Schneider said Germany and the EU wanted to spark new momentum in the "global phaseout of fossil fuels."
It's wouldn't just be good for the climate, but a chance for many countries to boost their economies and reduce dependence on energy imports, added Schneider in a statement.

Oil-producing states like Saudi Arabia, however, aren't interested in deals that will undermine their business model. At recent UN climate conferences, they've repeatedly blocked any final agreements including phaseout plans.

Even China, despite its massive expansion of wind and solar energy over the last 20 years, could be against the idea. The economic superpower traditionally rejects any outside demands, proposals or interference concerning its national decisions on energy policy.
Climate financing 'far from what's needed'

Every country in the world is affected by climate change, with loss and damage calculated in the hundreds of billions from heat, drought and storms. Worst hit are vulnerable countries in the Global South and island nations, who are at risk of disappearing as sea levels rise.

That's where money comes into play, with developing countries calling for more support to protect their citizens from the harms of global warming. At the 2024 UN climate talks in Baku, Azerbaijan, industrialized nations agreed to free up at least $300 billion annually in climate financing by 2035.

blocks.caption: Island nations and coastal communities in places like Panama (above) are at risk of rising seasImage: Martin Bernetti/AFP

blocks.text: But where exactly all those funds will come from remains hotly debated. At the same time, several major developed countries — most notably, the US — have cut their development aid.
The German government only paid out €4.7 billion from its 2025 budget for international climate financing, down from €6.1 billion in 2024.
"The level of financial support for developing countries today is far from what's needed," said Jan Kowalzig, a climate expert at Oxfam Germany.

Breaking financial promises like this comes at the expense of losing the trust of developing countries and, as a result, the diplomatic power, on which Germany and other industrialized nations rely to shape policy to fight climate change.
Concrete action would make COP31 a success
Cosima Cassel, who focuses on climate diplomacy at the independent think tank E3G in Berlin, believes Turkey's push to turbocharge electrification during an oil crisis could be successful.
Kenya's young climate influencers driving real change
For Cassel, a successful outcome at what are expected to be difficult negotiations in Antalya would reveal actual political will behind the grand agreements.
When it comes to electrification, that means taking the expansion of electricity grids and battery storage capacity seriously — not to mention removing the barriers to further electrification.
This article was originally written in German.

blocks.text: November 8, 2026 | 1:15pm
Workers are seen constructing Marikina’s flood control projects on May 30, 2023, ahead of the rainy season.
The Philippine STAR / Walter Bollozos
MANILA, Philippines — A labor group has urged newly-appointed Chief Justice Rodil Zalameda for a speedy disposition of labor cases across the judiciary.

In a statement on Saturday, November 7, Federation of Free Workers (FFW) National President Sonny Matula appealed for a comprehensive review of aging labor cases currently pending before the Supreme Court and the Court of Appeals.

“For a worker who has lost a job, every year of litigation means food, tuition and medicine that the family must struggle to afford. Ang manggagawa, arawan ang sahod; sana ang hustisya, hindi dekada ang hintayan,” Matula said.

(For a worker who has lost a job, every year of litigation means food, tuition and medicine that the family must struggle to afford. A worker's wage is earned daily; hopefully, justice won't take decades of waiting.)

Matula also urged the high court to implement stricter monitoring against dilatory motions, establish digital court services for low-income litigants and introduce a proposed "Writ of Manggagawa" designed to expedite cases involving workers exercising their right to unionize.

“Hindi sapat ang panalo sa papel. Workers must receive the wages, benefits, reinstatement, or separation pay finally awarded to them while these remedies can still make a meaningful difference in their lives,” Vilma Garcia, FFW Board Member and President of the De La Salle Health Institute Employees Union said in a statement

(A victory on paper is not enough. Workers must receive the wages, benefits, reinstatement or separation pay finally awarded to them while these remedies can still make a meaningful difference in their lives.)

“Habang nakabinbin ang kaso, tuloy ang pamasahe, bayarin sa pagkain, pag-aaral, at pagpapagamot. Kailangang maramdaman ng manggagawa ang hustisya habang kaya pa nitong maiahon ang kanyang pamilya,” she added.

(While the case is pending, transportation, food, education and medical expenses continue to pile up. Workers must feel the effects of justice while it can still help lift their families out of hardship.)

Labor leaders also highlighted the need for urgent Supreme Court action regarding lower court injunctions against wage orders, specifically pointing to the Regional Trial Court injunction halting Metro Manila’s Wage Order No. 27.
FFW noted that the blocked wage hike leaves over one million minimum wage earners in the National Capital Region without expected financial relief.

“The RTC injunction blocking NCR Wage Order No. 27 is a grave injustice to more than a million minimum wage earners in Metro Manila,” Jun Mendoza Ramirez, FFW National Vice President and President of the Vishay Philippines Inc. Employees Union said.

“We respectfully urge the Supreme Court to act urgently on the challenge to the injunction. Bawat araw ng pagkaantala ay dagdag na pagkakait sa dagdag-sahod na inaasahan ng mga manggagawa at kanilang pamilya,” he added.

(We respectfully urge the Supreme Court to act urgently on the challenge to the injunction. Every day of delay is an added denial of the wage increase that workers and their families are counting on.)
RELATED: SolGen asks Pasig court to resolve motions on wage hike freeze order

Meanwhile, Matula noted that Justice Zalameda’s previous rulings—such as Ascent Skills Human Resources Services v. Manuel and Keng Hua Paper Products v. Ainza—demonstrate an understanding of workers’ realities.

“We hope Chief Justice Zalameda will bring that attention to the administration of the entire judiciary. The constitutional promise of full protection to labor must be felt in both the fairness of decisions and the time it takes to obtain and enforce them,” Matula said.
“Speedy labor justice must become a reality that workers and their families can experience, " he added.

articles.title: Gencorp counsel skips Sara Duterte impeachment trial on Nov. 9, cites medical reason
articles.summary: The corporate counsel of Gencorp Industries Inc. will not attend Vice President Sara Duterte"s impeachment trial when it resumes on Monday, citing a scheduled medical examination.

blocks.text: Published November 8, 2026 1:04pm
The corporate counsel of Gencorp Industries Inc. will not attend Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial when it resumes on Monday, citing a scheduled medical examination.

According to House Lead Prosecutor Representative Gerville Luistro on Sunday, the prosecution team received a notice that Gencorp lawyer Suzette Balucang-Punay would be unable to attend the hearing due to a scheduled magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan.

"That is correct, and the anticipated date for her presentation will be on Wednesday kasi ‘yung subpoena na na-issue sa kanya (Balucang-Punay) I believe is from Monday to Wednesday, but with the excuse of having this scheduled MRI, definitely, walasiya bukas,” Luistro told Super Radyo dzBB.

(The anticipated date for [Balucang-Punay’s] presentation will be on Wednesday. The subpoena issued to her, I believe, covers Monday to Wednesday. However, since she has a scheduled MRI, she will definitely not be attending tomorrow.)
The Senate impeachment court will convene at 10 a.m. on Monday, November 9. The Senate will then have a session in the afternoon and resume the trial after the session.

According to Luistro, the expected witnesses are engineer Jaime Adalin, Davao City assessor; engineer John Kenneth Enumerables, Island Garden City of Samal assessor; and Cindy Colina, barangay captain of Matina Crossing, Davao City.
“So, our anticipation for the first witnesses on Monday… will dwell on the testimony of the Land Registration Authority,” Luistro said.

Meanwhile, law professor Dean Ralph Sarmiento, who was initially expected to testify for the defense in the impeachment trial, earlier withdrew as a witness, citing the need to preserve his independence and impartiality as a constitutional law expert.

"I have decided to decline participation as a witness in the proceedings. This is a personal decision to preserve the independence of my constitutional law scholarship and the impartiality of my legal views and opinions," Sarmiento said.
Luistro also expressed confidence that the defense would have a hard time challenging the prosecution's witnesses, saying their testimonies are evidence-based.
The prosecution has dropped three Articles of Impeachment, of which they were able to present evidence on Articles I and IV.

Article 1 tackles alleged misuse of confidential funds, Article 3 on alleged bribery of Department of Education officials during Duterte’s tenure as Education chief, and Article 4 on alleged threats against President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta Marcos, and former House Speaker Martin Romualdez.

Impeachment court presiding officer Sen. Francis Escudero, however, said the freedom to discuss the allegations in the withdrawn articles does not authorize the unrestricted disclosure or dissemination of the evidence presented in connection with them. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: ‘Ayo Ayo sa Nangayo’ puts Bohol’s environmental struggle into perspective
articles.summary: Through local folklore and the story of a century-old narra tree, the award-winning Bohol film asks how much of the environment humanity is willing to lose in the name of change

blocks.text: CEBU, Philippines – For generations at Jagna Central School in Bohol, a century-old narra tree stood as part of every student’s childhood.
More than a decade ago, the same tree was cut down over fear that it would fall on nearby buildings during typhoons. Students and alumni protested, even bringing their concerns to the municipality.
For most Boholanos, losing that tree meant losing a piece of their childhood.
This incident became the inspiration for Ayo Ayo sa Nangayo, a film by Boholano director Gerard Jamora, executive producer Pia Piquero, and writers Leon Junel Garsuta and Anne Paradiang.
The film took home the awards for Best Short Film, Best Director, Best Screenplay, and other major awards at the SINEBOHOL Film Festival 2026.

Developed during a SINEBOHOL filmmaking workshop in partnership with United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO), the film explores environmental preservation and the cost of development through a story inspired by elements of Boholano folklore.

What began as an assigned theme, “Dili Ingon Ato (not like us),” eventually led Jamora back to the Jagna tree cutting incident. He saw in it an opportunity to tell a bigger story about how nature often “falls prey” to proposed developments that promise progress in communities.

At the center of the film is an Agta or a tree-dwelling spirit portrayed by Angelo Vidal whose home is cut down for the construction of a new classroom. The spirit then seeks help from the same principal, played by Marvin Ablao, who ordered its removal to find a new place to call home.
For Jamora, the story goes beyond the conflict between two characters. It is about people’s growing tendency to think only of themselves.

One line he hopes audiences remember is the Agta’s “Ija-ija, aho-aho” — a familiar Boholano expression that the film uses to describe how people prioritize what is theirs while overlooking what happens to everything around them.
“That’s the reality of human beings. It’s up to us on how we must find a solution to this,” Jamora said.

In May 2023, Bohol became the Philippines’ first UNESCO Global Geopark, recognizing its geological heritage and the importance of conserving its natural landscapes. Yet, the province continues to face environmental concerns, from tree-cutting applications in upland areas to controversies involving infrastructure projects.
One of the latest is the P3.5-billion Loboc River Protection Project, which has drawn scrutiny from provincial lawmakers, residents, and tourism stakeholders.

Critics have raised concerns over the installation of steel sheet piles and the removal of natural riverbank vegetation, warning of possible consequences for biodiversity, firefly habitats, and the river’s tourism appeal.
The controversy surrounding the Captain’s Peak Resort in March 2024, which was built on the foot of Chocolate Hills in Sagbayan town, Bohol, also raised questions about environmental regulation.

Piquero shared her frustration over the increasing number of private developers seeking permission to cut trees in upland areas, noting that while some applications are questioned or deferred, others are approved without delay.
“[Just] because you don’t feel the impact of environmental danger doesn’t mean that it does not happen,” she said.

In the film, the Agta’s displacement from its home — the ancestral tree — despite not being directly visible to human characters, reminds audiences that environmental destruction affects more than what people can immediately see. For Piquero, this was also what made the story personal.
“When I write stories, I want it to be human or connect it to humans, and after pitching the story, I got so invested in it,” she shared.
For Jamora, he hopes that Ayo Ayo sa Nangayo reaches audiences beyond Bohol and encourages them to become more critical of the environmental changes happening around them.
While the film draws from an incident in Jagna, the filmmaker believes its message remains relevant to the wider realities of environmental development and preservation.
“We hope our message resonates with the audience, because that is the goal, to let people know that this tree-cutting issue is still very much relevant,” Jamora highlighted.
He also hopes the film reminds viewers that there is still time to protect the environment.
“The film is about how we want to tell the audience that it’s not too late as human beings. We need to preserve what was given to us by nature,” Jamora said. – Rappler.com
Joshua Eli Narajos is a Cebu-based Mover and a communication student from the University of the Philippines in Cebu.

articles.title: Uyghurs facing deportation by Thailand say they will be ‘like slaves’ in China
articles.summary:
Activists fear Bangkok will give in to pressure from Beijing despite reports of torture and human rights abuses against the mostly muslim ethnic minority

The deportation of two more Uyghurs…

blocks.text: The deportation of two more Uyghurs to China from Thailand would put their lives in grave danger, activists have said, with one of the men saying he would be “like a slave” if he was sent back.
Now, two more men fear becoming the latest victims of Beijing’s repressive crackdown against the largely Muslim ethnic group, condemned by the UN as a potential crime against humanity.
The girlfriend of one of the men said her boyfriend, whose name is being withheld for security reasons, told the Guardian he wanted to go “anywhere else but China”.

Human rights groups said two Uyghur men were at risk of deportation after recently being transferred to an immigration detention centre and they feared Thai authorities may once again give in to pressure from Beijing.

Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch, called for the men to be allowed to travel to a safe third country. “Previous Thai governments have kept Uyghurs in inhumane detention for years and then complied with Beijing’s demands to send them to China, where they were forcibly disappeared,” she said.

The men had been serving a seven-year prison sentence for offences related to an attempted escape from immigration detention in January 2020. They were part of a group of more than 200 Uyghur men, women and children who were apprehended by Thai police in 2014 near the border with Malaysia after they fled from China.

Since 2014, women and children in the group have been released to Turkey, while the men have been deported to China, in separate batches, attracting criticism from the United Nations and the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio.

blocks.caption: Uyghurs are taken away for questioning in 2014 in Thailand after crossing to south-east Asia through China’s southern border.   Photograph: The Asahi Shimbun/Getty Images

blocks.text: Uyghurs, a Turkic minority mainly from the Xinjiang region in China, have been subjected to decades of oppressive and discriminatory treatment from the Chinese authorities. This has included the incarceration of hundreds of thousands of people in detention camps aimed at stamping out their cultural identity.
Beijing has defended its policies in Xinjiang as being aimed at poverty alleviation and counter-terrorism.

In July, Marzeyya Kasem’s (who asked to be referred to by her Islamic alias) boyfriend wrote to her in a letter that he would be “like a slave” if he was sent back to China. “Sometimes I thought why I’m a human being. What I do wrong against China … no want to go back to China,” he wrote. She shared the letter with a Thai rights group.
The two men facing imminent deportation reportedly pleaded their case to Thailand’s office of the National Human Rights Commission on Wednesday.
Relatives of Uyghurs have said the Chinese government was “paranoid about Uyghurs going to a safe country in large numbers and living together”, and preferred to have them deported.

It is not clear whether China has issued a formal extradition request for the two men. But Chaipruak Doungprapat, Thailand’s national security council chief, told reporters that the men, along with three other Uyghurs who are still in prison, had arrest warrants outstanding in China.

blocks.caption: A detention centre in China’s Xinjiang region, where treatment of the Uyghurs has been condemned by the UN as a potential crime against humanity. Photograph: Mark Schiefelbein/AP

blocks.text: Some have questioned whether criminal warrants could be credible considering that at least one of them, Kasem’s boyfriend, was a minor when he left China. “If they are really wanted for a crime in China, why didn’t China immediately issue a [Interpol] red notice [when they were detained in 2014]?” asked Kasem.
Kasem believes that because Thailand was criticised for last year’s mass deportation, this time the authorities were trying to establish a more credible legal basis for the move.

A spokesperson for China’s foreign affairs ministry said: “The cooperation between China and Thailand in combating cross-border illegal and criminal activities such as smuggling is consistent with the laws of the two countries, international law and international practice.”
A spokesperson for Thailand’s foreign affairs ministry declined to comment.

articles.title: [Two Pronged] My husband’s porn consumption seems extreme
articles.summary: 'Is it normal — as my husband says and that I should just accept — that he watches pornography all the time?'

blocks.text: Rappler’s People section runs an advice column by couple Jeremy Baer and clinical psychologist Dr. Margarita Holmes.

Jeremy has a master’s degree in law from Oxford University. A banker of 37 years who worked in three continents, he has been training with Dr. Holmes for the last 10 years as co-lecturer and, occasionally, as co-therapist, especially with clients whose financial concerns intrude into their daily lives.
Together, they have written two books: Love Triangles: Understanding the Macho-Mistress Mentality and Imported Love: Filipino-Foreign Liaisons.
Dear Dr Holmes and Mr Baer,
I don’t know if you remember me, but five years ago, we had three video calls. I am Maria, from Turkey. I had a French partner and you helped me deal with him better.
I left my French boyfriend. I now have a husband. He is also French. I also need help with him.

Is it normal — as my husband says and that I should just accept — that he watches pornography all the time? He finishes work at lunchtime and when he comes home and I am cooking, he is watching porn. When he finishes his lunch and I am washing our dishes, he watches porn.

My husband leaves the house before 5 am so he is not late for his work. It starts before 6 am. This is why he is tired so right after lunch, he takes a nap. Before he takes a nap, he watches porn because he says it helps him relax. He even saves many of the pictures he sees. Many of these girls are nude, and some of them are so extreme, with their legs wide open, and their tongues always licking their lips or something that looks like a penis.
I do not like it. But if it is normal, I have to accept it. What should I do? Please help.
– Maria
Dear Maria,
Thank you for your message.

Now that almost anybody can access the internet, pornography is freely available, ubiquitous, and can be viewed anonymously. This has radically altered attitudes towards porn and in many circles it is no longer viewed as negatively as previously.

This is not to say that porn consumption is necessarily harmless. Although in some cases it can satisfy sexual curiosity, alleviate stress or boredom, combat loneliness, heavy usage can on the other hand influence sexual preferences, undermine trust and reduce intimacy in relationships, leading to feelings of inadequacy and even emotional abandonment.
Secrecy surrounding usage is also problematic, though this is not apparently an issue in your case, Maria.

It seems that your husband is quite open about his use of porn. He claims it helps him relax and sleep. Why he saves all those pictures however is perhaps less clear. The question then is: what is your objection to it?

For example, is it a matter of principle for you; do you believe all porn use is by definition bad? Is it that it has altered his sexual habits e.g. he wants to copy what he sees in videos? Is it perhaps that porn has reduced his ardor or increased his desire for novelty?
How has it affected your relationship? Has it changed his attitude towards you and if so, in what way? Has it reduced the intimacy between you? How else does it manifest?

Once you have a clearer idea of the answers to these and any related questions, then you will have a basic framework for another conversation with him about how his use of porn impacts both you individually and you as a couple.

This conversation should be non-judgmental and avoid blame, with each listening to the other’s point of view so as to understand and discern where future boundaries might be established. You might even consider counseling.

If this does not yield a compromise that you find comfortable and acceptable, you will need to weigh the pros and cons. Should he be unwilling to change significantly, are the negatives of his porn use something you can just live with? Alternatively, do they undermine your marriage to the extent that you want to take action?
An open and frank conversation aimed at improving mutual understanding and exploring options can hopefully bring greater intimacy and deepen your relationship.
Best wishes,
– JAF Baer
Thank you very much for your letter, and yes, I remember you with great fondness. I am glad you decided to write Two Pronged. This way, Mr Baer’s insights will also be included.

I agree with what he says about trying to understand what porn truly means to you. This would include not only your present — something totally unacceptable, his insisting you both try things he’s seen and insisting you try together things you do not want to? — but also your past — what you observed while growing up, what you were taught, etc.

I feel how I can help you most is to encourage what Mr Baer suggested, which is to explore more deeply “how (his porn watching) affected your relationship? And also “has it reduced the intimacy between you?”

At present, your relationship is unequal; where your husband (let’s call him Nathan) gets to say what normal is, with your having to accept it as normal and therefore, acceptable, because of nothing more than his opinion.
Your writing to Two Pronged shows a step in the right direction: wanting an outside resource to verify your “suspicions” vis-à-vis Nathan’s pronouncement that porn is normal.

For the avoidance of doubt it need not be Two Pronged per se that makes it the correct step, but any other resource that is both evidence-based and clearly distinguishes between science and mere opinion.
Perhaps, a realistically accessible guide for any person to gauge their partner’s “normality” would be the 5-D’s framework professors in Abnormal Psychology share with their undergrad students.
These include:

items: Deviance: Is Nathan’s porn watching significantly different from societal, cultural, or statistical norms? Not that being deviant is enough to label something as inherently a disorder. For example, possessing not just Patis Tesoro’s unsurpassed creativity but the grit and hard work to make such designs a reality is “deviant” (but not a disorder). That is the reason she is a national artist and we are not. This does NOT seem a relevant issue in your case.

Danger: Behaviors that pose a risk of harm to either Nathan or to others (like yourself) e.g. suicide ideation, aggressive violence etc. which would require immediate attention. This does NOT seem a relevant issue in your case (at the moment).
Dysfunction: resulting in a person’s inability to handle daily life e.g. working or maintaining relationships. This is a relevant issue in your case, as it is affecting the quality of your marriage.

Distress: The emotional pain, suffering, or anguish the behavior or condition causes the individual. This does NOT seem a relevant issue in your case, because the distress mentioned here refers only to Nathan. One might even comment that distress seems the very opposite of what Nathan feels when he watches porn.

Duration: How long the symptoms or behaviors have lasted. Temporary emotional reactions to a stressful life event are normal, whereas porn watching that persists continuously over an extended period points toward a clinical disorder. This does NOT seem a relevant issue here since this only focuses on how long your husband has been watching porn, not you.

blocks.text: If you can move beyond asking a credible resource what normal is, and have the confidence to ask yourself what you would consider normal in a marriage, then that would be a bigger/better step towards achieving even better mental health!
That saying, “What is normal for the spider is chaos for the fly,” fits your situation perfectly!

You do not have to have an evidence-based, ultra logical reason for not wanting to experience your Nathan’s constant porn watching. Everyone in your barkada (friend group) may think it ok, but the fact that you do not, that it causes you distress, is enough reason to talk about it with Nathan and find a solution acceptable to both of you.

In my clinical experience, a marriage where both partners feel safe because they feel loved is a relationship that does not insist on outside experts to convince the other an issue is worth focusing on.

If it distresses one’s partner, that alone is sufficient reason to try and find solutions that work for you both. All you need to say is “This makes me sad/angry/feel humiliated, please stop” to the partner. Because he loves and respects his wife, he will at the very least try. Nathan is definitely not at that stage yet.

How long you want to wait until he does…IF he does…depends entirely on you. That decision can be difficult. Please remember, dearest Maria, that we are right here to help you make it should you want us to.
Wishing you the clarity and courage to decide what is best for you.
– MG Holmes
Life got complicated? Write to our Two Pronged duo at twopronged@rappler.com.

articles.title: One Pinoy dead in Persian Gulf tanker explosion
articles.summary: The DMW said that the incident occurred aboard the MT Velos Sapphire, a Marshall Islands-flagged vessel, while it was en route to Sitrah, Bahrain.

blocks.text: November 8, 2026 | 10:56am
Photo showing MT Velos Sapphire
Department of Migrant Workers via Facebook

MANILA, Philippines — One Filipino seafarer has died after an explosion aboard an oil products tanker in the Persian Gulf in the early morning hours of November 5, the Department of Migrant Workers (DMW) said.
In a statement on Saturday, November 7, the DMW said that the incident occurred aboard the MT Velos Sapphire, a Marshall Islands-flagged vessel, while it was en route to Sitrah, Bahrain.

While initial reports suggest a drone attack may have caused the blast, authorities noted that the exact cause of the explosion remains unverified. The DMW said no environmental damage or oil spillage has been reported following the blast.
Meanwhile, 21 other Filipino crew members were reported safe and unharmed
The vessel's licensed manning agency has notified the bereaved family after receiving official confirmation from the shipowner, and is currently providing guidance and assistance.
The shipowner has also extended its condolences and pledged full support to the victim's relatives, according to the DMW.
Migrant Workers Secretary Hans Leo Cacdac said that the government is taking immediate steps to assist the family.
“We will provide all the support and guidance the bereaved family needs during this difficult time," Cacdac said.

The DMW confirmed it is also maintaining close coordination with both the shipowner and relevant international authorities to track ongoing developments, investigate the circumstances behind the blast, and ensure all necessary aid reaches the victim's family.
