articles.title: Cold blast brings springtime snow to alpine regions as temperatures plummet across Australia’s south-east
articles.summary:
Thredbo, Perisher and Mount Hotham all recorded falls, along with kunanyi/Mount Wellington in Tasmania

  • Get our

blocks.text: Snow has fallen across parts of NSW, Victoria and Tasmania as an unseasonal cold blast whips through Australia’s south-east.
Thredbo, Perisher and Mount Hotham all recorded falls, while snow also fell on Kunanyi/Mount Wellington in Hobart.

The snow had been forecast by the Bureau of Meteorology (BoM), and though uncommon, it is not entirely unusual – many of the places hit by snow in the past 24 hours also recorded a fall in November 2022.
The falls brought a rush of posts on social media from those puzzled by the unseasonal spring weather.

blocks.caption: The Perisher Valley snow stake at 8:18am, on Sunday 8 November 2026. Photograph: Perisher Valley

blocks.text: “You will not believe this, it’s springtime in Australia, in November, and it’s snowing,” Madeleine McVie, a retail manager at Thredbo, posted on Instagram on Saturday afternoon.
“Like, not just a little bit. It’s fully snowing.”
McVie posted another clip on Sunday morning of her riding empty chairlifts through the park as the snow continued to fall.
Kingston Crows cricket club in Tasmania posted an image of the Kingston Beach Oval on Saturday that showed it coated in hailstones.
after newsletter promotion

The BoM said a weather system, filled with cold air moving north from towards Antarctica, had caused the wintery chill with apparent temperatures much cooler than forecast maximums. South-westerly winds were also causing the apparent or “feels like” temperature to be lower.
At midday, Adelaide, Melbourne, Hobart, Canberra and Sydney all had temperatures that felt cooler than 13 degrees.
The highest temperature at that time was in Adelaide, with a top of 17.5C that felt like 12.3C, with Canberra the lowest (a maximum of 12.9C that felt like 5.3C).
Brisbane, Perth and Darwin, meanwhile, were all enjoying temperatures in the 20s or 30s.
Warmer temperatures are forecast for Monday, and all capital cities are expected to reach at least 20C by Tuesday.
It may be one of the last cold snaps of the year – the BoM, as well as the UN and other bodies, have warned about the likely impacts of a “jaw dropping” supercharged El Niño.

blocks.caption: Vehicles are submerged and damaged on a flooded street following heavy rainfall in Erbil, Ira. Severe downpours caused widespread flooding across the city, leaving cars trapped in rising waters, on November 7, 2026. Photograph: Ahsan Mohammed Ahmed Ahmed/Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: The climate crisis, caused by pollution from fossil fuels, is already supercharging extreme weather and killing people. The El Niño is expected to ratchet up the effects even further, and has already begun to affect regions across the planet as weather patterns are altered.
The southern hemisphere summer is predicted to be hotter and drier as a result of the huge El Niño, meaning greater wildfire risk and droughts in Australia and southern Africa.

articles.title: Rodrigo Duterte defense opposes prosecution's bid to submit expert report to ICC
articles.summary: The defense team of former president Rodrigo Duterte has opposed the prosecution's bid to submit an expert report as evidence in his crimes against humanity of murder case before the International…

blocks.text: November 8, 2026 | 10:34am

MANILA, Philippines — The defense team of former president Rodrigo Duterte has opposed the prosecution's bid to submit an expert report as evidence in his crimes against humanity of murder case before the International Criminal Court (ICC), questioning its late submission and the inclusion of related materials.

In an 8-page request originally filed on October 30 and released on November 6, defense lawyer Peter Haynes asked ICC Trial Chamber III to dismiss the prosecution's fourth application under Rule 68(3), arguing that it failed to seek permission to include the expert report and its associated materials in its list of evidence.
The report, prepared by prosecution witness P-1400, was received by the prosecution after the deadline for submitting its list of evidence, according to the defense.

On October 23, prosecutors informed Trial Chamber III that P-1400, whose field of expertise remains undisclosed, had provided an expert report covering redacted topics relevant to Duterte's case. They also sought to introduce 15 associated items alongside the report under Rule 68(3).
Haynes said the prosecution had not explained why it did not seek leave to submit the report earlier, despite having received it weeks after the deadline.
The defense argued that the timing could affect Duterte's ability to prepare his case.

"This omission affects Mr Duterte's ability to prepare his defence, particularly as P-1400 is expected to be the [REDACTED] witness called by the Prosecution and the associated materials are extensive," the filing read.

The defense did not generally oppose the use of expert reports under Rule 68(3). However, it questioned the inclusion of two other studies cited in P-1400's report, saying the witness did not sufficiently discuss or explain their contents.

"In reality, the Prosecution is attempting indirectly to introduce material prepared by other professionals who are not on its witness list via the instant Expert Report which - by its own admission - only '[REDACTED]'," the filing read.
"These additional materials do not form an integral part of P-1400's evidence," it added.
Haynes also objected to documents they considered repetitive and of little relevance to the proceedings.
"Their introduction would be redundant, and would burden the Chamber with evidence of negligible relevance, contrary to its express directions," the filing read.

The defense asked the chamber to dismiss the prosecution's application or defer its consideration until the judges decide on the request to add the documents to the list of evidence. It also asked the chamber to reject the proposed redacted materials as associated evidence under Rule 68(3).
Prosecutors submit updated witness list
In a separate filing dated November 6, the ICC Office of the Prosecutor submitted an updated list of witnesses following an order from Trial Chamber III.
The prosecution identified witnesses who may testify through audio-video link (AVL) technology and updated their anticipated order of appearance.
The chamber had directed the prosecution to provide the number of witnesses expected to testify remotely, their anticipated calling order and any foreseeable issues with AVL testimony.
The prosecution said it would inform the chamber, the parties and participants if circumstances would allow the witnesses to testify in person.
"The Prosecution does not currently foresee any issues with respect to AVL testimony," the filing read.

The updated witness list was attached as a confidential annex because it contains sensitive witness information. The public filing did not disclose the names or number of witnesses included in the list.
The submission was signed by Acting Prosecutor Mame Mandiaye Niang.
Duterte's trial set to open Nov. 30
Duterte's trial before the ICC is scheduled to open on November 30 at 10 a.m. in The Hague, Netherlands.

The judges will first verify whether Duterte understands the charges against him and ask him to enter a plea. The prosecution and the legal representatives of victims will then deliver their opening statements, followed by the defense if it chooses to make one.

The prosecution has been given six hours to present its opening statement, while the victims' representatives have three hours. The first prosecution witness is expected to testify after the opening statements.

The ICC confirmed all charges of crimes against humanity against Duterte on April 23, 2026, and committed him to trial. He faces three counts involving alleged murders and attempted murders linked to the war on drugs.

articles.title: Elks to face Alouettes in Grey Cup after beating Lions in West final
articles.summary: Cody Fajardo used his legs and his arms to engineer two fourth-quarter touchdowns to guide the Edmonton Elks to a 28-16 win over the B.C. Lions in the West Division final on Saturday.

image.caption: Elks quarterback Cody Fajardo throws a pass under pressure from Lions linebacker Darnell Sankey during the CFL West final on Saturday in Edmonton. (Codie McLachlan/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: CFL·Breaking
Cody Fajardo used his legs and his arms to engineer two fourth-quarter touchdowns to guide the Edmonton Elks to a 28-16 win over the B.C. Lions in the West Division final on Saturday.
113th Grey Cup goes Nov. 15 at McMahon Stadium in Calgary
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Nov 07, 2026 9:29 PM EST | Last Updated: 30 minutes ago

With 40,183 noisy fans at Edmonton's Commonwealth Stadium — the CFL's largest crowd of the year — two key Fajardo second-down runs of 11 and 14 yards ended with rough play penalties against B.C. The Elks capitalized both times with Fajardo scoring on a five-yard run and later hitting Austin Mack with a 23-yard touchdown strike for a 25-16 margin.

Justin McInnis fumbled after a pass reception and Edmonton's JJ Ross returned it to the B.C. 20. Three plays later Vincent Blanchard's third field goal of the night gave Edmonton a 28-16 lead with three minutes left.
The Elks will meet the Montreal Alouettes in the Grey Cup in Calgary next Sunday. Montreal earned its spot earlier Saturday with a hard-fought 33-23 win over the Winnipeg Blue Bombers.

items: Montreal Alouettes defeat Winnipeg Blue Bombers in CFL East final

blocks.text: The first time either team started a drive in the opponent's side of midfield came midway through the third quarter. Montrell Washington returned a punt 35 yards to the B.C. 54 but two straight penalties promptly moved the Elks back to their own 49. Fajardo then ran for 15 yards and a rough play penalty put the Elks on the B.C. 18-yard line. A 13-yard pass to Mack set up Fajardo's run for the game's first major and a 16-9 lead.

The Lions instantly responded. Four straight successful passes, including a 33-yarder to James Butler, left the lions second and two on the Edmonton eight. Quarterback Nathan Rourke broke loose over the left side and pushed his way into the end zone 37 seconds into the fourth quarter.
Another Fajardo run, this one for 15 yards, and a second rough play penalty set up Blanchard's 46-yard field to put Edmonton back ahead 19-16 at 3:15.
Both offences struggled through the first 30 minutes that ended with B.C. up 9-6 on the strength of three Sean Whyte field goals. Blanchard kicked a pair of field goals for Edmonton.

The Elks opened the game with a 10-play, 42-yard drive that ended with Blanchard's first field goal, from 21 yards. A 48-yard boot by Blanchard at 11:36 made it 6-0 but Edmonton's next four possessions ended with punts.

The Lions got three second-quarter field goals from Whyte of 13, 29 and 42 yards. The visitors had only one sustained drive, seven plays for 52 yards. But Rourke began to find some cracks in Edmonton's No. 1 ranked defence with lengthy passes to set up Whyte's kicks.

articles.title: Gifting with a purpose: Filipino brands doing more than just selling
articles.summary: These small businesses give back to the communities they serve

blocks.text: Every holiday season, we remember that the most important thing about gifts is making our recipients feel seen and special. There’s nothing quite like watching joy bloom on someone’s face as you hand them something they’ve always wanted or that makes their life easier. There’s also nothing quite like using your gift to support others along the way. What if your gift could help the sick, or stop rivers from being clogged? What if your gift could give back to a community in need?

Standing for “Alternative Nest and Trading/Training Hub for Indigenous or Ingenious Little Livelihood seekers”, true to their name, they help our indigenous groups have a space and name in the market. This is the place if you’re looking to gift stylish woven apparel, accessories, home decor, or even whole fabric by the meter, along with custom orders and alterations. Moreover, Anthill has sustainable zero-waste programs: bringing life back into scrap fabric via their reweave project, accepting unwanted fabric in their circulatory hub, and offering lifetime repairs and consults. So in a world of fast fashion, rest assured any gift you buy from them will reduce fabric waste and last long-term.
Get them here:
https://anthillmarkets.com/ https://anthillfabrics.com/

For over a decade, LoveHopeFaith Group has been helping people fight the Big C— cancer— with charities and donations. Their Lifesaver watches are not only affordable, classic, and stylish, but 50% of their proceeds go to their sponsored cancer patients.
View this post on Instagram A post shared by Brave Story (@thebravestory)

As cheesy as it sounds, art brings us together. And we wouldn’t have art without the people behind it who trained their craft to show their hearts. Kâtha is one such place that supports local artists. If you’re looking for everything about art, from illustration to artisanal works and fashion, you can find it at Kâtha, and it goes beyond putting their work on the market: Kâtha also does training, workshops, advocacy campaigns, and brings their artists’ voices to policy reworks.
Visit their instagram page here.

Cara Welfare is an animal welfare organization that cares for stray cats and dogs. While we don’t recommend gifting pets, we definitely recommend sponsoring care for a furry friend or two in the giftee’s name. And hey, in the future, your giftee can foster on their own terms, or adopt them into a fur-ever home.
Visit their website here.

The water hyacinth is a non-endangered aquatic plant notable for its rapid reproduction… and the invasive effects of its proliferation on the ecosystem and living communities. To help keep its population in check, Jacinto and Lirio source their plant-based leather from the water hyacinth and turn it into a variety of leatherworks, like accessories, bags, and stationery. They also provide custom orders.

A shameless plug. There’s no shame in supporting the press, so why not gift a subscription to independent investigative journalism? It also comes with audio articles, exclusive articles, and, depending on your plan, discounts on other Rappler media and exclusive events. You can also gift one-time donations in your giftee’s name.
Whichever gift you choose from this list, you’ll know it’s a gift that gives back in the Filipino spirit. – Rappler.com

This piece was written by Rappler intern Czarina Yasmin Sia. Czarina is an earnest creator whose works focuses on the little things and helping others. She enjoys engaging with unconventional ways to tells stories and is eager to write about life’s overlooked aspects. A graduating Communication Arts student from De La Salle University Manila, she aims to inspire people to find wonder.

articles.title: The Trump coalition is shattered - what will Republicans do now?
articles.summary: Republicans can stick with Trumpism or chart a new path, writes BBC Washington correspondent Daniel Bush.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
ByDaniel BushWashington correspondent and Madeline Halpert
Republicans are in soul-searching mode after the coalition that powered Donald Trump to three straight presidential nominations imploded in spectacular fashion in the 2026 midterms.
The stunning election defeat immediately raised questions about the party's future post-Trump.
But there are no easy answers as Republicans face the choice of doubling down on Trumpism or trying to chart a new path forward in his final years in office.
The depth of the problem was captured by outgoing Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, who called the midterms "close to an extinction-level event for Republicans".

Others struck a more optimistic tone. Vice-President JD Vance, who blamed the midterm results on public anger over the war with Iran, argued the party could turn things around. Nevertheless Vance acknowledged the fallout will be messy.
"There will be a lot of infighting and arguing over what happened and why," Vance said.
The wide range of reactions on the right highlights deep fault lines in the party that formed around Trump's improbable rise to the presidency in 2016 and never really went away.
It's too early to tell which faction will win out. But while Republicans are still licking their wounds, the intraparty battle Vance predicted is already under way.

The party must decide whether it will be "centred on one figure, one guy, or on a wider set of ideas like conservatism that can win outside the deepest red places," Rina Shah, a Republican strategist, told the BBC.

Critics on the right - the "Never Trumpers" who opposed his first White House campaign - are pushing for a return to the Republican Party's pre-Trump roots, citing the historic losses around the country on election night.
But simply turning back the clock on Trump will be extremely difficult if not impossible to do.

The party has been wholly transformed during Trump's decade-long reign. Most Republicans have shifted to the right on domestic issues like immigration, and rejected the interventionist foreign policy of the George W Bush era that led to the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan.

In Congress, the more moderate establishment wing of the party that disliked Trump from the start has almost entirely disappeared, replaced by conservative Trump backers who echo his nativism and populist rhetoric.
That trend continued this year, as old-guard Republicans like John Cornyn in Texas and Maine's Susan Collins, both of whom clashed with Trump over the years, were voted out of office.
Three days after the election Trump appointed Stephen Miller as his new White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles.

The move signalled Trump has no plans to moderate his policies or message in his remaining years in office. Miller, who had been serving as the president's chief domestic policy adviser, is a longtime Trump aide known for his hardline immigration policies.
One of the architects of the Make America Great Again (Maga) movement, Steve Bannon, predicted a "civil war" in the party after the midterms.
Afterwards, he blamed the Republicans' defeat on the economy and "foreign wars". "I don't think we implemented the Maga programme," he said, calling on Trump to double down on mass deportations.
But other Republican strategists said the midterms were a wake up call for Make America Great Again (Maga) loyalists who want Trump's political movement to outlast his presidency.
"There's still plenty of Maga voters out there who have supported Donald Trump through thick and thin," said Whit Ayres, a Republican strategist.
"But there is also a significant portion of the Republican Party that's non-Maga, and that's a majority now."

blocks.caption: Trump shows Maga hats to supporters in Ohio

blocks.text: Should Republican hopefuls distance themselves from Trump?

The party lost control of the House and Senate, as well as governorships and state legislatures in red states like Texas and Kansas where Democrats had been shut out of power for decades - and where Trump won by double digits when he was on the ballot.
The stunning upsets underscored the fickle nature of political coalitions.
Trump expanded the Republican base in 2024, increasing support with Latinos and younger voters among other key groups. Republicans hailed the gains as a sign of future strength for the party.

Just two years later, the party lost ground with nearly every critical voting bloc. According to a New York Times analysis of voter data, Latino support for Democratic candidates increased by 29 percentage points from 2024-26. Support from young voters 18-29 years old increased by 33 points.
The swings reflected polling ahead of the midterms that found widespread disapproval with Trump's handling of the economy, immigration and the war with Iran.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Tuesday night saw Trump's Republicans lose in states they had comfortably held for decades

blocks.text: Tuesday night saw Trump's Republicans lose in states they had comfortably held for decades

Democrats also capitalised on a public perception that the Trump family and administration is rife with self-dealing and corruption. The president's focus on the White House ballroom and other Washington construction projects also contributed to a sense among voters that he was more focused on his legacy than addressing affordability issues.

It's a sentiment shared by Benjamin Shrader, the leader of the Young Republicans in Austin, who was still shell-shocked when he spoke to the BBC in Texas the morning after his party was almost wiped out in the state by a Democratic "blue tsunami".
Shrader said Trump was still a "force of nature" when asked to reflect on how the president had used his first public appearance after the results to show off the White House ballroom project.
He hesitated before adding: "I would focus on issues that are not ballrooms, that are not renaming things. I would focus on what matters."
The evidence in the immediate aftermath of the midterms suggests that Republicans could benefit by distancing themselves from Trump ahead of 2028.
With Congress flipped, what does Donald Trump do next?
'Vance was the favourite - now the race is wide open'

Vance tried to thread the needle with his midterm assessment blaming the Iran war and calling for a return to "America First." It was a nuanced critique that broke with Trump on an unpopular war, but embraced a broader political brand that remains popular with the Maga base.
Trump's next moves on Iran will be watched closely by the party for their 2028 implications. An escalation would risk fuelling the concerns voiced by Vance and other "America First" proponents.

In his postmortem statement on X, Vance also echoed the growing calls on the right to reexamine US support for Israel. But he also signalled an openness to making some immigration enforcement changes. That clashes with Miller, a Vance ally who has speared the administration's second-term immigration agenda.
Party strategists said the midterm drubbing complicated Vance's path to the nomination.
"Before this midterm, JD Vance was the odds-on favourite to win the Republican nomination in 2028. After this midterm, the nomination battle is completely wide open," Ayres said.

Potential Trump successors have some time to consider their options, but they'll have to make up their minds relatively soon. Any 2028 presidential hopefuls will face pressure to announce White House bids in the next few months. Some could launch campaigns before the end of the year.
Vance's election analysis was widely interpreted as an unofficial signal of his plans to run. It will likely be a crowded primary field.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Both Vice-President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are seen as contenders for the 2028 nomination

blocks.text: Both Vice-President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are seen as contenders for the 2028 nomination

Other rumoured White House contenders include Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, Florida Governor DeSantis, former US ambassador to the United Nations Nikki Haley and former New Jersey Governor Chris Christie, to name a few.

In the next election cycle, Republican presidential and congressional candidates alike will have tough decisions to make on key issues of the day, from US support for Israel to tariffs to the AI boom.

Trump's power may be diminished as he enters the final two years of his second term, but he'll still have the loudest voice in the party over the next two years. It's unclear whether he will get deeply involved in the process or take a hands-off approach.
Trump has praised Vance and Rubio at different times, but typically deflects questions about who he'd like to see succeed him.
His endorsement will loom as the biggest wildcard in the 2028 Republican primary race.
"It remains to be seen who will jump into that race," Ayres said.
"But I think it's going to be a lot larger and more diverse than we anticipated before the midterm election."
'Hopefully things get done': Americans react to historic political shift

blocks.caption: unspun

blocks.text: Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here. Those outside the UK can sign up here.

articles.title: Germans wrestle with what to do with Hitler's destroyed Eagle's Nest retreat
articles.summary: While some believe the site should be partially or completely rebuilt, others want it abandoned and all memory of its Nazi past forgotten.

blocks.text: Fire engulfed Hitler's mountaintop Eagle's Nest retreat in Bavaria last month

Perched on a ridge high up in the spectacular scenery of the German Alps lie the burned-out ruins of a mountain house called The Eagle's Nest, which is now at the heart of an intense debate about Germany's Nazi past.

Known in German as Kehlsteinhaus, the retreat was built by the Nazis in 1938, and frequented by Adolf Hitler and other high-ranking Nazis and their guests. After World War Two it was classified as a historical monument recalling the Nazi era.
Last month it was gutted by fire in a suspected arson attack, and some believe it should be completely destroyed, the site returned to nature and all memory of its Nazi past forgotten.
But others want it either partially or completely rebuilt, wary of the risk of turning it into a site for Neo-Nazi pilgrimage at a time when Germany is witnessing the resurgence of the far-right.
Germany has an "everlasting responsibility to communicate, to deal with our Nazi past", said Isabel Heinemann, professor of contemporary history at Munich's Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität (LMU).
But rebuilding the site completely, she warned, would mean putting "highly ideologised or highly ideological architecture" back in place.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Adolf Hitler used the mountain retreat to welcome guests

blocks.text: Image source, Galerie Bilderwelt/Getty Images
Adolf Hitler used the mountain retreat to welcome guests
Before it was burned down during the evening of 23 October, the Eagle's Nest had been a popular tourist attraction, owned by the state of Bavaria and operating for many years as a restaurant.
Visitors would take a bus and then ride the original brass and mirror-panelled lift through the mountain to the Kehlsteinhaus to savour the magnificent views above the town of Berchtesgaden.
Once there, they could eat sausages in the beer garden on the Obersalzberg at 1,834m (6,017ft) above sea level, overlooking the Alps.
Unlike Hitler's nearby summer residence, the Berghof, which was bombed in World War Two and demolished in 1952, the Eagle's Nest survived the war.
Tens of thousands of tourists visited each season, providing an important source of income to the region.
In the 1990s, amid concerns that the site did not do enough to confront the crimes of the Nazi past, a museum, the Obersalzberg Documentation Centre, was opened close by.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Before it was burned down, the Kehlsteinhaus or Eagle's Nest had long been a tourist destination in Bavaria

blocks.text: Image source, Universal Images Group via Getty Images
Before it was burned down, the Kehlsteinhaus or Eagle's Nest had long been a tourist destination in Bavaria
Around 15 years ago, a photo exhibit was opened in the Kehlsteinhaus about its history.
Although the Eagle's Nest itself was "largely destroyed" by the fire, according to police, the documentation centre survived unscathed.
The authorities have not commented on a possible motive, but a 33-year-old man with a history of mental illness has been detained in a secure psychiatric hospital on suspicion of arson.
Some feel this is the moment to allow the site to fade into history.

"It's been torched now. It's been destroyed. I think they should just clear away the rubble and leave the mountain as it should be in its natural state," said Prof Sir Richard J. Evans, a specialist in Nazi Germany at the University of Cambridge.

That has happened with "quite a few other Nazi sites", he argued, including the bunker in Berlin where Hitler killed himself: "The bunker was filled in with concrete and a children's playground put on the top of it on the ground."
The Kehlsteinhaus was just "a Nazi vanity project" since romanticised by the name Eagle's Nest, he said.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Police say the old Nazi retreat was largely destroyed by last month's fire

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Police say the old Nazi retreat was largely destroyed by last month's fire
But Bavaria's authorities take a different view about the site's future.
Both the state's interior minister, Joachim Herrmann, and its minister for the arts, Markus Blume, have spoken out in favour of rebuilding the Kehlsteinhaus.
"We can hardly leave a ruin standing there," Herrmann said.

Sven Keller, head of the Obersalzberg Documentation Centre, believes it is important not to leave the site in ruins, as that could encourage Neo-Nazi pilgrims, who would be able to hike up there completely undisturbed.

"We have quite some experience at Obersalzberg with what happens if we clear those sites. Hitler's Berghof was demolished in the 1950s, and in our experience, this does not remove such sites from the mental maps of people," he told the BBC's Today programme.
Nor does he believe "a one-on-one reconstruction" of the site is possible, and Blume has made clear on Bavarian radio that "it should not and must not cost the taxpayer anything".

blocks.caption: Image caption, After Hitler's downfall, US soldiers captured the mountain-top retreat and are seen relaxing here on 4 May 1945

blocks.text: Image source, ERIC SCHWAB/AFP
After Hitler's downfall, US soldiers captured the mountain-top retreat and are seen relaxing here on 4 May 1945
Herrmann said they would look for a sensible solution in consultation with historians, given the historically complex circumstances surrounding the building.
Heinemann, who also heads the Leibniz Institute for Contemporary History, believes full-scale reconstruction should be "out of the question".

"I rather think we can document the state left by the fire and also document the historical remains of the Kehlsteinhaus, and then reconstruct parts in a modern design, to make clear the different layers of time that can be seen in this building," she told the BBC.
Germany and Austria have long struggled to deal with the fraught legacy of buildings and sites connected to the Nazi era.
With the recent rise of the far-right AfD and the Austrian Freedom Party, the debate over Erinnerungskultur (Culture of Remembrance) has taken on a new urgency.

A row broke out recently in Germany when AfD and conservative CDU councillors in a town in Saxony decided to ban "stumbling stones" memorials - embedded small brass plaques in the streets - to victims of the Nazis.
In Austria over the summer, a police station was opened in the house where Hitler was born in Braunau am Inn. It followed years of controversy about how the house should be used.
The Austrian government said the police presence would help prevent neo-Nazi pilgrims.
But others had wanted the house to become a centre of responsibility, actively confronting the Nazi past.
As one resident of Braunau am Inn told me, it was a delicate balance between how much to remember and how much to forget.

articles.title: UFC boss Dana White says he's meeting with Trump after press secretary job offer
articles.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump said Saturday that he has offered the job of White House press secretary to his friend and UFC boss Dana White, an announcement unconventional even for the norm-busting…

image.caption: U.S. President Donald Trump and UFC president and CEO Dana White are seen at the White House on June 14. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

U.S. President Donald Trump said Saturday that he has offered the job of White House press secretary to his friend and UFC boss Dana White, an announcement unconventional even for the norm-busting president. White said Saturday that he plans to meet with Trump on Monday at the White House.
U.S. president has attended several UFC events with close friend White

Trump, while he was at his golf club in Florida, posted on social media that he made the offer to "the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior" to become the Republican president's chief spokesperson.

White, who was in London on Saturday for a boxing event, was asked at a news conference about Trump's post and responded by saying that he planned to fly to Washington right after and meet with Trump on Monday.
When asked how he would balance the job with the current positions he has in the fighting world, White seemed confused by the question and then said, "Yeah, I got a lot of jobs already."
He declined to say what conversations he'd had with Trump but said, "I'm sure I'll have more to talk about after that."

items: How the UFC became a stage for Trump

blocks.text: Before the news conference, the UFC head shared an image of Trump's post on Instagram, along with an image of himself standing behind the podium in the White House press briefing room with the words "On to the next chapter."
The White House and a spokesperson for the UFC did not respond Saturday to messages inquiring about the Truth Social post.

Trump said in his post that he requested that White bring along several UFC fighters as "assistants," adding, "We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left. Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other. Dana, please take the job!"

While White didn't make it clear if he was seriously considering the position of becoming the primary spokesperson for the president of the United States, he did elsewhere in his news conference describe his ambitions to expand the Zuffa Boxing organization he also runs with Saudi Arabian backers and hold more of its events around the world.
Transition period

Trump's post came as his White House is in a period of major transition and struggling with his party's deep losses in Tuesday's midterm elections. The historic wins by Democratic candidates, including in areas that Republicans had held for decades, led to the GOP losing control of both chambers of Congress.

Trump on Friday announced he was replacing his longtime adviser Susie Wiles, who was seen as something of a tempering force on the president's impulses, with aide Stephen Miller to serve as the next chief of staff. Miller is known as the architect of the administration's hard-line immigration policies and is among the most determined of Trump's inner circle.

items: Trump names Stephen Miller as new chief of staff after midterm drubbing

blocks.text: The shake-up at the heart of his administration follows the brief but tumultuous week when Trump tried out a new press secretary in Katie Zacharia, who seemed uncomfortable in her sole appearance with reporters before leaving the job after five days.
The post had been vacant since Karoline Leavitt left at the end of August. Trump remains without a chief spokesperson.
Close friends
Trump is close friends with White and has attended several UFC events with him since returning to the White House in January 2025.

He brought White and the sport to the White House's South Lawn in June for the celebration of America's 250th year of its independence and the president's own 80th birthday. A wire-mesh Octagon was constructed near the executive mansion under "the Claw," a spaceship-like metal arch fitted with lights, sound equipment and large screens.

items: Trump gets ringside seat at White House UFC event on his 80th birthday

blocks.text: "It was an amazing experience, this was a one-of-one," said White afterward.
White also spoke at the Republican National Conventions in 2016, 2020 and 2024.

articles.title: Victoria Barracks in Sydney and Melbourne to remain in public hands after partial backtrack on defence property selloff
articles.summary:
Four heritage-listed defence properties to be preserved for community use after backlash from veterans and former PMs

  • Get our

blocks.text: Four heritage-listed defence sites, including Sydney’s Victoria Barracks, will remain in public hands after the Albanese government yielded to public backlash against their sale.

The sites, along with 63 others around the country, were identified in an independent audit as being underutilised by defence, not fit for purpose and costly to maintain, and were earmarked for sale to recoup $3bn in the federal budget.

But the plan to sell off the heritage-listed sites drew fierce opposition from public campaign group Save Victoria Barracks Sydney, veterans and high-profile politicians including former prime ministers John Howard and Paul Keating.

Ahead of an important cabinet meeting on the budget on Monday, the Albanese government confirmed on Sunday that four sites – Victoria Barracks in Sydney and Melbourne, and Fort Queenscliff and RAAF Base Point Cook in Victoria – will remain publicly owned and their historic elements preserved for community use after they are vacated by defence personnel.

The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, said Victoria Barracks Sydney held a “special place in our nation’s history” while the defence minister, Richard Marles, said the military needed to focus its spending on keeping people safe.
“Given the strategic landscape we face, we cannot afford to be wasting money. We need to look at how we best use defence money for defence capability,” Marles said.
“By moving personnel off these sites, and working to open them up for the public we are ensuring that the history of Victoria Barracks is one that can be protected and returned to all Australians.”
The government will work with the Australian War Memorial once the sites are free to transform the sites into public spaces that tell the history of Australia’s military.
Sydney’s Victoria Barracks was built between 1840 and 1848 and was originally occupied by the British army. It is also the site of the city’s oldest wine cellar.
The shadow defence minister, James Paterson, said questions remain about whether the military should have a presence and capability in Melbourne and Sydney.

“While this is a win for Australia’s defence heritage, it is only the beginning. The Coalition will continue to fight to save other critical defence sites, including HMAS Penguin, Lancer Barracks, Irwin Barracks, and more,” he said.
The NSW opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, said the site was an “irreplaceable part of our military heritage that deserves to be protected for future generations”.
“Our military heritage and defence capability must come before a short-term cash grab,” she said.
The multi-year audit, completed in 2023, was tasked with identifying surplus and costly property holdings, often costing millions to maintain.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: Victoria Barracks in Melbourne. The sales of the Sydney and Melbourne Victoria Barracks had been expected to raise $1.3bn, given their prime locations in the biggest capital cities. Photograph: Michael Currie/AAP

blocks.text: The audit found underutilised sites are “draining resources from higher priority needs” for defence.

“Today’s estate footprint comprises numerous legacy sites without a clear ongoing link to current or future capabilities. Urgent interventions are needed to correct the unsustainable trajectory that has resulted from decades of deferred decisions on contentious estate issues,” it said.
The sales of the Sydney and Melbourne Victoria Barracks were expected to raise $1.3bn, given their prime locations in the biggest capital cities.

Up to $2.4bn was expected to be raised from the sale of 26 major metropolitan sites, saving about $3bn in upkeep and security costs over 10 years. These include sites in Randwick, Sydney; Sandringham and St Kilda in Melbourne; Petrie Terrace in Brisbane; and Fremantle in Western Australia.
The government hopes the sales will free up land for new housing developments with a long-term target of 6,000 new dwellings.
Defence expects personnel will have vacated six sites by the end of the year.

The announcement comes as cabinet’s expenditure review committee, which determines budget decisions, meets on Monday after the official interest rate was lifted to an 18-year high of 4.85% in a bid to combat persistent inflation this week.
The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, said this week higher fuel prices due to the Middle East conflict were the “primary driver” of inflation rather than the government’s budget.

articles.title: Israel's president tasks opposition leader Eisenkot with forming government
articles.summary: Neither PM Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc nor that of his rival secured a majority in last week's election.

blocks.text: Israel's president says he will task opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot with forming a new coalition government.

Isaac Herzog has been holding talks with political parties after neither Eisenkot's bloc nor that of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu secured a majority in Israel's parliament, known as the Knesset, following last week's election.
Eisenkot will now have 28 days to try to form a new administration, with a potential 14-day extension.
"Now is the time to form a national emergency government. I will do everything to ensure we are worthy," the former military chief wrote on X.
No political party in Israel has ever won an outright majority, meaning all governments have been coalitions.

Netanyahu's right-wing Likud party and its far-right and ultra-Orthodox Jewish allies won 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, while Eisenkot's centrist Yashar party and three other Jewish opposition parties in his bloc won 48.
Two Arab-led alliances, the United Arab List and the Joint List, together won an unprecedented 19 seats following a surge in turnout among Arab voters.
That positions them as potential kingmakers. However, all but one of the Jewish parties pledged before the polls not to work with them to form a government.
Herzog said that, after consulting all parties during the week, he would give Eisenkot the first chance to form a government.
A statement from the president's office said he had informed both Eisenkot and Netanyahu of the decision.
Following consultations with delegations from the incoming Knesset members, Eisenkot received 67 recommendations for the premiership and Netanyahu 46, the statement said.
The president has broad discretion to pick someone they believe has the best chance of building a coalition and does not have to choose the leader of the party with the most seats.

The election results had implied three possible options for the formation of a government: a national unity administration involving both Netanyahu and Eisenkot, a right-wing coalition involving Netanyahu and defectors from Eisenkot's bloc, or an Eisenkot-led government supported by the Arab parties.
Eisenkot and every member of his bloc bar one has previously refused to enter government with Arab parties, but there has been speculation that an agreement could be reached.
He could also attempt to reach a deal with ultra-Orthodox parties, but that too would be difficult.

There is precedent for a unity government. In 2020, following three deadlocked elections, Netanyahu and his centrist rival Benny Gantz agreed a power-sharing deal in which the leadership rotated between the two.

During his consultations with the parties, Herzog had said that to prevent another round of elections and to build a stable government, he expected "factions and their representatives to understand that, in the current reality, not every commitment and promise can be fulfilled".
In the period 2019 to 2022, one of the most politically fractured in Israeli politics, there were five separate elections as Netanyahu and his rivals struggled time and again to co-operate.

articles.title: 'Flat', 'tired', 'cynical': Unusually gloomy Kiwis deliver New Zealand's tightest election in years
articles.summary: The national mood is low, and faith in politics even lower - with voters deserting the major parties at the polls.

blocks.text: New Zealand voted in a new government as fog choked the capital, Wellington, on Saturday - and the mood was as palpable as the grey weather.
"It's pretty flat," 21-year-old Imogen Vlutger says. "There's this kind of apathy and a bit of dread."
"Tired. I think we're all tired," Symone, 28, admits.
"I didn't even vote," one man in his 40s sheepishly confesses. He couldn't bring himself to tick any of the boxes, he explains, declining to chat further.
"Wellington's a bit of a bubble," another voter says, expressing a caveat I heard often, before describing feeling disillusioned.
But polling shows this is a pervasive sentiment across the country: the national mood is low and faith in politics is even lower.
More than half the country no longer sees it as a land of opportunity, a recent study found, while a similar portion fears that the future looks even worse.

Many Kiwis feel the economy is in ruins, there are no jobs, the cost of living has become sky high, the sense of community that used to be a source of national pride is breaking down and there's no sense of genuine progress on policy solutions.
A record number of them are abandoning ship in search of brighter futures elsewhere.
Saturday's election also saw a record number of voters desert the two major parties, giving neither a clear mandate.

But it brought new highs for parties across the spectrum: the left-leaning Greens, the right-wing libertarian Act Party and the centrist Opportunity Party – the latter of which had never won a seat in parliament before but could now hold the balance of power with seven.
Many who spoke to the BBC said the country's decline accelerated into a dive during the Covid pandemic.

Unemployment is now at an 11-year high and rising. For Kiwis aged under 24, things haven't been this bad in three decades: jobs are so scarce that one in three either cannot get enough work or have none at all.
Michael Dawson says he did everything he thought he was supposed to: finished school, studied a trade and obtained a qualification, and has applied for dozens of jobs.
But it's been a year now and the job market is so dire he hasn't had a single interview.
"It has sucked. A lot... I'm somewhat cynical with the way I think [about the future] now," the 20-year-old says.
Zainab Ali, chief executive of support service Youth Inspire, has never seen demand so high, with waitlists for its employment aid workshops stretching into the hundreds.
The young people who do make it through their doors on the outskirts of Wellington are disheartened.
"The things we used to hear from everyone's grumpy uncle around the Christmas table sometimes, our young people are now starting to give us that same feedback: like, 'What's the point?'"

Meanwhile, household electricity bills have jumped drastically, partly driven by global supply shocks. New Zealand remains one of the least affordable places on Earth to rent or buy a home. High inflation means every dollar is having to stretch further.

The island nation produces enough food to feed its population eight times over, but about a quarter of adults are skipping meals because the price of groceries – set by a supermarket duopoly – is among the highest in the developed world.

And the headlines are full of healthcare crises: long waiting lists, chronic understaffing, crumbling health infrastructure and climbing costs for patients. Few stories have captured the state of the system like the death of a man who collapsed in an emergency department toilet after a nine-hour wait in July.

"There's a segment of the population that are facing real material hardship... and then there's another segment of New Zealanders that are quite anxious that they could be next," political scientist Luke Oldfield, from Victoria University of Wellington, says.

Increasingly polarised public debate – around topics like Māori rights and the Treaty of Waitangi, healthcare for LGBT+ people and immigration – have added to the mental load for many in those communities.
"There's been a few groups feeling like they're being used as a political football," Dr Lara Greaves, who studies Indigenous politics, says.
This perfect storm is driving about 180 people to leave the country every day – a record-breaking exodus that is dividing families, shrinking communities and draining talent pools.

Siblings Sam and Emily tell the BBC that they love New Zealand but find it hard to keep finding reasons to stay. Their friends are leaving en masse and even their parents have considered moving to Australia.
"It's not just that you're being rewarded for going to Australia, it's that you're kind of actively being punished for staying here," Sam says.
Many of these issues affecting New Zealand are global trends - and it's undeniable that Kiwis' standard of living is better than many others.
But these issues are having a corrosive impact on its national identity.
"It leads to a crisis of confidence about what New Zealand is and where it's going," Helen Clark, who was prime minister from 1999 to 2008, tells the BBC.

Her foundation surveys New Zealanders every year about social cohesion, and its most recent report found Kiwis - in particular young poeple - feel far more isolated than they did a generation ago, attitudes towards multiculturalism are souring and the population is becoming less hopeful.
Faith in institutions and leaders has taken an alarming turn: only two out of five New Zealanders trust the government to do the right thing, while less than half of the country trusts the courts.
"There's a feeling that, really, there's no-one who cares," Clark says.

articles.title: Poland: Gunman kills 6 in Krakow main square
articles.summary: A gunman who fired from a car killed at least six people, including a British tourist, in Krakow's main market square. Officials said the shooter was fascinated with "radical" and "far right'…

image.caption: Krakow's 'Rynek' market square is a popular tourist destination Image: Jakub Włodek/Agencja Wyborcza.pl/REUTERS

blocks.text: At least six people were killed and sixteen injured in a shooting on the main market square in the southern Polish city of Krakow on Saturday.
The perpetrator, a 25-year-old Polish man who acted alone, was wounded during an exchange of fire with police, authorities said.
"Until now in Poland we haven't had such drastic cases of terrorism," Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk told reporters in Krakow.
"That's what we have to call this cruel attack on people's lives here in Krakow," he added.
Shooter aimed at random people, police say
The gunman aimed at random people as he drove through the city's main square, which is a popular tourist attraction.
"At around 3 pm (1400 GMT), a man who had driven into the market square in a car began shooting at random people from inside the vehicle," police said on X, adding officers were among the wounded.
Deadly shooting in popular Krakow tourist spot
"The perpetrator was shot by police ‌officers and is currently being ‌transported ​to a hospital," police said.
Later Saturday evening, Polish police chief Marek Boron said a British citizen was among those killed.
"There are six fatalities: four women and two men; three Polish women, one British national, and two people who have not yet been identified," Boron told reporters.
Krakow police had earlier said that five of the sixteen people injured in the shooting were non-Polish nationals.
Authorities later clarified that the man drove to multiple spots in the square and opened fire at each with an automatic weapon.

blocks.caption: Police secure an area near the city's main market squareImage: Jakub Włodek/Agencja Wyborcza.pl/REUTERS

blocks.text: Bodies found in shooter's house
On Saturday night, Tusk said that the bodies of two women and a man were found in the shooters home by police.
There was "much to suggest that they are members of the [suspect's] immediate family."
The residence is located Ostrowiec Swietokrzyski, a city about 150 kilometers (93 miles) northeast of Krakow.
"We have the next acts of this tragedy," Tusk told reporters.
Shooter fascinated by 'far-right' views
Polish Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski said that the shooter, whom she declined to identify, was "fascinated by far-right ideologies" and held "ultranationalistic" and "very radical" views.
The shooter wore military-style fatigues and a bulletproof vest and used a long gun in the attack, said Katarzyna Cislo, a spokesperson for the Krakow police,
Numerous other weapons and ammunition were found in the gunman's car.

blocks.caption: Police personnel at the site of shootingImage: Jakub Włodek/Agencja Wyborcza.pl/REUTERS

blocks.text: Poland to observe 2 days of mourning
Prime Minister Tusk posted to X that police were investigating the attack and called it a "tragic" incident.
Tusk later said Poland would observe two days of mourning for the victims of the shooting.
Polish President Karol Nawrocki wrote on X that his thoughts were with the victims and wounded, as well as their families.
'Poland does not stand alone,' European politicians show support
The European Union's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said the shooting was a tragedy that will be felt far beyond Poland, adding that "Poland does not stand alone."

"I am deeply saddened by the events in Krakow. My thoughts are with the victims and their families," German Chancellor Friedrich Merz wrote on X, adding that "Germany stands alongside Poland as a friend and partner during these difficult times."
Krakow is located about 250 kilometers (155 miles) from Warsaw, the capital of Poland.
With a population of over 800,000, Krakow is Poland's second-largest city, as well as a popular tourist destination.

articles.title: Ebola: Why is there still no vaccine?
articles.summary: Ebola has been known about for decades, but there is still no vaccine against the Bundibugyo strain of the virus causing the current outbreak. New research raises hopes of protection against the…

image.caption: Researchers are working to develop a vaccine against the strain of Ebola responsible for the current outbreak Image: Sebastien Kitsa Musayi/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: 1976: A hitherto unknown disease breaks out near the Ebola river in the country then known as Zaire, now the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). This was the first scientifically documented Ebola epidemic.

Now, 50 years on, the DRC once again finds itself at the center of a major Ebola outbreak. This time the pathogen is the less common Bundibugyo type of the genus Orthoebolavirus. The virus was identified in 2007 during an outbreak in Bundibugyo, Uganda. Another outbreak occurred in the DRC in 2012.
Bundibugyo: Preparations could have been made
How can a virus that has been known for decades continue to infect thousands of people, yet there is still no licensed vaccine or official treatment?

Torsten Feldt, a doctor of tropical medicine at Düsseldorf's University Hospital, sees this as a missed opportunity. "We had come across the Bundibugyo virus in two previous outbreaks: 2007 in Uganda and 2012 in DR Congo. So we had enough time to develop vaccines and therapeutic options. But we didn't make use of this opportunity, meaning crucial time was lost during the current outbreak."

Leonie Mayer from the German Center for Infection Research (DZIF) and the Institute for Infection Research and Vaccine Development at the University Medical Center in Hamburg-Eppendorf agrees. "They could of course have developed a vaccine and run pre-clinical trials before," Mayer told DW. She stressed, however, that their effectiveness can only be assessed and confirmed during an actual outbreak.
Mayer is the lead author of a recently published study that examined whether Ervebo, an Ebola vaccine that has already been licensed, can be used against other types of Ebola as well.
Congo's Ebola crisis: Fear, mistrust and a growing outbreak
Why Ebola is a good candidate for vaccine development

From an immunological point of view, and compared to — for example — influenza or HIV, Ebola is a very worthwhile candidate for a vaccine. Influenza viruses are constantly mutating, and the human immunodeficiency virus is particularly good at evading our immune defenses. Ebola is far more predictable.
"I think — and perhaps it's kind of a blessing in disguise — that it will be relatively straightforward to develop a vaccine against Bundibugyo," says Mayer.

Herein lies the paradox. From a scientific point of view, Ebola is a good vaccine candidate, yet there is still no licensed form of prevention against the Bundibugyo variant that is currently circulating.

Mayer explains that vaccines cannot be developed as a precautionary measure against every potential pathogen. Lack of funding or the prioritization of other pathogens often have a role to play. Many researchers had assumed that a fresh outbreak of the Sudan Ebola virus was more likely, and vaccine development for this strain is more advanced.
Different types of Ebola

Another part of the problem is that Ebola is not one single virus. The known, highly dangerous orthoebolaviruses include Ebola virus (EBOV), previously called the Zaire Ebola virus (ZEBOV), the Sudan virus (SUDV), and the Bundibugyo virus (BDBV). The existing vaccine, Ervebo, was developed and licensed for use against the Zaire variant. But there is still no approved protection against the others.
This is why the existing Ebola vaccine has been of only limited use to people in the areas of the current outbreak.

Another factor may also be relevant: The Bundibugyo virus appears to be less aggressive than the Zaire variant. At first, that sounds like good news, but it may make it harder to contain, as people remain mobile for longer after being infected, and can pass on the virus without realizing.
Ervebo vaccine: Immune response to Bundibugyo

In the recently published study, Mayer's research team from the DZIF investigated whether the already licensed Ebola vaccine could trigger an immune response not only against EBOV, but against other types of Ebola as well. They found cross-reactive T-cell responses against Bundibugyo, and also, to a lesser extent, against the Sudan virus.

For Mayer, this is already an important finding: "We now know that the immune cells can most likely also recognize the Bundibugyo virus." But she also observes: "Our data does not enable us to answer the question of whether this immune response actually provides protection, or if it results in a milder progression of the disease." This is currently an important gap in our knowledge.
Why the existing vaccine cannot currently be deployed
If there's a vaccine that has already been licensed, and indications that it could protect people, why isn't it simply being deployed?

Mayer explains the dilemma. For one thing, she says, it's not ethical to deploy a vaccine if you're not sure whether or how well it works. Also, if it were used on a large scale, it would no longer be possible to establish whether it actually works: A reduction in cases could also be a result of other measures, or the epidemic might already have passed its peak.

Jürgen May, a specialist in tropical diseases at the Bernhard Nocht Institute, also warns against mass vaccination: "Mass vaccination without proof of efficacy could create a false sense of security, forfeit trust, and, if it does not provide sufficient protection, make study impossible."

It's very important for there to be acceptance on the ground. "If we inoculate people with a vaccine on a large scale, and afterwards it turns out that it was nothing like as effective as we expected, it's very difficult to communicate that to people on the ground," Mayer says. In a worst-case scenario, people could subsequently refuse inoculation with more effective vaccines.
Why Ebola is still so difficult to contain

But the current outbreak also shows that medical innovation alone is not enough. Conflicts, difficult transport routes, attacks on healthcare facilities, and gaps in contact tracing all make it harder to contain.

blocks.caption: The DRC has had more than 10,000 cases of Bundibugyo since May. Recently, it has also been reported in Kenya and NigeriaImage: Andrew Kasuku/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Torsten Feldt says identifying Bundibugyo is no longer a problem in itself. What is often limiting is the practical availability of diagnostic tools. "In remote or conflict-affected regions, samples often have to be transported over long distances," he explains.

Here we see another Ebola paradox. The world is getting ever better at diagnosing infections, but it still struggles to contain outbreaks fast enough. The authors of an article in the current issue of Nature come to the same conclusion: The problem is often not identifying cases, but the speed with which people react. Finding Ebola is often easier now than stopping Ebola, they write.
From a Bundibugyo vaccine to a pan-Ebola one?

Many researchers believe the current crisis could potentially also provide a great opportunity. The so-called Tumaini study, which is testing different vaccine candidates, has now been launched in the DRC.
These include Ervebo, developed by Oxford University, and a Moderna mRNA vaccine. The study aims to provide the first reliable data about their efficacy against the Bundibugyo virus.

Whether these vaccines could still help control the current outbreak is uncertain. There is hope, but experts estimate that, realistically, it will be several months before any such vaccine is available for widespread use; perhaps not until mid-2027.

"Ideally, we will develop cross-reactive pan-Ebola vaccines," Christof Geldmacher, a co-author of the DZIF study, says of their long-term plans. This is also something that is being worked on. For now, though, the focus is on developing an effective vaccine against the Bundibugyo variant of the virus.
This article has been translated from German.

articles.title: Richard Lloyd, founding member and guitarist of punk band Television, dies aged 75
articles.summary:
Known for sophisticated musical style in band that played significant role in emerging 1970s punk rock movement

Richard Lloyd, known for his sophisticated musical style as a founding member…

blocks.text: Richard Lloyd, known for his sophisticated musical style as a founding member and guitarist for the influential punk band Television, has died at the age of 75.

His family confirmed that Lloyd died Saturday morning at his home in Chattanooga, Tennessee. “His loving wife Sheila and his dog Willie Mays were with him at the end,” his family said in a statement to Rolling Stone.
According to his family, Lloyd’s death was caused by cholangiocarcinoma, a form of bile duct cancer that he was diagnosed with in March 2026.
A crowdfunding campaign had revealed that Lloyd had developed tumors in his liver and, crucially, there was one that could not be surgically removed.

Television, which formed in 1973, played a significant role in the emerging punk rock movement that grew up around CBGB, the legendary former music venue on the Bowery in New York City. The group was among the earliest punk acts to perform at the downtown venue, which had previously focused mainly on country and bluegrass music.

During a 2007 interview, Lloyd reflected on his role in shaping the club’s history, declaring: “CBGB’s is the most famous rock ‘n’ roll club to have ever existed and I fucking created it! I was the invisible force behind it.”

Television recorded just two studio albums during its peak in the late 1970s. The band’s first album, released in 1977, was Marquee Moon, which has since earned widespread recognition as a landmark recording. Rolling Stone ranked it No 107 on its 2023 list of the 500 greatest albums of all time. The record is still considered one of the most influential guitar-driven albums in rock history.

In a 2005 review, the Guardian described his performance, writing that “Lloyd’s guitar was the louder in a lopsided sound mix, so it was impossible to overlook the amount of ground he was covering. Crisp, crunchy chords, dextrous fills and torrential Van Halen-style solos tumbled from his fingers.”

articles.title: FAA announces first US digital air traffic control towers in Florida and Alaska
articles.summary:
Systems provide 360-degree view of airport operations, but concerns have been raised about the technology

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has announced that the first digital air…

blocks.text: The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has announced that the first digital air traffic control towers in the US are officially operational, bringing new technology first to smaller airports in Florida and Alaska as the Trump administration presses ahead with updating the country’s ageing aviation infrastructure.

The systems are now online at the Bartow executive airport (KBOW) in Florida and the Kenai municipal airport (PAEN) in Alaska, with five additional regional airports slated to receive the technology next.

The digital towers use advanced camera systems and digital displays to give air traffic controllers a continuous, 360-degree view of airport operations, including runways, taxiways and surrounding airspace, according to the agency.

The FAA maintains that the technology is not intended to replace human controllers. Instead, the systems are designed to provide greater visibility and additional information to help controllers perform their existing duties.

“Our air traffic controllers continue to do the critical job of keeping aircraft safely separated, and we’re giving them better technology to do that,” said the FAA’s administrator, Bryan Bedford, in a statement.
“Digital towers provide controllers with greater visibility of airport activity and more information to make critical decisions,” he added.

Bedford is scheduled to appear before the House transportation and infrastructure committee next week, where he will face questions about the progress and challenges surrounding the administration’s ongoing $12.5bn modernization initiative.
The effort aims to replace decades-old equipment still used throughout the aviation system, including copper telecommunications lines, floppy disks and paper strips used to track aircraft.

Congress approved $12.5bn over five years in June 2025 to support air traffic control reforms, but the Trump administration is seeking another $30bn from the legislative branch to fund additional improvements.

Concerns about the types of technology being implemented within air traffic control have been gaining traction alongside the increasing unease about artificial intelligence as a whole. In September, the FAA rolled out a new AI software tool called the Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories (Smart).
Trump has been heavily criticized for his response to a national shortage of air traffic controllers following last year’s government shutdown.

Staffing levels in control towers and many related aspects of US air traffic safety systems have been under especially close scrutiny since a midair collision between a passenger jet and a military helicopter on the outskirts of Washington DC in 2025 that killed 67 people. It was the deadliest crash in the US for more than 20 years and the authorities later deemed it “100% preventable”.

articles.title: Israeli president tasks Gadi Eisenkot with forming government
articles.summary: President Isaac Herzog has picked former Israeli military chief Gadi Eisenkot, leader of an anti-Netanyahu alliance, to take the first shot at trying to form a government, with tricky coalition talks…

image.caption: Gadi Eisenkot leads a broad coalition of parties aligned against current leader Benjamin Netanyahu Image: Shir Torem/REUTERS

blocks.text: Israeli President Isaac Herzog has chosen Gadi Eisenkot to have the first opportunity to form a new Israeli government, according to a statement released by his office on Saturday evening.

The statement said Eisenkot was informed of Herzog's "intention to task him with forming a government" and would be invited to the president's residence, where a formal ceremony will take place on Sunday.
The decision comes after a neck-and-neck race with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Israel's October election.

Eisenkot's wide-ranging group, fashioned in opposition to Netanyahu, won 48 of the Israeli parliament's 120 seats in October's elections. Netanyahu's camp secured 53, leaving neither with the required majority of 61 seats.
Former Israeli military chief Eisenkot is the leader of the centrist Yashar party and heads an anti-Netanyahu alliance.
While Netanyahu ruled out working with Arab parties to gain a majority, both Arab majority lists had announced during the week that they would recommend Eisenkot to be next prime minister.
Can Netanyahu survive his last big fight?
What happens next?
The move is the first step toward what will almost certainly be complicated coalition talks.

Should Eisenkot succeed in forming a government, he would take over as prime minister from Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving premier, whose religious-nationalist coalition lost its majority in the election, despite emerging as the largest bloc.
Although Eisenkot was runner up, he managed to secure endorsements from leaders of Arab parties, which are opposed to Netanyahu.
Eisenkot faces a tricky path to forming a government, involving difficult constellations of Arab and ultra-Orthodox parties. He will have 28 days to round up the 61 votes needed to form a government.
Herzog can provide a 14-day extension if Eisenkot comes up short before the mandate must be offered to someone else.
If no candidate succeeds, Israel will head to fresh elections.
Could Arab voters hold the key in Israel's election?

articles.summary: US President Donald Trump has offered the job of White House press secretary to Dana White, the chief executive of the Ultimate Fighting Championship.

image.caption: President Donald Trump and UFC CEO Dana White arrive for the "UFC Freedom 250" mixed martial arts event on the South Lawn of the White House on June 14. Image: Kent Nishimura/AFP

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump announced on Saturday that he has asked Dana White, the CEO of Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC), to serve as White House press secretary.
"I am pleased to announce that the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior, has been offered the job of Press Secretary of the United States," Trump wrote on his Truth Social account.
"Dana, please take the job!" Trump said, calling on the longtime fight promoter to bring "assistants" with him "even though some are not from our country."
Dana White has been president of the UFC since 2001 and its CEO since 2023.
The White House does not have a press secretary as yet.
Katie Zacharia left the high-profile job on October 16 after a shaky debut press briefing. She was out as press secretary in less than a week after her appointment to the job.
