articles.title: UK cannot 'cherry pick' EU single market deal, Barnier tells BBC
articles.summary: The former Brexit negotiator says EU countries would reject any British attempts to follow economic rules "a la carte".

blocks.text: The EU's former Brexit negotiator has warned that the UK cannot "cherry pick" which elements of the single market to which it subscribes, after Andy Burnham said he wanted to explore closer economic ties with Europe.
The prime minister has said rejoining the bloc's internal market was among options he could pursue as part of a reshaping of ties since the UK's exit from the EU nearly six years ago.
But Michel Barnier told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that EU members would insist on the UK readopting certain conditions, such as the free movement of people, to gain access.
He said there was not a "single market à la carte" menu from which the UK could pick and choose what elements it wanted to adopt.

Barnier - who led the EU delegation during Brexit talks between 2016 and 2021, and had a three-month spell as French prime minister in 2024 - said the "door is open" within Europe to the UK rejoining as an EU member.
But he insisted that any move to rejoin the single market - which allows for goods to be freely traded without border controls - would require the UK to follow the same terms as other members.

He added that this included compliance with regulations designed to promote the circulation of goods, services, capital and people, referred to collectively within EU institutions as the "four freedoms".
"There will be no possibility to have one freedom and not the other. The four freedoms are clearly the four conditions to be inside a single market."

Since becoming prime minister in July, Burnham has suggested he could commit Labour to pursuing a much closer future relationship with Europe, including asking to rejoin the organisation as a full member, though he has ruled out major changes before the next election.
His predecessors have struck a series of deals with the EU on different aspects of how the UK and EU interact post-Brexit.
Both sides are hoping to use a meeting in Brussels in 10 days' time to unveil deals on food standards, youth visas and re-linking British industry to the EU's carbon trading regime.
Of the four freedoms, the free movement of people - which allows EU citizens to live and work elsewhere in the bloc without a visa - was a key issue during the 2016 Brexit referendum.

Burnham's immediate predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer, ruled out re-establishing it for the UK in Labour's 2024 election manifesto and any move to advocate it again would prove a key dividing line with the Conservatives and Reform UK at a future poll.

Burnham recently said in an interview that he would not re-establish free movement of people without a referendum, prompting Downing Street to clarify that he was not advocating its return at this point.

He has previously said he wanted to lay out "different options" for the relationship with Europe at the Brussels summit later this month, before trying to find a consensus with the British public on a new relationship.

Barnier also predicted that EU countries would reject reinstating the British financial rebate, first negotiated in 1985, that lowered UK contributions towards the EU's annual budget while it was a member.
The UK's decision to leave the bloc had created "a new situation", he said, meaning a new rebate would be "off the table".
Barnier also compared Reform leader Nigel Farage to French politician Marine Le Pen. He said: "We have our own Farage. It is Mrs Le Pen. The same populism, the same lies, the same false promises."

Asked by Kuenssberg to clarify what he was referring to with his accusation of lies, Barnier said "for instance, when Mr Farage and Mr Johnson promised the UK people to get back [£350] million per week, it was not true, it was not possible. It was a lie".

The Vote Leave campaign, of which Boris Johnson became a key figure, has been criticised previously for the slogan on the side of their campaign bus that said Britain sent £350m a week to the EU, adding: "Let's fund our NHS instead".

Johnson said in 2017 that "once we have settled our accounts, we will take back control of roughly £350m per week. It would be a fine thing as many of us have pointed out if a lot of that money went on the NHS".
Critics have said that the £350m per week was an approximate sum which represents a "gross contribution" and did not take into account the UK's £75m-a-week rebate nor the EU's investments in the UK.
Johnson has since defended the claim, saying the £350m was based on the UK's gross contribution to the EU, and was in fact an underestimate as UK contributions were due to rise.

​In his memoirs published in 2024, Johnson said EU money spent in the UK was not "democratically controlled by the British people", and "even if the net figure was only £175m, that was still a hell of a lot of money".

Farage, who led Leave UK and was not part of the Vote Leave campaign so not connected to the £350m claim, said: "It is the same old Barnier - arrogant, out of touch and a bully. He vindicates our decision to leave every time he opens his mouth."

articles.title: Rodrigo Duterte defense challenges expert report bid
articles.summary: PRAGUE, Czech Republic - Among the expert reports that International Criminal Court (ICC) prosecutors are seeking to admit as evidence, former President Rodrigo Duterte"s defense is challenging one…
articles.byline: ANDY PEÑAFUERTE III, JAY-VEE MARASIGAN PANGAN

blocks.text: PRAGUE, Czech Republic – Among the expert reports that International Criminal Court (ICC) prosecutors are seeking to admit as evidence, former President Rodrigo Duterte’s defense is challenging one that cites external materials not considered an “integral part” of a witness’s evidence.

In a publicly redacted request released on November 6, Duterte’s counsel, Peter Haynes, opposed introducing and using two external studies as associated materials for P-1400’s Expert Report, calling it an “improper attempt” by the Office of Prosecution (OTP).

It may be recalled that on October 23, prosecutors informed Trial Chamber III that P-1400 – an expert in a currently undisclosed field – provided the Expert Report covering redacted topics relevant to Duterte’s ICC case.
Aside from this document, the prosecution requested to admit 15 associated items in its fourth application under Rule 68(3).
In his response, Haynes said that the defense does not object in principle to introducing P-1400’s Expert Report via Rule 68(3), rather than full viva voce testimony.
However, he argued that the expert report “contains [REDACTED] footnotes citing other sources, [REDACTED] of which the Prosecution now seeks to introduce.”

Haynes noted that P-1400 “has not meaningfully used or explained” the two studies in question and that they “are not integral” but “merely reproduce information already provided in” the witness’s report.
“Their introduction would be redundant, and would burden the Chamber with evidence of negligible relevance, contrary to its express directions.”
In the filing, Haynes stated that a redacted individual or entity contributed to the first study, whose “treatment of the considerably wider findings of this item is extremely limited.”
He also mentioned another study – whose topic and preparer remain concealed – that contains “contextual information that does not form part of the P-1400’s own inquiry.”

“In reality, the Prosecution is attempting indirectly to introduce material prepared by other professionals who are not on its witness list via the instant Expert Report which – by its own admission – only “[REDACTED],” Haynes argued.

During the final status conference on November 2, Haynes described P-1400’s expert report as “difficult” and told Presiding Judge Joanna Korner that the defense would need “a couple of hours” to cross-examine.
In the filing, Haynes noted that there would be “merit” in hearing a redacted testimony “concurrently with that of the Defence expert”.

Additionally, he asked Trial Chamber III to either dismiss the OTP’s application for P-1400 or consider this request from the defense in a pending decision on the prosecution’s prior request to add the documents to its List of Evidence after the deadline.
Some witnesses may testify remotely
In a separate filing also dated November 6, prosecutors submitted an updated list of witnesses ahead of Duterte’s trial.

Trial Chamber III had ordered prosecutors to identify witnesses expected to testify through audio-video link, or AVL, and provide their expected order of appearance and any foreseeable problems with remote testimony.

At the November 2 status conference, senior trial lawyer Julian Nicholls told Korner that about 29 witnesses would participate via an audio-video link, and that the number could be broken down into categories.
In the latest filing, the prosecution said it has now marked in its confidential list the witnesses who may testify via AVL and updated their anticipated calling order.
The public filing does not disclose the number or identities of the witnesses because the updated list is in a confidential annex.
Prosecutors said they would inform the Chamber if circumstances later allow these witnesses to appear in person.
At present, the prosecutors said they do not foresee any issues with testimony through an audio-video link.
During the status conference, Director of the ICC Division of Judicial Services Marc Dubuisson told Korner that "everything is on track" regarding the preparations for AVL witnesses.
Dubuisson suggested that the schedule for AVL witnesses be started earlier, citing the seven-hour time difference.
"If we do it [this suggestion], we have to finish at 8:00 p.m. in the Philippines -- if the hearing ends at 1:00 p.m. in The Hague, that won't fit the schedule," Dubuisson told Korner.
For the defense, Haynes told the chamber of the logistical challenges of starting hearings at 8 a.m. in The Hague, including the need to transport Duterte to and from Scheveningen Prison.
Trial Chamber III has yet to release an order regarding the schedule for AVL witnesses.
Duterte is facing three counts of crimes against humanity involving murder and attempted murder allegedly committed during his terms as Davao City mayor and Philippine president.
His trial is scheduled to open on November 30 before Trial Chamber III, composed of Korner and Judges Keebong Paek and Nicolas Guillou. —VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Stephen Miller, Trump’s incoming chief of staff, pledges ‘total devotion’ to the president
articles.summary: Hardline aide offers ‘unwavering commitment’ to president amid fears White House will double down on far-right immigration agenda Stephen Miller, Donald Trump ’s most controversial aide and the…

blocks.text: Stephen Miller, Donald Trump’s most controversial aide and the architect of his sweeping immigration crackdown, has lavished praise on the president after his appointment as White House chief of staff.

In his first public remarks since the move was announced, Miller – who begins the role on Monday – pledged “total devotion” to Trump amid concern the administration is now poised to double down on its far-right, nativist immigration agenda.

“If it wasn’t for President Trump the United States of America would not exist right now,” Miller, standing alongside his boss, declared at an event on Friday evening. “This man saved America. He saved our military from collapse. He saved our economy from destruction. He saved our border from annihilation. He saved our country from threats at home and abroad which would have been the end of the American dream for ever.”

His appointment was unveiled after Americans punished Trump’s Republican party in this week’s US midterm elections, unleashing a blue wave that swept through parts of the country where Democrats have not won in decades.

As of Saturday morning, Republicans have lost seven seats in the Senate, and Democrats hold narrow leads in the two races – Alaska and Mississippi – that have yet to be called. Republicans have also lost 42 seats in the House of Representatives, and five governor races.

Despite this extraordinary array of losses nationwide – which senior Republicans including JD Vance have blamed on the Iran war and tariffs, key pillars of Trump’s agenda – Miller praised the president on Friday for having “saved the Republican party from the ash heap of history and has made it stronger, more popular and more resilient than ever before”.

Miller added: “It is the honor of my life to be President Trump’s chief of staff, and I swear to you, and I pledge to you, Mr President, my absolute loyalty, my unwavering commitment, and my total devotion to your success and the success of this country.”

The speech will likely add to concerns that the Trump administration is set to continue pursuing its hardline immigration agenda, which Miller had been leading in his previous role as deputy chief of staff.

Miller’s appointment has been met with dismay by Democrats and some Republicans, with Marlin Stutzman, the Republican congressman from Indiana, describing the move as a “horrible decision” in comments to Politico.

Don Bacon, the outgoing Republican congressman from Nebraska, predicted that Miller will “have an antagonistic relationship with many”, telling CNN: “He cost us seats in Texas and Arizona by alienating many Hispanic voters who voted for Trump in 2024.”
after newsletter promotion
Miller’s appointment was announced as Trump said he expects to make “a few changes” to his team.
“I love my cabinet. I think they’re good. But I’ll do – be doing maybe a few changes. I don’t want to mention who,” Trump told 60 Minutes, in an interview due to air on Sunday.

Asked if he has confidence in his defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, who has faced questions over his future in the role as the scale of the Republicans’ midterm losses became clear, Trump said “I do”, but notably stopped short of crediting him for what the president said were military successes.
Last month, after reports he might replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff, Trump was unequivocal: there is “zero chance” that will happen, he told reporters.

articles.title: Journalism and AI: Who owns the news?
articles.summary: Publishers say AI chatbots are using their reporting to answer readers' questions while sending back less traffic and less money. Should the companies that build these tools pay for the journalism…

image.caption: Image: Matteo Della Torre/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Millions of people now use AI chatbots as a source of news to find quick answers to questions about current events.

A 2026 survey by the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism, which questioned more than 90,000 people worldwide, found that 10% use AI chatbots for news on a weekly basis, a figure that is significantly higher among younger audiences.

Explaining what is happening in the world, why it matters, and what it means has traditionally been the work of journalism. Media organizations send reporters into the field, commission investigations and conduct research, producing stories that help audiences understand global events. But as more people turn to AI tools for information, the relationship between those producing journalism and those distributing it is changing.

"In the past, search engines like Google indexed our websites and directed users to their articles, generating traffic in return," Julia Becker, publisher of Funke Media Group, told a panel at the Global Media Forum (GMF) in Berlin. "But now that exchange has broken down."

"AI companies draw on our quality reporting to generate answers, yet the reporting itself often remains largely invisible by the end of this process," said DW Director General Barbara Massing in a keynote address at the forum.

Their remarks reflect a worry that is growing across the media industry. Publicly available news is copied and summarized by AI chatbots, while news organizations are becoming less and less able to rely on the money and visibility that used to come from distributing that work.

blocks.caption: Publishers, legal experts, and tech companies debated who should pay for journalism used in AI systems at the Global Media Forum in BerlinImage: Stephanie Englert/DW Images

blocks.text: Journalism and AI: A growing imbalance?

There has been growing concern about how copyrighted material is collected, used, and reproduced by artificial intelligence, and whether the companies that build those systems should pay the people and organizations that created the material.
Media houses are now pressing "Big Tech" companies to ask permission before using their work and to pay for it.

In October, German broadcasters ARD and RTL, along with the country's Federal Association of Digital Publishers and Newspaper Publishers (BDZV) and the Association of Private Media (VAUNET), called for stronger copyright protections for media companies.
In the US, lawsuits are adding pressure. The New York Times has sued internet company Brave Softwar for allegedly using its content without permission and getting around its paywall.
Meanwhile, legal institutions in the EU, including the European Court of Justice (ECJ) are examining whether AI-generated answers can themselves infringe copyright.

In February, a coalition of media organizations, including the Guardian, the BBC, and the Financial Times, called for rules that would give publishers more control over how AI systems copy and reproduce their content.
The problem goes beyond whether AI companies may use journalism. It also concerns how publishers and journalists can get paid when their work becomes part of the answers AI systems generate.
"AI systems shouldn't just use quality journalism. They should also pay for it," Massing said.
Is the internet dying?
How could AI companies pay for the content they use?

Professor Martin Senftleben, who directs the Institute for Information Law at the University of Amsterdam, separates two ways AI companies use journalistic material: Training their models and generating responses to individual user questions.
Payment for training is a more complicated legal question, he said. The more urgent issue is what happens when an AI system uses journalism to answer a question in real time.

He argued that European copyright law may already offer a way to address part of the problem. Under existing EU law, publishers and journalists may be able to claim payment collectively, without waiting for a new legal framework.
"What are we waiting for? Germany is a large member state. This should be introduced in Germany," he told the forum.

One option, Senftleben suggested, is a legally required payment system in which every AI response that draws on journalism triggers a payment. A collecting organization would gather the money and distribute it among publishers and journalists, in the same way that music royalties are collected and distributed.
Once such a system exists, publishers and authors could use its rates as a starting point when negotiating individual licensing deals with AI companies.
Existing deals and concerns about too much regulation

Lutz Mache, senior manager of government affairs and public policy at Google, told the GMF panel that Google is willing to negotiate agreements with German media companies and to discuss new AI products with them.

Google has also started testing other ways to pay publishers for their contributions to AI-generated answers. Its "AI Contribution" pilot, which is being tested with selected publishers, aims to reward content that plays a significant role in answers produced by products such as Gemini and AI Overviews. But the program is still an early experiment, not a general payment system open to all publishers.

blocks.caption: Google says its ancillary copyright agreements cover more than 800 German publications with payments already being madeImage: Stephanie Englert/DW Images

blocks.text: Microsoft, Anthropic, and OpenAI have recently said they support clearer, standardized signals that let website owners state whether their content may be used to train AI models.
However, not everyone thinks more regulation is the answer.

Jörg Heidrich, a lawyer who specializes in technology law and serves as AI commissioner at the German media company Heise, warned against adding new rules without considering their effects on the wider tech sector.
Europe has already fallen behind in the global AI race, he argued. More regulation, he warned, could make it harder for European companies to compete with major providers based elsewhere.

Heidrich also pointed to smaller players, including startups, independent developers, and research institutions. They depend on access to data to build and train AI systems. He argued that the debate over copyright and payment risks overlooking these groups, and that new restrictions could hurt their work.
Digital clones, real money: how athletes are trying to cash in on AI

articles.title: National Trust votes to seek banking partner more in tune with its environment policies
articles.summary: Charity’s AGM decided overwhelmingly to begin a tendering process amid criticism of current bank Barclays fossil fuel investments The National Trust has voted overwhelmingly to seek a new banking…

blocks.text: The National Trust has voted overwhelmingly to seek a new banking partner in a significant victory for members who have long argued that its relationship with Barclays was at odds with its commitment to protecting the natural world.

The resolution, passed at the charity’s annual general meeting on Saturday with the backing of its board of trustees, instructs the organisation to begin a competitive tendering process for its banking arrangements.
That process will, for the first time, centre on the condition that the new bank demonstrates a positive commitment to protecting biodiversity and reducing the human-induced climate crisis.

Campaigners said the result, 53,256 votes for and 4,094 against, sent a message that charities should apply the same environmental standards to their financial relationships as they do to their investments and suppliers.
But others questioned the significance of the success, with insiders suggesting that the tendering process will not take place for at least a year.
“This result highlights a profound shift in NGO accountability,” said Drew James, a proposer of the resolution and a member of Christian Climate Action.
“Civil society looks to charities, universities and faith groups to sever ties with financial institutions failing to match their ethical standards.”

The move follows years of pressure from members concerned about Barclays’ financing of the fossil fuel industry. The bank has been criticised for its support for oil and gas expansion, including fracking and methane gas infrastructure, while the National Trust has repeatedly identified the climate emergency and the decline of nature as the greatest threats to the landscapes, wildlife and historic properties in its care.

The vote came as the trust faces mounting consequences of extreme weather across its portfolio of countryside, coastline and historic buildings. A wildfire at Dunwich Heath in Suffolk in July destroyed 104 hectares (256 acres) of ancient heathland, with campaigners estimating that the damage would take 25 years to recover. Other trust properties have faced the effects of flash flooding, prolonged drought and increasingly severe weather.

blocks.caption: Smoke and ash from the wildfire at Dunwich Heath in Suffolk in July that destroyed 104 hectares of ancient heathland.  Photograph: Justin Minns/National Trust/PA

blocks.text: James said the relationship with Barclays was particularly difficult to reconcile with the Trust’s public position on the climate crisis. “For years, our trustees have declared climate change and the decline in nature to be the biggest threat to the places in our care. Each is human-induced, and the pace is quickening,” he said.

He pointed to comments made by the trust’s chief executive at a seminar during the Labour party conference, in which the executive identified keeping fossil fuels in the ground as the most significant response to the climate breakdown.
“Meanwhile our bank, Barclays, undermines our conservation mission by channelling billions of dollars into fossil fuel expansion,” James said.

The resolution’s supporters argued that the trust’s association with the bank was inconsistent with its responsibilities under the National Trust Act 1907, which established its duty to preserve places of historic interest and natural beauty for the benefit of the nation.

They also pointed to the Trust’s previous advice to the public, encouraging them to bank ethically. “It is contradictory for the organisation to hold its own banking provider to a lower standard than its suppliers and investment portfolio,” said James.
after newsletter promotion

However, the National Trust has made clear that the tender will not be restricted to specialist ethical banks. In its supporting statement for the vote, the board said the tender “must remain open to the major UK clearing banks”.

It added that “while some members may understandably aspire to the use of a specialist ethical bank, the evidence presented to the board of trustees indicates that no such provider currently has the combination of cash handling capability, lending capacity, payments infrastructure and operational scale required to support an organisation of the Trust’s size and complexity”.

Barclays has defended its relationship with the National Trust and its wider approach to financing the energy sector. A spokesperson said: “It is our privilege to support and bank the National Trust and we value their engagement on these important topics.

“As a leading energy financier, we recognise the interconnectedness of economic growth, energy security and affordability and decarbonisation to meet society’s needs. Over the past three years, we have facilitated more than $300bn (£225bn) of sustainable and transition finance, including billions for cleaner energy projects here in the UK, and invested millions into climate tech.”

Campaigners, however, dispute the significance of the $300bn fund, pointing to Barclays’ latest annual report which states that fossil fuel entities can access it, provided the money is not designated directly for oil and gas activity.

“This means that a reduction in carbon intensity, such as a switch from tar sands extraction to natural gas, could qualify for sustainability backing even if it results in a net increase in total carbon emissions,” said James.
Restore Trust, a group of National Trust members, has said the vote shows the organisation is straying from its core purpose.
Cornelia van der Poll, its chair, called the vote “a distraction from the National Trust’s charitable purpose of properly maintaining all the historic buildings and countryside in its care”.

articles.title: Prosecution rejects claim of failure in Sara Duterte impeachment trial
articles.summary: The House prosecution panel rejected remarks from Vice President Sara Duterte"s spokesperson claiming that the prosecution had failed, with one lawmaker asking: “In what alternate universe did we…

blocks.text: The House prosecution panel rejected remarks from Vice President Sara Duterte’s spokesperson claiming that the prosecution had failed, with one lawmaker asking: “In what alternate universe did we fail?”
Duterte’s spokesperson, Atty. Salvador Paolo Panelo Jr., made the remarks about the impeachment trial, saying the prosecution had failed.
During a news forum on Saturday, House prosecutor and Bicol Saro party-list Representative Terry Ridon said Panelo must have woken up in a bad mood.

“In what alternate universe did we actually fail at this point? Kasi ang totoo naman, if we failed, hindi pasok yung mga ebidensya na ito. Hindi sila maco-compel na sagutin po yung usapin, point per point in this defense presentation of evidence,” Ridon said.

(In what alternate universe did we actually fail at this point? The truth is, if we had failed, this evidence would not have been admitted. They would not have been compelled to address the issues point by point in this presentation of evidence by the defense.)

“So hindi ko alam kung masama lang yung gising ni Attorney Panelo pero hindi ko alam kung saang universo hinugot itong pagtingin po niya sa aktwal na estado ng paglilitis po niya ngayon,” Ridon added.
(So I do not know if Atty. Panelo simply woke up in a bad mood, but I do not know which universe he is getting this assessment of the actual state of the trial from.)

Meanwhile, House prosecution spokesperson Jay Tolosa said that declaring the prosecution unsuccessful would mean that its efforts had been futile. However, he pointed out that the defense had already lined up several witnesses.
“Sa first week pa lang, they already want to present 24 witnesses. So parang hindi masyadong consistent ito,” Tolosa said.
(In just the first week, they already want to present 24 witnesses. So that does not seem very consistent.)

Asked about surveys showing that Duterte’s defense panel had earned more favorable public opinion, Ridon said the prosecution was not dismissing the polls but stressed that the impeachment trial was not a popularity contest.

“Hindi naman ito Miss Universe. Hindi po ito beauty contest. Hindi po ito pasikatan. Hindi po ito popularity contest. Gagawin ng prosekusyon ang kailangan niyang gawin para patunayan yung ebidensya, para patunayan ang paratang laban sa Pangalawang Pangulo,” Ridon said.

(This is not Miss Universe. This is not a beauty contest. This is not about gaining fame or popularity. The prosecution will do what it needs to do to establish the evidence and prove the allegations against the Vice President.)
Ridon also said the survey results showed signs of partisanship, citing differences in the results across the regions where the poll was conducted.
Tolosa, for his part, described the particular survey as “stale,” noting that it was conducted before the article on unexplained wealth was presented.
Ready for Duterte
Tolosa said the prosecution was prepared for whatever the defense had planned, including the possibility of Duterte herself taking the witness stand.
“Kahit sino yung ma-presenta nila na witnesses, we will welcome it, even if they will finally call to the stand, the Vice President herself, we will of course, welcome that,” Tolosa said.
Tolosa added that several surveys indicated that the public wanted Duterte herself to explain the allegations against her.

With many of the defense witnesses reportedly consisting of staff members, Tolosa was asked whether they could simply claim that errors had been made in filing financial records and that Duterte had nothing to do with them.
Tolosa explained that many of the allegations stemmed from the Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN), a document that Duterte herself had signed.
“We all know, the Vice President, of course, is also a lawyer. So, alam niya kung ano yung significance, kapag pinirmahan niya yung isa dokumento and much more kapag notariado,” Tolosa said.
(We all know that the Vice President is also a lawyer. So she understands the significance of signing a document, especially when it is notarized.)
Discussing dropped articles could cause delays
In a report by Vonne Aquino on “24 Oras Weekend,” the prosecution team said the defense should no longer be allowed to present evidence on Articles I, III, and IV, which had already been withdrawn.
“Sana ma-address na head on itong issues sa unexplained wealth para ma-wrap up na rin natin itong unexplained wealth, the sole remaining article. Hopefully, [by] the end of the year,” Tolosa said.
(I hope the issues surrounding unexplained wealth, the sole remaining article, can be addressed head-on so we can wrap up the proceedings. Hopefully, by the end of the year.)

“Kung mag pe-presenta pa sila ng ebidensya para doon, it will not serve any legitimate purpose kasi nga, at the end of the trial, ang pagbobotohan nalang dito, kung dapat ma-convict o hindi ang bise presidente, yung unexplained wealth nalang,” Tolosa said.

(If they still present evidence on those articles, it will serve no legitimate purpose because, at the end of the trial, the only issue to be voted on is whether the Vice President should be convicted based on the remaining article on unexplained wealth.)
The defense had been given 30 days to answer the four articles of impeachment. Tolosa said it would only be reasonable to shorten the period following the withdrawal of three of the charges.
“Dapat ma-set po yan, kung ilang days na lang talaga yung binigay sa kanila so that they will not be allowed to drag this indefinitely,” Tolosa said.
(That should be set in terms of how many days they will actually be given, so they will not be allowed to drag this out indefinitely.)
The impeachment trial will resume on Monday, November 9, at 10 a.m. —VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Son of Iran's shah receives 'Freedom Prize' in Frankfurt
articles.summary: 18,000 people gathered in Frankfurt to show support for Reza Pahlavi, the son of the Iranian monarch ousted in 1979. Factions in the opposition have accused him of not distancing himself from his…

image.caption: Pahlavi received the 'Freedom Prize' in Frankfurt's historic St Paul's Church from an institution linked to the pro-business Free Democrats (FDP)Image: Hannes P. Albert/AFP

blocks.text: Iranian opposition leader Reza Pahlavi on Saturday received a "Freedom Prize" in Frankfurt in the central German state of Hesse.
Some 18,000 people rallied to show support for Reza Pahlavi, according to a police statement.
The event was held at St Paul's Church. The building hosted the Germany's first-ever elected parliament in 1848-1849, known as the Frankfurt Assembly.
Pahlavi is the son of the last shah of Iran, Mohammed Reza Pahlavi, an autocrat who fled into exile after being deposed in a 1979 revolution.
The 1979 revolution was followed by the transformation of Iran into an Islamic republic and the consolidation of power around the Shiite Muslim clergy.
Pahlavi was handed the prize by the Friedrich Naumann Foundation, which is tied to the pro-business Free Democratic Party (FDP).

blocks.caption: Thousands of supporters, mostly of Iranian origin, rallied in Frankfurt in Pahlavi's supportImage: Hannes P. Albert/AFP

blocks.text: What did Reza Pahlavi say about the prize?
Pahlavi said that Iran "is a country not waiting to be taught democracy, this is a country being prevented from practicing it."
"A people ready to die for the right to vote is willing to exercise the right to vote," he said.
Rights groups say thousands were killed in a government crackdown on protests in January.
"You could not have chosen a people who better understand the meaning of the word 'freedom,'" he said.
He also stressed that he was receiving the prize only as a "trustee" until a democratically-elected government comes to power in Iran.
"I hold it only temporarily," he said. "One day I will place it in the hands of its rightful owners, not on foreign soil but in the capital, Tehran."
The speech was accompanied by chants of "Long live the shah, long live Iran!" from the crowd.

Pahlavi has in the past offered to lead a transitional government in the event of a democratic transition in the West Asian country and has said he does not aim to use this proposed position to reinstate the Iranian monarchy under his father's dynasty, instead planning to leave the decision to a later referendum.

blocks.caption: Some in the audience of Pahlavi's speech yelled out 'long live the shah, long live Iran!'Image: Hannes P. Albert/AFP

blocks.text: Iranians criticize Freedom Prize for Pahlavi prince

While Pahlavi has emerged as a figurehead for factions within the anti-government protest movement, others have criticized him for his vocal support for Israel and have accused him of failing to distance himself from his father's autocratic rule.

Around 200 prisoners held in Iran signed a letter protesting Pahlavi's receipt of the prize, Sahar Sanaie, spokeswoman for the Society for German-Iranians in Hesse, was cited by the AFP news agency as saying.
The letter described him as the symbol of a "bygone dictatorship."

The Frankfurt branches of the center-left Social Democrats (SPD) and the environmentalist Greens boycotted the event and said he could not be considered a legitimate representative of the Iranian people.

Meanwhile, the socialist Left Party argued that the church could not by used as a venue for the event due to Frankfurt city statutes that prevent the use of places of worship for political gatherings.

articles.title: After victory in the midterms, what next for US Democrats?
articles.summary: Donald Trump's Republican party has lost its majority in both chambers of the US Congress. But the president still has a lot of power — and the Democrats have yet to agree on how best to use theirs.

image.caption: Democrats across the US, as here in Des Moines, Iowa, celebrated spectacular victories in the midterms on November 3Image: Vincent Alban/REUTERS

blocks.text: A "blue wave" has rolled across the United States. Some are even calling it a "blue tsunami." The Democrats scored a decisive victory in the midterm elections on November 3, wresting the majority from President Donald Trump's Republicans in both the US House of Representatives and the Senate. They also won gubernatorial elections in former Republican strongholds such as Texas.

Pictures from Tuesday evening show Democrat politicians and supporters across the country celebrating, hugging, even weeping with joy. However, as the White House reminded Americans in a post on X the day after the elections: "Trump is still your president."

Trump has the power to veto any proposed legislation Congress puts before him, and his veto can only be overruled by a two-thirds majority. Also, in the past he has, on occasion, simply ignored the Congress's decision.
How much power do the Democrats have?

Patrick Malone, professor at the public administration and policy department at American University in Washington DC, told DW that a presidential veto is not necessarily the end of the matter — even though the Democrats don't have a two-thirds majority in either Congressional chamber.

"There are Republicans, especially on the House side, who are not going to want to tie themselves that closely to Trump anymore," says Malone. "The Republicans that survived had a very strong message sent to them. It would be illogical and foolish for them to point to a neighboring district [that turned blue] and say, 'Well, that can't happen here.'"
For that reason, Malone predicts that Republicans and Democrats may come together to overrule a Trump veto. "It could happen very easily."

blocks.caption: The day after his party's dismal showing in the elections, Donald Trump focussed on the construction of his White House ballroomImage: Mandel Ngan/AFP

blocks.text: Will Trump be impeached again?

A question at the front of many people's minds is: Might the Democrats make another attempt at impeachment? One possible basis for this would be that Trump started the war with Iran without congressional approval. The US Constitution says only Congress has the power to declare war. But as commander-in-chief, the president also has a degree of military authority. How far this extends without Congressional approval is legally disputed.

From January 2027, Democrats will have the simple majority required to bring charges against him in the House of Representatives. They will not, however, be able to muster the two-thirds majority in the Senate that would be needed for a conviction and Trump's removal from office. Some Democrats say it is nonetheless imperative that the impeachment process be initiated, as a way of keeping the president in check.

Others remain skeptical. "If we make Donald Trump the center of our focus, we will lose this moment in history," the Democratic senator Cory Booker said. "We need to deal with the American people's problems."

This does not mean that Democrats won't try to launch investigations into Trump, or into members of his family or government. Quite the reverse. Malone believes the Democrats in Congress take their control function very seriously and will definitely initiate investigations. These, he says, serve a purpose beyond the documented outcome: "Another thing about Congressional investigations: They have a much stronger impact on public opinion than on legislation. They catch people's attention."
What a Democrat-led Congress could mean for EU, trans-Atlantic unity
Will Hegseth be sacked as secretary of defense?

While Trump will most likely get to keep his job, Pete Hegseth might be about to lose his. Observers assume the Democrats will demand a different secretary of defense. "There's a lot of speculation about what's going to happen to Pete Hegseth," says Brandon Conradis, a former DW journalist who is now an editor at Bloomberg Government in Washington DC. Whether Trump will actually fire Hegseth is a decision for the president. All the Democrats can do is exert political pressure.

From January onward, the Democrats will have a majority in Congress, which is where decisions are made on how government funds are spent. Conradis says one possibility for the Democrats to get their way would be to link the financing of Trump's pet projects to specific conditions. "One thing Democrats might do is say, 'Look, if you want more funding for these conflicts, Pete Hegseth needs to go.'"
As secretary of defense, Hegseth is being held at least partially responsible for the US's relative lack of success in the war with Iran. This could also be a reason for Trump to fire him.
Democrats not a unified bloc

After their success in the midterms, the Democrats have been enjoying a brief moment of unity. But Malone says it won't last. "The Democratic Party was unified for maybe 24, 36 hours. Now they're not really going to unify for a bit."

Unlike Germany, the US does not have governing coalitions at the federal level. There are, however, various political groupings within the Democratic Party itself. On the left wing of the political spectrum there are the progressive Democrats, including, among others, the prominent young representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. "[Progressives] have very aggressive policy ideas, whether it be environment or social programs," comments Malone.

blocks.caption: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez campaigning for the Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, who was elected senator for MichiganImage: Andrew Roth/ZUMA/IMAGO

blocks.text: In the middle are the mainstream liberal Democrats, who see themselves as politically pragmatic and good at compromising. But there are also moderates. "This is an important group on the Democratic side," Malone says. "There were a lot of Democrats [in the midterms] who won elections in former red districts or really, really conservative blue districts. They won't be able to go back to their districts and say, 'Look, AOC wants this.'"

It will be no easy task for Democrats in Congress to agree on one clear direction. But many believe that it's vital that they do. "They're going to have to figure out a positive governing agenda that they can all agree on," says Malone. Just opposing Trump won't be enough for the Democrats to sustain their current success, the pundit argues.
This article has been translated from German.

articles.title: Italy's Meloni blames pro-Russian hackers for cyberattack on minister
articles.summary: Antonio Tajani has said hackers published personal data stolen from him as Giorgia Meloni blamed pro-Russia criminals for the incident. The news follows a string of bomb threats that have grounded…

image.caption: Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani says neither he nor the Italian government will be intimidated by threatsImage: Francesca Bolla/AGF/SIPA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Italy's Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani on Saturday announced that personal data had been stolen from him and published on the Darknet.

In a statement on the social media platform X, Tajani said he had been targeted because of the Italian government's "position on Ukraine," and claimed criminals were "prepared to pay for other details on me and my loved ones," adding, "For days, cybercriminals have been spreading my personal data on the dark web and seeking other information, in fact exposing me and my family to new threats and intimidation."
Italy, like other EU and NATO member states, has provided humanitarian and military assistance to Ukraine as it continues to defend itself against a nearly five-year Russian invasion.
The foreign minister did not specify what kind of information had been shared but suggested the criminal activity targeting him remained ongoing.

"I will not allow myself to be intimidated in any way," he said, adding, "I will continue working to defend my ministry, and Italy, and I will further strengthen the ties and cooperation to protect ourselves together."
What did Italian Prime Minister Meloni say about the hack?

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni was unambiguous in her assertion that "pro-Russian hackers" were behind the security breach, calling it "a matter of grave concern that must be addressed with the utmost determination."
Accusations of Russian involvement in the Tajani hack come as Europe reels from a dizzying number of suspected "hybrid attacks" thought to be orchestrated by the Kremlin.

These have included drone incursions and sabotage in NATO territories, as well as attacks on food supplies, and most recently, threats against media outlets as well as a string of bomb threats that have forced the cancellation and rerouting of airline flights in the bloc.

articles.title: Yemen: 33 killed in strike near Sanaa, Houthis say
articles.summary: The Iran-backed Houthi rebel group accused Saudi Arabia of hitting several homes in the village of al-Shariya near the Yemeni capital. There was no initial comment from Riyadh.

image.caption: Coalition forces led by Saudi Arabia have carried out numerous airstrikes on Sanaa and other Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen [FILE: October 24, 2026]Image: Mohammed Huwais/AFP

blocks.text: The death toll from airstrikes on the village of al-Shariya near the Yemeni capital Sanaa killed has risen to at least 33 people, the Health Ministry for Yemen's Houthi rebels said on Sunday.
At least 39 people were wounded, Houthi health ministry spokesman Anees Alasbahi added in a post on X.
Earlier, Alasbahi told the Associated Press that Saudi Arabia had carried out the strikes.
He said in another post on X that that the strikes had hit several homes.
The Houthi-linked Al-Masirah broadcaster showed purported footage of the attack showing piles of debris and wounded people in a hospital.
There was no initial comment from Saudi Arabia on the reported strikes.
More fighting between Yemen's Houthis, Saudi Arabia
What is the state of the war in Yemen?

The Iran-backed Houthis have controlled Sanaa and large swathes of western and northern Yemen since the outbreak of the southern Arabian country's civil war in 2014, while Saudi Arabia backs Yemen's Aden-based internationally recognized government.

A yearslong truce in the war fell apart over summer, with the Houthis pushing forward in an offensive and taking more territory along the Red Sea coast in September, including the port city of Mokha and strategic islands in the crucial Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The rebel group has also hit targets in Saudi Arabia, including oil facilities and military infrastructure, and has also targeted Saudi shipping in the Red Sea.
The United Nations says over 1,600 people have been killed and more than 300,000 displaced since the intensification of fighting.
Also on Saturday, pro-government media reported that Yemeni government forces had pushed back a Houthi attack on the al-Aqroud front in the contested Taiz province in southwestern Yemen.
Saudi-led coalition forces also reported that they had intercepted a Houthi missile launched towards Saudi Arabia's Riyadh province.
On Friday, an airstrike on a market in southern Yemen killed at least 30 people, according to Houthi officials.

articles.title: New Zealand facing weeks of uncertainty with election ‘too close to call’
articles.summary:
National party will be largest in parliament but ultimate shape of next government won’t be settled for some time

New Zealand could be facing a weeks-long wait to know the shape of its next…

blocks.text: New Zealand could be facing a weeks-long wait to know the shape of its next government, after its nail-biting election failed to hand a decisive victory to either the incumbent rightwing coalition or opposition left bloc.

On preliminary results, the centre-right National party, led by prime minister Christopher Luxon, managed to secure enough seats to govern alongside his two traditional coalition partners, the libertarian Act and populist New Zealand First parties.

But with some seats won by very slim margins, and a large tranche of special votes yet to be counted, that success is precarious, resulting in an election too close to call until official results are released on 27 November.

Special votes, which include overseas votes and ballots cast outside a voter’s electorate, are yet to be counted. In 2023, 600,000 votes were issued, or 21% of the total. These votes tend to favour the left – in 2023, special votes resulted in Te Pāti Māori (the Māori party) and the Greens gaining three seats between them.

With nearly 100% of the votes counted on Saturday night, National secured 42 seats, Act 13 and New Zealand First 12. The combined 67-seat majority is wafer thin, with the left bloc just 3 seats behind.

Speaking to a room full of the party faithful at Auckland’s Viaduct events centre just before midnight on Saturday, Luxon said the results were “too close to call” and the special votes would need to be counted before negotiations could get under way.
National was still the largest party in parliament, he said, and had “a pathway to forming the next government”. National pipped Labour by 0.02% in the party vote.

Labour – led by Chris Hipkins – meanwhile, secured 35 seats, while its traditional coalition partners the Greens won 16 and Te Pāti Māori won five. Even with the seven seats from the centrist newcomer party – Opportunity – the left bloc is three seats short of forming a government.

blocks.caption: Labour party leader Chris Hipkins speaks to a rowdy crowd of supporters at the Cosmopolitan Club in Upper Hutt on Saturday. Photograph: Hollie Adams/Reuters

blocks.text: Before a rowdy crowd of supporters at the Cosmopolitan Club in Upper Hutt, north of Wellington, Hipkins joked that New Zealand had spoken but “it may take a bit longer to work out what they’ve said”.

“As things stand tonight, it is clear that we are not going to know the shape of our next government for a little while longer yet,” Hipkins said, promising that Labour would get “straight to work” should the final vote land in its favour.

The collapse of the two major parties, amid a sluggish economy and stubbornly high ⁠inflation, is feeding record support for the smaller parties, including Act, New Zealand First and the Greens. It is also helping propel Opportunity into parliament for the first time.

Opinion polls in the lead-up to the election had Opportunity placed to become the kingmaker. At this stage, the right bloc does not need them to govern, but if special votes change the landscape, their predicted role could come to fruition.

Currently at 5.9%, the centrist party has met the threshold needed to enter parliament, a historic first. Since New Zealand adopted the mixed-member proportional (MMP) electoral system in 1996, no new party has been able to meet that threshold – all the minor parties have been born from MPs or groups splintering from other larger parties.
The party’s leader, Qiulae Wong, told her supporters in Auckland she was “stoked”.
“It’s looking very promising for us,” she said. “Let’s just see how the rest of the votes fall.”
In New Zealand, voters get to make two votes: one for an electorate MP and one for a party. The system is meant to produce a parliament that reflects each party’s share of the nationwide vote.
However, if New Zealanders vote for more electorate MPs from a particular party than their party vote would entitle them to, they get to keep the extra MPs in what is called an overhang.
Te Pāti Māori, Act and New Zealand First urged voters to embrace strategic voting to try to maximise their share of MPs.
National has won more seats that its party support allows for, meaning it could gain an additional five seats to make up the balance.

That will be good news for its path to power, but comes with some significant trade-offs for the party. Four of its most senior ministers, including Nicola Willis, Paul Goldsmith, Chris Bishop and Gerry Brownlee will not return to parliament because they did not win a seat, or the party didn’t win enough votes to bring in list-only MPs.
On the other side of the house, Te Pāti Māori picked up five overhang seats.
With those extra seats, there could be 130 seats in the next parliament – a record under MMP – which means 65 seats are needed to form a coalition.

The country will now face a two-week wait until special votes are announced, followed by the possibility of weeks of negotiations. Caretaker government conventions will apply in the meantime, Luxon said.
“For now, I want to tell New Zealanders that well established caretaker conventions apply … The daily business of government will continue.”

articles.title: LifeLabs in B.C. ordered to pay $32K for misgendering transgender, non-binary patients: Human Rights Tribunal
articles.summary: B.C.'s Human Rights Tribunal has ordered LifeLabs and a subsidiary to pay three transgender and non-binary people $32,000 for "injury to their dignity" after the staff at the company misgendered and…

image.caption: LifeLabs was found to have discriminated against three non-binary and transgender people based on their gender identities in 2019, according to the B.C. Human Rights Tribunal. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia

B.C.'s Human Rights Tribunal has ordered LifeLabs and a subsidiary to pay three transgender and non-binary people $32,000 for "injury to their dignity" after the staff at the company misgendered and outed them at service centres in Vancouver and Burnaby in 2019.
LifeLabs ordered to ensure patients can have privacy to discuss their gender, sex
B.C.'s Human Rights Tribunal has ordered LifeLabs and a subsidiary to pay $32,000 to three transgender and non-binary people for "injury to their dignity" after separate instances of discrimination.

Tribunal member Theressa Etmanski said in her decision, posted last week, that LifeLabs and its subsidiary Excelleris Technologies misgendered and outed the three patients at service centres in Vancouver and Burnaby in 2019.
Etmanski also ordered LifeLabs to pay almost $3,000 in lost wages and $11,100 for an expert report.
'Exhausted and upset'
In one of the incidents, LifeLabs "refused to recognize" a person's non-binary gender identity and misgendered them, according to the tribunal decision.
Noa Moses said they brought a lab requisition form to a LifeLabs location in Vancouver in October 2019.

The form, which was filled out by their doctor, did not have "M" or "F" in the sex field, but staff repeatedly asked Moses whether they were male or female in front of the waiting area, where Moses believed other people could hear.
Moses said they were neither, but the response wasn't accepted and staff repeated the question.
Moses testified they weren't offered a private space to have the conversation.

items: More stories from Vancouver-South Coast

blocks.text: Another staff member said they were going to call Moses' doctor to "find out which gender marker to use."
When LifeLabs staff couldn't reach Moses' doctor over the phone, staff "informed Noa that if they did not choose a male or female gender marker, staff would not draw their blood."

After responding "10 to 15 times" that neither binary marker was appropriate, the decision says a staff member approached Moses with a piece of paper with "M" and "F" written on it. They asked Moses to point to one.
"Noa says they were so exhausted and upset by that point that they just pointed to a letter on the paper."
LifeLabs staff wrote a binary gender marker on Moses' requisition form.
Moses testified that their experience was demeaning and made them feel like a child being chastised, according to Etmanski's decision.
More instances of misgendering, outing
The tribunal also found that LifeLabs wouldn't allow Devan Snow to update his gender identity in their system and instead used the sex assigned to Snow at birth.
Snow also said he was forced to discuss his gender identity at the counter in front of an occupied waiting area at a LifeLabs centre in Burnaby in October 2019.
"Snow said everyone in the waiting room could hear what he was saying, and that his requests had become a 'huge thing.'"
Snow described feeling othered and unimportant because of the experience at LifeLabs, according to the decision, and also felt embarrassed because the incident was public.

Etmanski also found that Vincent Viezzer was discriminated against at a LifeLabs location in Vancouver in 2019 when, despite his gender marker typed as "M," Etmanski said staff added the letters "FTM" to the form. LifeLabs disputed this, but Etmanski accepted Viezzer's evidence.

Viezzer understood the letters to mean "Female to Male" and told the tribunal he had an emotional, physiological reaction to seeing the letters and scribbled them out with a black marker. He left LifeLabs without having his blood tested that day, according to the decision.

Etmanski said while the initials "may not appear to be particularly egregious or virulent," and can still be used in some settings, they also can be an "oversimplified and inaccurate way to describe some peoples’ lived transgender experience."
She said there is no requirement that something be understood as universally offensive for it to have a discriminatory impact.
Etmanski also noted disclosing someone's transgender or non-binary identity publicly "can place them at risk of harm."
Etmanski awarded $15,000 each to Snow and Moses and $2,000 to Viezzer.
LifeLabs was also ordered to correct the misgendering of Moses and Snow and to ensure transgender and non-binary patients have a private space to discuss their sex or gender within six months.
LifeLabs must also develop training on trans and non-binary patients' privacy considerations and give it to all staff and management in B.C. within a year.

articles.title: Ukraine's power network suffers further damage after fresh Russian strikes
articles.summary: The attacks come before Ukrainian and Russian delegations are due to take part in trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi next week.

blocks.text: Overnight drone and ballistic missile attacks damaged Ukrainian energy infrastructure, President Volodymyr Zelenskyhas said, causing blackouts and disrupting water supplies.
Zelensky said 12 Ukrainian regions came under attack with the capital Kyiv hit hardest.
Nine people are reported to have been hurt across the country, including one child, in the wave of attacks that consisted of more than 30 ballistic missiles and over 170 drones.
The attacks come before Ukrainian and Russian delegations are due to take part in trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi next week.
Zelensky wrote on Telegram, external that Moscow was preparing for the talks by launching attacks on Ukraine's "critical infrastructure".
Temperatures are dropping in Ukraine, and parts of the country have had the first winter snow.

"The situation in the capital is difficult, with disruptions to electricity, water, and heating supplies. Residential buildings, the North Bridge, and a kindergarten have been damaged," Zelensky said.
"In the Kyiv region, there were strikes on substations that connect the Rivne and Khmelnytsky nuclear power plants to Kyiv and central Ukraine."

In his latest update, Kyiv's Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the city's water supply system is back to operating normally. He also said around 60% of the city's apartment buildings were connected to the heating system.
The energy minister, Denys Shmyhal, said there were power cuts in five regions but did not say how many homes were affected.
Zelensky added that beyond Kyiv, substations were damaged in Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Rivne, Kharkiv and Dnipro regions.
The latest attacks come after US First Lady Melania Trump hosted Russian and Ukrainian delegations at the White House on Thursday.
She called for a "more enduring" ceasefire in Ukraine following a truce last week in the southern region of Kherson.

Hundreds of residents of the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky facing starvation and constant bombardment were able to evacuate during a six-day ceasefire, which both Moscow and Kyiv credited Trump with brokering.
"The lives of innocent people must transcend the division of war. I hope Oleshky inspires greater peace," she said.
Earlier this week, a number of people were killed when glide bombs hit an aid centre near Zaporizhihia, with the death toll rising to 55 as teams search deeper into the ruins.
Zelensky added in his Telegram post on Saturday following the latest attacks that Ukraine was counting on increased bilateral support from the United States.
He wrote: "We are counting on unity between both parties on issues of security, support for Ukraine, condemnation of Russian aggression, and increased sanctions pressure on Putin.
"The resolve and consistency of the United States in supporting Ukraine are of great importance in bringing peace closer."
Meanwhile, Zelenksy's spokesperson would not be drawn on reports that the Ukrainian president is to be invited to the UK for a state visit next year.
Additional reporting by Daniel Wittenberg

articles.title: Two men arrested after boy injured in Gloucester sword attack
articles.summary:
Armed police attended the scene, which led to two nearby schools going into lockdown on Friday

Two teenagers have been arrested after a 17-year-old was injured in a suspected sword attack…

blocks.text: Two teenagers have been arrested after a 17-year-old was injured in a suspected sword attack near a Catholic school in Gloucester.

Officers were called to Chalford Road, near St Peter’s high school, in Tuffley, shortly after 8.50am on Friday. It was reported that two men – one in possession of a sword – had been seen chasing two 17-year-old boys. The suspects then fled the scene on foot.
One of the victims sustained a “superficial wound believed to have been caused by the sword”, Gloucestershire constabulary have said. The other boy involved was not physically injured.
Armed police attended the scene to search for the suspects. St Peter’s high school and the nearby Willow primary academy were put on lockdown on Friday after the incident.
A 19-year-old man was arrested overnight, while an 18-year-old handed himself in to the police on Saturday morning. Both of the men are from Gloucester and remain in police custody for questioning.
Police said a woman had been arrested on Friday on suspicion of assisting an offender, but was released on police bail pending further inquiries.

A pupil named Jimmy at St Peter’s high school told the BBC that the situation was “really scary”, and students were locked in their classrooms for several hours. “At the time I was scared,” he said. “My heart was racing.”

Parents also received messages from the secondary school, explaining there had been an incident but that the situation was under control. DI Sophie Dawkins, from the constabulary’s CID, said: “We completely understand the concern this incident would have caused, especially when it happened near a school at drop off time.
“We’ve had armed officers searching the area, along with support from our drone unit and the National Police Air Service, and work is ongoing to identify and locate those involved.
after newsletter promotion
“Numerous inquiries have been taking place and officers from the neighbourhood team have been in the area throughout the day to reassure parents that there is not thought to be a wider threat.
“We are now keen to hear from anyone who has not already spoken to police who witnessed what happened or who has dashcam or any other footage.”

articles.title: Is the Alberta government engaging in American-style gerrymandering?
articles.summary: Political science experts told CBC’s West of Centre that Alberta’s electoral map-making process should be reexamined to stave off American influences.

image.caption: Normally a dry, administrative affair, this year’s electoral boundary redrawing process has been marked by accusations of U.S.-style gerrymandering. (Jason Franson/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Edmonton
Political science experts told CBC’s West of Centre that Alberta’s electoral map-making process should be reexamined to stave off American influences.
Take political parties out of electoral map-making, former Manitoba commissioner says
NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi has called the proposed redrawing of Alberta’s electoral boundaries a “Trump-style MAGA gerrymandered map.”
Premier Danielle Smith says rural-urban hybrid ridings are common, and serve communities well.

So which is it? Alberta’s electoral boundaries commission turned what is normally a routine process into a politically charged conversation this week. Political science experts told CBC’s West of Centre that Alberta’s map-making process should be reexamined to stave off American influences.
The new boundaries report comes on the heels of the U.S. midterm elections, where Republican efforts to redraw district lines weren’t enough to stop a blue wave of Democrat wins.

Greg Anderson, a political science professor at the University of Alberta who studies Canada-U.S. relations, says some U.S. states have commissions, but redistricting is generally understood to be driven by partisan efforts to gain advantage.
Here in Alberta, he sees echoes of that practice in the way the map lumps in some urban Lethbridge voters with those in surrounding counties.
“Just the way that the lines have been drawn as an effort to water down the impact of an urban area, it smells a lot like the gerrymandering that you see in the United States.”
Anderson said it’s common to see newly-drawn maps tied up in U.S. courts.
“That's sort of a sign that the stakes are really high.”
The Alberta NDP has already threatened to take the province to court on constitutional grounds, if the proposed map becomes law.
Alberta NDP accuses Smith of ‘Trump-style’ gerrymandering in new electoral map
Per the usual process, Alberta had a bipartisan commission propose a new electoral map last spring.
But in an unprecedented move, the two UCP members on the commission submitted their own report and map in protest against the majority proposal.
Both maps were rejected by the government.
A UCP-majority committee struck a second commission, which created a third map — the one currently before the legislature.
A map showing a sole Lethbridge urban seat, as well as three hybrid electoral divisions combining parts of the city with vast surrounding rural regions. (Advisory panel on electoral boundaries)
Mount Royal political scientist Lori Williams says the first commission’s division and the subsequent re-do represent a breakdown in political norms.

“I think one of the strengths of Canada is the fact that we've got independent bodies — to some degree independent — even if they're multi-partisan bodies making decisions about these electoral boundaries.”
“It's the violation of that standard, that norm that's causing so much controversy here.”
Alberta’s Justice Minister Mickey Amery repeatedly told the legislature this week that the redistricting was non-partisan and independent.
There’s another way
Richard Sigurdson, a political science professor at the University of Calgary, said in an interview that there’s a way Alberta could avoid continuing down this road.
Sigurdson served on Manitoba’s 2008 electoral divisions boundaries commission and describes the process as completely non-partisan.

Manitoba’s commission is made up of its chief justice, chief electoral officer and three university presidents in the province. As dean of arts at the University of Manitoba, Sigurdson was brought on in the president’s place, as outlined in legislation.
He blames partisan appointments for the division that plagued Alberta’s first commission.

“Having any kind of partisanship in these commissions, in my view, is problematic and opens you up to criticism that you're not interacting above the board — that it's not really independent of government.”
A future without partisan appointments is Williams’ preferred outcome.
“If the rules aren't clear on this, there's going to be a temptation for some people to make it more to their advantage and to have more influence.”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Emily is a reporter and producer with CBC's West of Centre podcast. Previously, she covered Edmonton city hall. She can be reached at emily.williams@cbc.ca.

articles.title: New Zealand election too close to call with over 95% of votes counted
articles.summary: Initial results in New Zealand show the two main parties neck-and-neck with fewer than 4,000 votes separating them. Official results aren't expected until later this month once special votes have…

image.caption: Incumbent Luxon said his National Party has a 'pathway' to forming a governmentImage: David Rowland/REUTERS

blocks.text: The two main parties were effectively deadlocked in New Zealand's close-fought general elections on Saturday, with the rising cost of living and general economic problems the main issues at stake.
Results with 95% votes counted showed the ruling center-right National Party and the opposition Labour Party neck-and-neck with just under 30% of the vote.
The National Party held a slim lead of about 3,500 votes more than Labour late on Saturday night.
PM claims 'pathway' to power as opposition calls for 'common ground'
Incumbent Prime Minister Cristopher Luxon, who heads the National Party, said that his party "is once again the largest party in parliament, and we have a pathway to forming the next government."

The National Party currently governs in coalition with the pro-business ACT and the right-wing populist New Zealand First. According to preliminary results, the three parties are set to net a total 67 seats in parliament, amounting to a wafer-thin majority.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins said that New Zealand's politicians would need to find "common ground" after the results showed neither his party nor the ruling National Party were likely to form a governing majority on their own.
"New Zealand has spoken. It may take us a little bit longer to figure out exactly what it is that you've said," Hipkins told supporters.
"Our next parliament is going to require all of us to compromise, to work together, and to find common ground."

blocks.caption: Hipkins served as PM for 10 months after succeeding Jacinda Ardern in 2023Image: Yuxin Liu/AFP

blocks.text: What to know about the election results in New Zealand

Special votes, including those cast from people overseas, are to be counted over the next three weeks. The votes typically benefit left-leaning parties and have shifted preliminary election results over the last three elections.
Final results are expected to be released on November 27.

If the right-wing bloc fails to hold on to its slim majority, the centrist Opportunity Party could act as a kingmaker. The party is projected to get seven seats, putting it past the 5% threshold to enter parliament for the first time since it was founded in 2017.
Luxon has previously ruled out cooperating with the Opportunity Party.
New Zealand has a mixed-member proportional system that requires voters to tick two options: a party and a local electoral candidate.

Electorate winners earn a seat in parliament, which typically has 120 seats, unless a so-called "overhang" leads to more lawmakers being returned to parliament, along with the highest-ranked members of the party based on their national party vote.

blocks.caption: New Zealand's parliament sits in WellingtonImage: picture-alliance/M.Moritz

blocks.text: Preliminary results on Saturday showed that parliament is set to expand to 130 seats because of the overhang, making it the largest parliament in New Zealand history.
The vote took against a backdrop of high prices for basic goods and the highest unemployment in more than a decade.
The voting took place under New Zealand's strict laws banning media reporting and political campaigning on the final day.

New Zealanders have, however, been able to cast their votes since October 26, with almost 1.7 million of the country's 3.8 million eligible voters already casting their ballots by Thursday, according to the electoral commission.

articles.title: Germany hopes to host world ice hockey championship — without Russia
articles.summary: International protests continue after a court ruled that Russia must be allowed to return to international ice hockey. Germany is seeking a solution that will allow the country to host next year's…

image.caption: The last time Russia competed at the IIHF World Hockey Championship was in December 2021 in Red Deer, AlbertaImage: Jonathan Hayward/The Canadian Press/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: A government spokesman has said that, despite talks with the German Ice Hockey Federation (DEB), the International Ice Hockey Federation (DEB) and others, the impasse caused by last week's Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruling remains.

Since the October 30 decision, several leading ice hockey nations — including Finland, Sweden and Czechia — have said they would refrain from playing against Russia in any tournament in which it is allowed to take part. Several key sponsors have also threatened to pull out, should the Russians be allowed to play.

The first tournament to be affected would be the Men's World Juniors, which opens in Canada in late December, followed by the IIHF's premier event, the Men's World Ice Championship, to be hosted by Germany in May.
Hosting Worlds 'practically impossible'

Stefan Kornelius, the spokesman for Germany's government, told reporters in Berlin on Friday that talks held with various stakeholders had made clear that Russia's participation would render the hosting of the championship "practically impossible — both from a sporting and an economic perspective."

Kornelius said talks would continue and the government still hoped for a diplomatic solution that would allow Germany to host the championship — as planned — in Gelsenkirchen, Mannheim and Düsseldorf in May.

"Our goal must be to hold the tournaments as scheduled," he said. "However, given the boycotts that would follow Russia's readmission, that would effectively be impossible. For this reason, we intend to explore — through dialogue — how we can still ensure the tournament takes place."
Following the CAS ruling that the IIHF must allow Russia to return to international play, DEB chairman Frank Lutz had conceded that Germany may be forced to consider withdrawing as championship host.
German visa restrictions on Russians in place

Asked at Friday's press conference whether Germany could issue visas to a Russian team for the tournament, a Foreign Ministry spokesman declined to answer categorically, but did indicate that this would be difficult under restrictions currently in place.
"At a time when Russia is waging a war of aggression against Ukraine, there can be no 'normalcy' — and we will certainly not pretend that there is," said spokesperson Martin Giese.
Earlier this week, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney categorically ruled out Russian players taking part in the World Juniors in Alberta.
"While Russia and Belarus are supporting this illegal, unjustified ​war in Ukraine, as long as that's going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada," he said.
"So, ​if you're asking specifically about the World Juniors," he said, "the Russians will not be there."
Consensus remains elusive
Russian President Vladimir Putin has also weighed in on the issue, accusing countries opposing Russia's return to international sport of violating the rights of his country's athletes.

The IIHF Council had originally called two days of meetings, on Monday and Tuesday, to try to reach a consensus on how to respond to the CAS decision — before extending discussions for a third day, on Thursday. By Friday, its members had evidently still not reached a consensus.

This comes as the Women's Ice Hockey World Championship, which is not affected by the CAS decision, opened in Denmark — and with the clock ticking toward the start of the World Juniors in Alberta on December 26.
