articles.title: Watchdog, House speaker agree to work on budget transparency
articles.summary: The People"s Budget Coalition (PBC) commended House Speaker Faustino “Bojie” Dy III who expressed commitment to greater transparency in the national budget process, signifying a constructive…

blocks.text: Published November 7, 2026 6:43pm
The People’s Budget Coalition (PBC) commended House Speaker Faustino “Bojie” Dy III who expressed commitment to "greater transparency" in the national budget process
This comes after the PBC met with Dy to discuss areas where the House could enhance its processes for scrutinizing and disclosing government projects.

“Thank you, Speaker Faustino ‘Bojie’ Dy III, for meeting with the People’s Budget Coalition... acknowledging the points for improvement in the House process, and committing to working with us budget watchdogs and civil society groups to open up these documents and deliberations so that every taxpayer can verify where our taxes go,” Abante said in a Facebook post.
His statement came after Dy said that the House was ready to disclose supporting documents for government projects and promote greater transparency in budget deliberations.

According to the civil society group, the development points to a significant shift toward constructive engagement between lawmakers and civil society organizations that have raised concerns about project documentation, technical descriptions and amendments in the proposed P6.793-trillion national budget for 2027.

The PBC said that instead of dismissing concerns raised by independent budget monitors, the House leadership has opened channels for dialogue and cooperation to reinforce public scrutiny of government expenditures.

To recall, Dy said the House of Representatives is open to disclosing supporting documents for government projects and make budget deliberations more accessible to the public, in order that proposed appropriations can be examined against their supporting studies, technical specifications, project locations and implementing agencies’ validation.
“Such disclosures would help distinguish properly documented and justified budget amendments from questionable allocations that require further scrutiny,” the PBC said.

The PBC added the House Speaker’s approach also backs the principle that government projects should be evaluated on their merits, supporting documentation and benefits to the public, instead of allegations alone. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Ombudsman Remulla flags BIR over taxation, abuse concerns
articles.summary: Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla on Saturday flagged alleged abuses within the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR), saying business leaders have raised concerns over taxation and permit processing.

blocks.text: Published November 7, 2026 5:53pm
Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla on Saturday flagged alleged abuses within the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR), saying business leaders have raised concerns over taxation and permit processing.
Speaking on his radio program on dzRH, Remulla discussed efforts to revive the investment ombudsman and shared concerns raised by business leaders during his conversations with them.
“Ang isang pinaka-malaking problema natin ngayon BIR… talagang ina-ano nila, para silang kasosyo talaga. Yung republika, may utang sa kanila palagi, yung nga taga-BIR,” Remulla said.
(One of our biggest problems right now is the BIR… they really, they are like an enterprise. The republic always owes them something, those in the BIR.)
“May nangyayari diyan, yung 70-30: 70 sa BIR, 30 sa bayan,” he added.
(What is happening there is a 70-30: 70 for the BIR, 30 for the nation.)
Remulla, however, did not elaborate on his 70-30 claim.
GMA News Online has reached out to the BIR for comment and will update this story once a response is received.
Remulla also raised concerns over the alleged abuse of Letters of Authority (LOAs).

In November 2025, the BIR suspended the issuance of LOAs following allegations that the documents were being used in money-making schemes. A technical working group was also formed to spearhead reforms in the system. —VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Ukraine: Russia hits Kyiv with airstrikes ahead of trilateral talks
articles.summary: The strikes hit a major bridge and energy facilities in the Kyiv region. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Moscow of trying to "push" Ukraine "into a blackout" ahead of talks in Abu Dhabi.

image.caption: Russian forces hit several sites across the Kyiv region overnightImage: Gleb Garanich/REUTERS

blocks.text: Russia launched strikes on Kyiv and surrounding areas overnight, Russian and Ukrainian authorities said on Saturday.
Russia's Defense Ministry said the strikes hit the Northern Bridge and the Meridian Plant.
Moscow said that the bridge was being used by the Ukrainian military to transport weapons and military equipment, while the plant is used to produce Flamingo cruise missiles.
It said the strikes damaged several energy and industrial facilities in the Kyiv region, as well as an electricity substation in the neighboring Zhytomyr region and a cargo vessel in the Black Sea.

blocks.caption: Russia has stepped up its attacks on Ukrainian cities as its ground offensive has stalledImage: Gleb Garanich/REUTERS

blocks.text: What have Ukrainian authorities said about the attacks?

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko confirmed the strikes on the Northern Bridge, adding that the Ukrainian capital found itself in an "extremely difficult" situation regarding power, heating and water supplies. Overnight temperatures dropped to 0 degrees Celsius (32 degrees Fahrenheit) in the city.
The Kyiv region's governor, Tymur Tkachenko, said energy facilities in three of its districts had been hit.
Ukrainian authorities said that one person was killed and eight were wounded in the overnight attack.
In a statement on social media, president Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Russia used 172 drones and 36 ballistic missiles during the attack.
He said that Russia was trying to "push Kyiv … and the entire country into a blackout" and repeated his call for increased support from the United States.
Russia has stepped up airstrikes on Ukraine in recent months, targeting energy infrastructure and major cities, and more recently hitting bridges.
Is Trump negotiating a new European security order with Russia?
Strikes come ahead of Russia-Ukraine talks
The strikes come days before a fourth round of trilateral talks between Kyiv, Moscow and Washington in Abu Dhabi in the United Arab Emirates.
Previous rounds of US-brokered talks have failed to achieve any breakthroughs, with territorial and security questions remaining major points of contention.
On Friday, US President Donald Trump said the war could be close to being settled and that he envisioned a "big, beautiful agreement" with Moscow that involves "all of Europe."
Last Friday, a six-day local ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in the southern Kherson region enabled the evacuation of some 800 residents.
The brief truce was brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump.
Oleshky evacuees recount survival under occupation

articles.summary: Remulla: Fake news peddlers want to disrupt institutions, influence courts

blocks.text: Published November 7, 2026 5:08pm
Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla slammed fake news peddlers, saying that they only want to "disrupt" institutions.
Remulla previously announced that he wanted to file charges against people who spread disinformation about his illness, despite him being cancer-free since 2023.
Speaking on his radio show at DZRH, Remulla spoke about the possible motivation behind the fake news against him.
“Gusto nila, alugin yung institution… Gusto nila influence yung korte. Kaya contemptuous yun,” Remulla said.
(They want to shake the institution… They want to influence the court. That is why that is contemptuous.)
Remulla had previously commented on former House speaker Martin Romualdez’s supposed security aide, where he disclosed that his office has garnered new enemies as well.
“Ang kalaban ng opisina ko ngayon, marami kaming kalaban na DDS (Diehard Duterte Supporters), at mayroon kaming kalaban na galing din sa… loob, sa hanay ng mga nakasama dati,” Remulla said.
(The enemies of my office now, we have a lot of enemies that are DDS, and now we have enemies from… inside, from the side of our allies before… this is rust, those detractors.)
Remulla said that if he was doing what his enemies were doing, it would be unfair to the people who are accused. He would only say that the evidence would speak for itself.
The Ombudsman said that he would let the Department of Information and Communications Technology handle the matter. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: What Ottawa's 'RRSP for life' plan means for Canadian seniors

image.caption: Tax and personal finance experts say that while the new 'RRSP for life' measure in the federal budget would be more convenient, it doesn't address seniors struggling under the rising cost of living. (Shutterstock)

blocks.text: Business·New
The federal budget proposes a tweak to Registered Retirement Savings Plans (RRSPs) aimed at simplifying financial planning for thousands of seniors every year.
Experts say the plan cuts complexity, but ignores bigger issues for many Canadian seniors
Canada's new federal budget proposes a tweak to Registered Retirement Savings Plans (RRSPs) aimed at simplifying financial planning for thousands of seniors every year.
Tax and personal finance experts say while the new "RRSP for life" measure would be more convenient, it does not address seniors who are struggling under rising living costs.

An RRSP is a Canadian savings account that lowers your tax exposure today, and lets your savings and investments grow without being taxed until you retire. They can hold a wide variety of financial assets, including cash, stocks, guaranteed investment certificates (GICs), and exchange-traded funds (ETFs).

For the 2026 tax year, individuals can contribute up to 18 per cent of their earned income in 2025, up to a maximum of $33,810. If you have a workplace pension, the value of those pension contributions is deducted from that 18 per cent limit.
What the federal budget means for your taxes | Hanomansing Live
What are the proposed changes?

Currently, RRSPs must be withdrawn or converted into a Registered Retirement Income Fund (RRIF) when the account holder turns 71. In the new federal budget, Ottawa proposes to allow Canadians to keep their RRSPs after they reach that age.
Currently, if someone dies after age 71 with a RRIF, the account can be transferred to a spouse without closing it or triggering tax paperwork. That's not the case today with RRSPs.

Ottawa's budget proposal would "allow a surviving spouse or partner to become a successor holder of an RRSP, and simplify tax-free transfers to qualified survivors after the death of the account holder."
A public consultation on the plan started on Thursday, and will run until Jan. 8, 2027.

items: 7 takeaways from the Carney government's 2nd budget
Carney's new budget aims to end homelessness in 10 years

blocks.text: Jamie Golombek, managing director, tax and estate planning at CIBC Private Wealth Management, says today most 71-year-olds choose to convert their RRSPs to RRIFs to avoid the tax applied if they choose to cash out.
"It's a complex administrative thing for hundreds of thousands at least every year," he told CBC News.
"What the government is saying is, 'Why not have an RRSP for life?' In other words, an RRSP that you basically have until the day you die."

Under the proposed change, the government would require RRSP holders to withdraw a minimum percentage of their savings each year, starting at age 72. These percentages are based on average life expectancy to ensure that retirement savings is paid out and taxed gradually for the rest of the owner's lifetime.
John Fragos, press secretary to Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne, confirmed to CBC News that under the government's proposal, RRSP account holders cannot contribute after age 71.
Budget 2026: Carney makes 'big bet' for investment, opposition blasts affordability moves
Why do the changes matter?

Aaron Hector, senior wealth advisor at Calgary-based Tier Wealth says simplifying the financial landscape for seniors is a smart move by the government. He also praises the proposal to allow RRSPs to be easily transferred after death.

"Not needing someone to go through the paperwork process of converting an RRSP into a RRIF just makes a lot of common sense for me," he said. "Heaven forbid it slips through the cracks. It could create some issues for people."

Li Zhang, director of social impact at Chartered Professional Accountants of Canada, sees the government's "RRSP for life" proposal as "more of a nomenclature change," that ignores bigger issues for seniors.
Firstly, she estimates only 33 to 37 per cent of Canadians actually have access to a pension.

"You're not actually talking about a lot of people who have a lot of retirement savings assets," she said. "If you've walked by food banks, and you look at the line, it's the really young or the really old."

items: From groceries to tax credits, how much is in the federal budget for your wallet?

blocks.text: She says another problem for RRSP holders is that the mandatory withdrawals can make it difficult to balance their income. "That then triggers higher levels of taxation," she said.
While the consultation period for this plan runs until Jan. 8, Golombek expects it could take much longer to enact these changes if Ottawa elects to make them.
"I think it's going to be a few years before we see the ultimate merger of these, or at least the elimination of the RRIF."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Jeff Lagerquist is a senior writer with CBC News based in Toronto. Originally from Erin, Ont., he studied journalism at Toronto Metropolitan University. Jeff previously worked as a senior reporter for Yahoo Finance Canada. He was also a reporter and digital producer for CTV National News, BNN Bloomberg and The Financial Post. In 2025, he was a Columbia University energy journalism fellow.

articles.title: The age of AI warfare has dawned. Is Canada ready?
articles.summary: Countries like the U.S., U.K. and China are pouring billions into AI-integrated military software and hardware, despite legal and ethical concerns. Canadian defence technology companies, military…

image.caption: A YFQ-44A Collaborative Combat Aircraft fires an air-to-air missile in a live-fire test in secluded airspace over California's Mojave Desert in July. (U.S. Air Force)

blocks.text: The drone looks like a small fighter jet. Artificial Intelligence is flying it, and it's firing a missile. A human approved the shot, but AI carried it out.
That's not science fiction. It may be the future of modern warfare.

In July, American defence company Anduril's YFQ-44A drone, known as Fury, fired an air-to-air tactical missile at a simulated target in California's Mojave Desert. In October, a pilot in an F-22 fighter jet was able to get the drone to carry out simulated combat tasks.
It's the latest step in the global race for autonomous weapons as armies try to gain a tactical edge.

With governments increasingly integrating AI into military software and hardware, Canada faces a question: should it join the autonomous arms race and start investing more in AI-enhanced weapons despite legal and ethical concerns?
'AI in a platform that is deadly'

YFQ-44A is a collaborative combat aircraft (CCA), designed to fly alongside manned fighter jets. It's meant to extend the jet's reach, while reducing risk to the pilot. The drone would use AI to carry out many fighter jet tasks, including firing weapons on command and eventually engaging in close aerial combat.
"You're getting artificial intelligence in a platform that is deadly," said Yvan Blondin, who commanded the Royal Canadian Air Force from 2012 to 2015.

items: Ottawa drone makers tool up for increased defence budget
As Canadian defence spending ramps up, London firms excited about opportunities

blocks.text: Blondin believes these drones will become integral to modern militaries by the 2030s.

The U.S. has two prototypes, including Fury. Australia has a Boeing-built CCA — and they're working on an underwater version built by Anduril. The U.K. is spending five billion pounds to boost drones and autonomous systems in their military.
Western armies say humans will stay in control and responsible for weapons using lethal force: it's part of NATO's policy on responsible use of AI.

Canadian officials told CBC that warfare must stay a fundamentally human endeavour, and said that no machine, weapons systems or algorithmic code can be held responsible for complying with International Humanitarian Law. But Blondin says other adversaries may not wait.
If one country uses autonomous AI in a conflict, Blondin wonders how other countries would respond — would they raise their ethical standards, or drop them entirely?
"In times of war, would China bother with the step of having a human in the loop?" he asked.
Canada's role

In a statement sent to CBC News, the Department of National Defence said the Royal Canadian Air Force is examining how these systems could be useful for Canada, but that no decision has been made about plans to procure CCAs.

The Canadian Armed Forces supports the development of autonomous functionality, the statement said, on the condition that it would be "operated within a responsible chain of human command and control and commits to uphold the reliable and lawful use of such weapon systems."

items: Military commander vows fast action on AI and robots, sees 'untapped potential' for Canada
In Canada's drone-killing 'Sandbox,' companies compete for a $1M prize

blocks.text: Canada has no collaborative combat aircraft, but Dominion Dynamics CEO Eliot Pence wants to change that.

His defence technology company is building Scout, a CCA that would fly ahead of a crewed fighter, three or four drones per jet, beyond the radar's edge — and be able to strike by firing a weapon, like a missile.

Dominion Dynamics CEO Eliot Pence stands in front of a subscale model of Scout, a collaborative combat aircraft that the Canadian defence technology company is building. Scout would fly ahead of a crewed fighter beyond the edge of its radar and be able to strike by firing a weapon, like a missile. (Nicolas Legault/CBC)

Pence, who previously worked at Anduril, says the need for CCA is about sovereignty, especially over the Arctic, which makes up about 40 per cent of Canada. The country doesn't have the fighter jets to cover all that territory, Pence argues, noting that leaves a gap in Canada's ability to carry out intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance — a gap Dominion is trying to fill.
"The best, most efficient and technologically advanced way of doing that is by pairing those jets with autonomous systems."
Dominion stands to benefit if Ottawa buys in.

Pence says he's raised about a third of the $500 million needed to build the prototype, and though Ottawa has bought into Dominion's simulation platform, there's no government contract for a prototype.
"We don't care. We're going to build it anyway."
Building in boundaries
Pence says Dominion wants a human to remain the last decision maker for the drone, and is building that boundary into the decision-making of its AI models.
But they have yet to figure out what, specifically, all those safeguards would be, says Benoit Breault, senior vice-president for aerospace engineering at Dominion.
Some boundaries are straightforward, Breault says — for example, any use of force will require human approval.

Benoit Breault, senior vice-president for aerospace engineering at Dominion, is working on safeguards to make sure a human is the last decision maker for the drone they want to build. (Nicolas Legault/CBC)
Other boundaries may seem less critical at first blush, but can become unexpectedly dangerous. For instance, if engineers want the drone to return home, can AI decide what route to take?
"You don't want to return to base straight into dangerous environments or contested airspace," Breault said.
He's also thinking about how to avoid overwhelming the pilot. Too much information from three or four drones could make it difficult for the pilot to maintain control of CCAs.

items: Drones and AI are rewriting the rulebook on naval warfare — with uncertain consequences

blocks.text: But right now, Breault acknowledges development of the human-machine interface is still "embryonic."

He says they're still trying to determine answers to important questions like, "How exactly are we going to provide information to the fighter jet pilots? How exactly are the decision recommendations going to be displayed."
Adequate human control

These details are central to ethical concerns about autonomous weapons systems, says Craig Martin, a former Canadian navy officer and an expert in armed conflict laws who teaches at Washburn University in Topeka, Kan.
"This is the million dollar question," he said. "What is the extent and the nature of the human control that's being exercised over that weapon system?"

Martin is worried about automation bias — where humans put too much trust in the machine, especially if, for instance, they have just seconds to respond. Martin says AI systems can also fail if they're used in environments where they weren't trained. For instance, a system trained for use in Afghanistan could make mistakes if it's used in Ukraine.
Such errors, he says, "can actually compound in sort of exponential feedback loops that result in biases that can possibly lead to the killing of civilians."

This month, diplomats will meet in Geneva to see if countries want to enter into negotiations about rules governing the use of autonomous weapons. Craig Martin, a former Canadian navy officer and an expert in armed conflict laws, wants Canada to lead that conversation. (Andrew Lee/CBC)
UN Secretary-General António Guterres wants a legally binding treaty on autonomous weapons by the end of 2026.

Guterres renewed that call in August, a month after a Russian drone, acting with no human operator, killed three civilians in Ukraine, the New York Times reported. The drone was reportedly a cheap, expendable weapon that picked its own target. It was in a different category from CCAs, but both that type of drone and CCAs are autonomous enough that they are able to make some of their own decisions.

Martin is calling for changes to international law that would ban fully autonomous weapons and restrict semi-autonomous weapons. This month, diplomats will meet in Geneva to see if countries want to enter into negotiations about rules governing the use of these weapons — and Martin wants Canada to lead that conversation.
Canada voted yes to a 2025 UN resolution calling on countries to lay the groundwork for possible negotiations on a treaty governing the use of lethal autonomous weapons systems.

DND officials say Canada will continue to participate in international talks about these weapons. It's also ramping up defence spending, having committed to NATO's target of spending five per cent of GDP on defence by 2035.
Whether or not Canada buys in to autonomous weapons, Blondin, the former RCAF commander, says they're coming.
"This is a discussion we need to have as a society."

articles.title: Regional gaps in safe sport rules remain a 'major' concern for Canada's sport integrity agency
articles.summary: More than six months on from a report that rang alarm bells about the prevalence of abuse and maltreatment in sport, the head of Canada’s sport integrity agency continues to have “major” concerns…

image.caption: (CBC Sports)

blocks.text: More than six months on from a report that rang alarm bells about the prevalence of abuse and maltreatment in sport, the head of Canada’s sport integrity agency continues to have “major” concerns about regional gaps in safe sport rules.

Sport Integrity Canada maintains Canada’s Safe Sport Program public registry, which includes the names of more than 80 people who’ve been sanctioned across more than two dozen different sporting bodies.

The registry captures violations of the Universal Code of Conduct to Prevent and Address Maltreatment in Sport, a set of rules governing behaviour around sport that all national sport organizations in Canada had to adopt as a condition of federal funding. It applies to coaches, volunteers, athletes and other leaders across sport.
A New Game Plan Series

items: A New Game Plan: How sports power Australia might offer Canada clues on how to fix its 'broken' system
Everyone into the pool: Canada's sports bodies grapple with push toward merging organizations
A New Game Plan: Sports Funding 101
A New Game Plan: What Australia can teach Canada about rebuilding its sports system
Canadian sports organizations, corporate sponsors see grassroots investment as key opportunity
Are Canada's aging sports facilities limiting development of the next Summer McIntosh?

blocks.text: Commissioner of future of sport says 'widespread abuse,' 'culture of silence' exist at all levels

The behaviours captured in the registry range from physical, psychological and sexual maltreatment to neglect and retaliation, among others. Some of the people on the list have been convicted of crimes. Some have been banned from sport permanently. Others faced sanctions such as suspensions or additional education.
It’s a snapshot of abuse and maltreatment in sport in Canada, but far from a fulsome picture.

That’s because most provincial and local sporting organizations aren’t required to adopt the Universal Code of Conduct. Details of maltreatment at those levels may not appear on Sport Integrity Canada’s registry.

“We know that individuals who cause harm in this way can move from one sport to another sport at one level to another level, where their names aren’t being appropriately placed on a registry so people know about it,” Sport Integrity Canada president and CEO Jeremy Luke said.

“It's a major concern for us. It was a very clear recommendation coming out of the Future of Sport in Canada Commission report and it needs to be put in place in Canada to protect participants who are participating in these sports.”

It’s also not a new concern. Reporting from CBC’s Shattered Trust project chronicled the problems with implementing safe sport rules at the grassroots level, and the consequences of the gaps that exist there, over the last few years.
The evidence shows that despite growing awareness and policy efforts, maltreatment remains deeply rooted in Canadian sport.Future of Sport in Canada Commission report
The Future of Sport in Canada Commission’s final report, released in March, described a system with a longstanding “culture of silence,” and one where racism and discrimination are major issues.
The commission’s work began after a number of athletes spoke publicly and testified in front of Parliament about the harm they experienced during their sporting careers.

“The evidence shows that despite growing awareness and policy efforts, maltreatment remains deeply rooted in Canadian sport,” the commission, led by former Ontario Chief Justice Lise Maisonneuve, wrote. “It affects individuals at all levels, including at the grassroots. These systemic problems require immediate and sustained government action. Although it is not possible to eliminate maltreatment entirely, governments and sport organizations must work together to strengthen and align prevention and response measures so that all participants can safely experience sport’s benefits.”
There are plenty of rules at the national level, where Sport Canada has the power to withhold federal funding to national sport organizations that don’t follow safe sport rules.

It’s below the national level that a hodge podge of safe sport policies persist, from the education every athlete and coach receives, to something as simple and important as background checks, the commission found.
A New Game Plan: The Norway Model

“Participants noted major inconsistencies in safe sport policies across levels of sport and jurisdictions, emphasizing the need for a shared understanding of maltreatment and consistent standards ‘from coast to coast to coast,’” the commission wrote, describing interviews with more than 1,000 participants in the Canadian sport system. “They supported the development of clear and harmonized expectations and remedies for all participants, regardless of sport or level.”
‘Urgent’ need for harmonization
The Future of Sport in Canada Commission said there’s an “urgent” need for more uniformity when it comes to how maltreatment is handled across the country.

More than seven years ago, sports ministers from provinces and territories across the country signed the Red Deer Declaration, agreeing that sport should be a safe place free from maltreatment and abuse. They agreed to work together on issues like monitoring and education.

The declaration led to the Universal Code of Conduct at the national level, but implementation at the provincial and territorial level has been “uneven,” the commission found. Quebec has its own safe sport legislation, for example, while British Columbia created a non-profit called Sport Safeguarding BC to oversee complaints in that province.

Some jurisdictions still don’t have a centralized place for people to file complaints. Many rely on third parties to handle those complaints, a set-up that the commission described as “costly, inconsistent, and affected by perceived or real conflicts of interest.”

The commission called for a pan-Canadian safe sport program that would harmonize rules, education, and the handling of complaints. But that will “take time and political commitment to build,” the commission said.
Luke envisions a system where Sport Integrity Canada can take a leadership role and provide guidance on sharing information and making sure there are consistent rules.
That includes closing the gaps on the registry.
“I think it's a priority, but I also think we need to get to a place where a priority becomes action and that we can put in place the necessary systems to make it occur,” Luke said.

“There are some challenges around putting in place registries, but what's most important is that we protect people who participate in sport, particularly vulnerable people, and that we agree as a country that we want to have a registry so that we can properly protect participants in sport from the grassroots level all the way through to the national level.”
A New Game Plan: What Australia can teach Canada about rebuilding its sports system
Funding for safe sport
In the last year, the federal government has earmarked more than $1 billion, spread over several years, to a sport system in transition.

Sport Canada has put $17.3 million into Sport Integrity Canada in 2026-27, up from $12.6 million in the previous fiscal year. The Sport Dispute Resolution Centre of Canada also saw a boost, from $1.94 million, up from $1.5 million.

Adam van Koeverden, Canada’s secretary of state for sport, gather sport leaders from across the country for a national summit in Ottawa next Monday and Tuesday, and safe sport will likely be on the agenda.

“Sport Integrity Canada has been among the strongest organizations in terms of their ability to apply for additional funding and demonstrate very, very clearly where the gaps lie and what they need in order to achieve stronger and safer sport systems,” van Koeverden said in a recent interview with CBC Sports. “They're one of our most important partners and certainly a regulated, mandated organization within the Canadian sport system.”
But the real heavy lifting to close the gap will require a pan-Canadian solution, something the federal government alluded to in an October press release announcing sport funding.
It will take all provinces and territories on the same page with the same vision, and it’s not clear how long something like that might take.

“Addressing maltreatment is a shared responsibility that requires commitment and collaboration from all levels of government across Canada,” the press release from Sport Canada says. “The federal government continues to work closely with provincial and territorial partners to advance safe sport priorities, including independent complaint mechanisms, awareness and education initiatives, and the exploration of a national safe sport registry. Together, these efforts look to build a more coordinated, consistent and effective approach to safe sport from coast to coast to coast.”
Looking abroad
Sport Integrity Canada works with other sport integrity organizations across the world through the International Integrity Group. Canada will serve on the organization’s executive through 2028.
The group includes Sport Integrity Australia, the similarly named organization that has wrestled with many of the same issues as Canada has faced.

More than five years into its existence, Sport Integrity Australia is trying to tackle the fragmentation between levels of government by adding national integrity managers at the state level to help integrate safe sport policies. Australia is also a federation, with powers divided between the federal level and provincial/state bodies.

“It gives us that formal connection from the national to the state level,” Sport Integrity Australia CEO Dr. Sarah Benson told CBC Sports. “By having those integrity managers in place, they'll also be a connection through to the community level.”
Dr. Sarah Benson, CEO of Sport Integrity Australia, is spearheading a review on the effectiveness of national integrity framework that guides that country's safe sport. (Karissa Donkin/CBC)
Australia doesn’t have all the answers. Still a young agency, Benson is spearheading a review on the effectiveness of the national integrity framework that guides safe sport in Australia.
She’s also hoping to use a home Olympic and Paralympic Games in Brisbane in 2032 as a vehicle for culture change in Australian sport.

“How can we do things differently that would actually benefit and put the athlete at the centre of what we're doing?” Benson said. “How can we use sport to actually try and make a difference in those areas that we've really been challenged to really shift the dial on in the past?”
But Australia’s sport integrity framework is rooted in legislation that makes it easier to cooperate with law enforcement agencies that are investigating the same issue as the sport integrity body.
It’s something Luke said Canada is missing. Sport Integrity Canada regulates abuse and maltreatment, as well as doping and competition manipulation.

“They [Sport Integrity Australia] have a lot of authority being a government agency that enables them to be able to cooperate with law enforcement and cooperate with other governmental bodies and be able to investigate matters perhaps in ways that we can't in Canada, given we're not a government agency and we're not founded in legislation in the same sort of way,” Luke said.
“I think that's a model we want to continue to consider the pros and cons of as we look to implement some of these recommendations in Canada and whether that’s a place that we should be evolving to.”

articles.title: Tax relief could be coming for Canadian artists — but how does it work?
articles.summary: The newly proposed Canada Creative Credit tax relief is supposed to help artists. But how much can artists really expect in their pockets? Which kind of artists can benefit from it? And when — if…

image.caption: Prime Minister Mark Carney, left, and Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne arrive in the House of Commons to table the federal budget on Thursday. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: If you're a Canadian artist who followed Thursday's federal budget release, you might believe you're getting a windfall.

"In Budget 2026, we’re backing the Canadian artists who tell our stories," Prime Minister Mark Carney wrote on X, shortly after Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne made a similar announcement in the House of Commons, revealing the Canada Creative Credit.
This tax credit is aimed specifically at those earning their income from "original and creative artistic works" in the country, according to the budget.
"That means if you’re a Canadian artist, you won’t pay tax on up to $45,000 of income derived from your creative work," Carney added in his post.
But how much can artists really expect in their pockets? Which kind of artists can even benefit from this? And when — if ever — is this actually taking effect?
What the latest federal budget means for national museums in Ottawa
What is the Canada Creative Credit?

The budget says it will likely take the form of a non-refundable tax credit that would "provide tax recognition on up to $45,000 of annual qualifying net business income derived from original and creative artistic works."
A non-refundable tax credit is a set reduction in the amount of income tax someone owes at the end of the year, says Chris Raymond, a tax consultant and content creator.
In short, the government decides your total income tax based on your income. The credit is then subtracted from that amount to reduce your total taxes owed.

What makes credits like the Canada Creative Credit "non-refundable" is that they cannot reduce that amount below zero. If the credit is bigger than your taxes, you don't get to cash out the remainder as a refund.
"The taxable income is the number that we actually calculate how much tax you owe on," Raymond said. "Once that tax number is calculated, that's where the non-refundable credits come into play."
How much money could you get?
Canadians are already covered by a non-refundable tax credit called the Basic Personal Amount, which applies to roughly $16,000 for most incomes.

The Canada Creative Credit would likely cover the difference between the Basic Personal Amount and the government's goal of $45,000, says Robert Gillezeau, an assistant professor of economic analysis and policy at the University of Toronto.

"If you're an artist making whatever, $40,000, $50,000, all the way up to $100,000, this is going to be a meaningful shift in what your income looks like at the end of the day," he said, adding that it could amount to several thousand dollars annually for those eligible.
"It should be a large enough incentive that it will cause some people to work in this area who would otherwise work somewhere else."

items: Carney’s big federal budget bets
Your questions about this year's federal budget, answered

blocks.text: However, that ignores a potentially large additional source of tax, said Toronto-based chartered professional accountant (CPA) and content creator Mohammed Al-khooly.
"If someone wants to truly be exempt on the first $45,000 income, then the provinces would also have to propose a similar credit for the provincial taxes," Al-khooly said.
"It's not necessarily tax-free. It's tax-free for just federal purposes."
Who would be eligible?
This is where things get tricky.
CPA Sam Cao pointed out that the budget says the government will support young Canadian artists and "Canadian painters, sculptors, ceramicists, writers, musicians, actors are our storytellers."

But there is "no exact definition" within the budget that specifies which types of artists would be eligible. So there's little to no way to know whether, for example, a violin teacher or a filmmaker is more likely to be approved.
"They're going to have some type of prescriptive list that demarcates a bunch of workers being in, and other workers being out. It's going to be arbitrary in some ways," Gillezeau said.

"They talk about supporting creativity and the arts broadly; like, any type of writing could fall within that. And if, you know … any type of original writing is going to be eligible, the cost of this credit will just absolutely balloon."

When asked whether there was any firm definition of which artists would qualify, a Department of Finance official referred CBC News to the budget release. It said further details will be announced in the spring economic update in 2027.
Printed copies of the 2026 federal budget. (David Thurton/ CBC)
How likely is it to happen?
Far less than a confirmed payday, Raymond said, the Canada Creative Credit is more the proposition of a plan.

"Obviously the budget hasn't been passed. But they haven't said that if the budget is passed, that this is coming into play," he said. "What they have said is that they have an idea and a concept of how this would work. They're going to consult with people in the industry about it."

There are other targeted tax credits in Canada, such as for teachers and volunteer firefighters. Still, Cao said, if the Canada Creative Credit took a form even somewhat similar to how it is currently described, it would be a unique step.
"This is probably the first tax credit of its kind that specifically targets self-employed individuals through a non-refundable personal income tax credit," he said.
LISTEN | The federal budget explained:
The Current20:14Breaking down the federal budget

Gillezeau noted tax policies targeted at specific professions are typically disliked by economists, comparing the Canada Creative Credit's possible end-status to the "boutique" tax credits of the Stephen Harper era that ballooned the tax code to absurd lengths.
There are also similarities to subsidies for the arts seen in the New Deal of the 1930s, in which the U.S. government subsidized works of art for the public good.
What is different here is the proposal of large, profession-targeted tax credits for income, Gillezeau said. Though what it looks like should it come to fruition is still almost entirely a mystery.
"It's enough to think about [whether] it is a valuable piece of public policy or not," he said. "But the actual implementation details certainly are nowhere close to being there."

articles.title: Amid protests, France's rising debt costs threaten stability
articles.summary: France plans to spend an extra €4 billion on education amid nationwide protests. But with public debt mounting and interest costs climbing, how much fiscal room does the government have?

image.caption: The French government is facing protests over the rising cost of living, and is also grappling with mounting debt costsImage: Reuters

blocks.text: Deeply indebted, politically trapped in a standoff between extremes and led by a government without a parliamentary majority: These are the defining features of France's current predicament.

If, in response to nationwide protests, the government plans to provide €4 billion ($4.48 billion) in low-interest loans to renovate schools by 2030 and allocate a further €1 billion to universities by 2029, it is promising money the state simply does not have.

France's public debt stands at around 120% of gross domestic product (GDP). By comparison, Germany's debt-to-GDP ratio is roughly 65%, despite its €600 billion investment package for infrastructure and defense.

Germany still enjoys the highest possible AAA credit rating. France, by contrast, is rated AA, A+ or Aa3, depending on the credit agency. While Germany's outlook is consistently rated as stable, several agencies have assigned France a negative outlook.

As a result, the French government must pay higher interest rates on its borrowing than Berlin. The risk premium over German government bonds, known as the spread, is now at its highest level since the financial crisis. France pays nearly 1.6 percentage points more in interest than Germany on 10-year bonds.
A barometer of France's public finances
The spread acts as a kind of "fever gauge" for bond markets, explained Friedrich Heinemann, an economist at the Leibniz Center for European Economic Research (ZEW) in Mannheim.

"This fever gauge then forces a change of course. If the spread rises too sharply, France's financing conditions come under pressure, and anyone in France who needs a loan has to pay higher interest rates. Banks then get into trouble, and the crisis escalates further," Heinemann told DW.

"This could then slide toward a financial crisis, which would finally send a clear signal to everyone: Things cannot continue like this unless you are prepared to risk a genuine economic collapse," he said.

Landry Charrier, a researcher at the University of Bonn's Center for Advanced Security, Strategic and Integration Studies, however, does not expect France's debt-fueled spending spree to end anytime soon.

"French people are aware of the country's high public debt. But debt remains an abstract concept if its consequences are barely felt in everyday life. According to INSEE [the French national statistics agency — Editor's note], 56% of the population receive more in government benefits and services than they pay in taxes and social contributions. The majority therefore have a tangible interest in maintaining the status quo," Charrier told DW.
For more than half a century, France has regularly spent more than it collects in tax revenue. The last time it balanced its national budget was in 1974.
Echoes of eurozone crisis

France last paid a similarly high-risk premium at the end of 2011, during the eurozone debt crisis. What is particularly striking is how quickly it has risen: Since June 2026, the spread over German government bonds has more than doubled.

The main driver is not so much the general level of interest rates. Rather, it's the growing risk premium investors demand in response to high debt levels, political instability, large budget deficits and the recent unrest.

The higher the interest rates, the larger the share of the national budget that must be devoted to debt servicing alone. France is expected to pay more than €79 billion in interest on its total public debt in 2026. That figure is projected to exceed €91 billion in 2027 and could reach between €125 billion and €132 billion by 2030.

These figures include the costs incurred by social security funds and local authorities. The central government's interest bill alone is currently estimated at €62.6 billion by the Agence France Tresor, a French Treasury agency.

In the coming years, France will have to refinance large amounts of outstanding bonds that were issued when interest rates were at historic lows. At the same time, the country's substantial budget deficit means it must take on additional debt.
Warning shot for Germany
The trend of rising interest costs is also affecting Germany. The ZEW's Heinemann has calculated that German interest payments are likely to increase sharply by the early 2030s.

"For the federal government alone, which has so far paid around €30 billion, the figure will triple within a few years as both debt and interest rates rise. And it won't stop there — it will exceed €90 billion. Reaching €100 billion in annual interest payments in the federal budget is then no longer far off," warned the economist.
Could France's debt crisis become a problem for Europe?
In France, however, economic realities seem to have little impact on political debate. Both the far-right National Rally (RN) and the far-left France Unbowed (LFI) are campaigning on costly promises.

RN leader Marine Le Pen, for example, wants to reinstate the retirement age of 62 while promising €140 billion in savings. Jean-Luc Melenchon, LFI's leader, has even suggested that government bonds held by the French central bank should be "thrown into the fire."
"Nobody will ever notice they've disappeared," he has claimed.
'Fairy tales from the left and the right'
For Heinemann, this is "a good example of radical parties on both the right and the left simply telling economic fairy tales."
Their common message, he said, is that "there is a way out of this mess that requires neither fiscal consolidation nor painful cuts."
Charrier is convinced that many French people have yet to grasp the seriousness of the situation.
"The euro has made it easier for France to access cheap financing and has long softened the pressure to adjust," he pointed out.

"In the past, currency devaluations [of the French franc — Editor's note] made economic imbalances immediately felt through declining purchasing power and rising prices. Today, that warning signal is missing. This has created the illusion that necessary adjustments can be postponed indefinitely," Charrier said.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Texas mayor instructs police to limit co-operation with ICE
articles.summary: There has been months of public outcry in Houston after an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer fatally shot a man who was driving to work.

blocks.text: The mayor of Houston, Texas, has directed the city's police to limit co-operation with federal immigration officials.

The move by John Whitmire, a Democrat, comes on the heels of stunning victories by the party in Texas during this week's midterm elections. It breaks with policy set by Republican Governor Greg Abbott, who lost his re-election bid.
"I do this to begin a healing process," Whitmire said on Friday, and to "reduce fear and anxiety across our community". He added: "I also do this knowing that elections matter."
There has been months of public outcry in Houston after an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer fatally shot a man who was driving to work.

Houston police chief Noe Diaz said on Friday that officers will now only contact ICE if someone they arrest for a jailable offence also has an administrative ICE warrant, which are issued internally by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), within which ICE operates.
"For example, if our police officers pull someone over for a minor traffic infraction and they write a citation, that person receives a citation and goes about their day," Diaz said.

Under the previous rules, Houston police officers were required to inform ICE if anyone they were dealing with came up as having one of these warrants attached to their name when they were searched on the National Crime Information Center (NCIC) - a digital database that includes records on wanted persons, stolen property, certain missing people and those arrested and fingerprinted for serious offences.
Whitmire said on Friday that he had directed the Houston Police Department to make the changes through an executive order.
He also called on Congress to change federal immigration rules, saying "ICE needs better training. They need body cameras. They need to be trained in de-escalation."
He added, "But this can only be done in Washington. I can only control what I can control."

In response, a spokesperson for the DHS told Houston's NBC affiliate, KPRC 2, in a statement: "We remain disappointed that sanctuary politicians seek to limit cooperation with ICE, as our law enforcement are simply fulfilling their sworn duties to serve and protect our communities."
"Partnerships with law enforcement are critical to having the resources we need to arrest criminal illegal aliens across the country," the spokesperson added.
Another Texas city, Austin, has also begun implementing a similar policy change.
Democrats won both the US Senate and House of Representatives in Tuesday's midterms, taking control of Congress for the rest of Donald Trump's presidency.

Texas, a long-time Republican stronghold, was the site of one of the most stunning upsets in the vote, with the state electing its first Latina governor, Gina Hinojosa, as the first Democrat governor since 1995. It also elected its first Democratic senator since 1988.
Whitmire has previously faced criticism for abiding by immigration enforcement policies under the Trump administration.
He had resisted previous calls to implement similar changes over concerns that the White House could send a surge of immigration officials in response. , external
Abbott has also threatened to take pull millions in funds from cities like Houston, Dallas and Austin unless they allow police to cooperate fully with federal immigration officials.
The BBC has contacted Abbott's office for comment.
Whitmire's announcement comes a week after an ICE officer was charged with aggravated assault with a deadly weapon after he allegedly hit a man with a vehicle in Texas.
Earlier this year, large protests broke out in Houston after an ICE officer fatally shot a man driving to work.
The deceased, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a 52-year-old Mexican national who lived in the US as an undocumented immigrant for decades, was not the intended target, officials said after the incident.

articles.title: Meghan's father Thomas Markle under house arrest after child sex abuse material charge
articles.summary: The 82-year-old appeared in court in Florida after the FBI searched two Los Angeles-area storage units he rented.

blocks.text: Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, has been placed under house detention at his assisted living facility in Florida after being charged over possession of child sex abuse material.
Markle, 82, was arrested in Florida on a federal complaint alleging he held images that show child sex abuse, the US Department of Justice (DoJ) said.
He is charged with one count of possessing indecent images of children, the DoJ said. Markle has previously denied allegations of possessing images of child sex abuse, calling them "sick lies".
In a 30-minute court hearing on Friday he was also ordered to submit to electronic monitoring, but no plea was taken.
At the court hearing, the charges were laid out against him by federal prosecutor Courtenay Derry, according to the BBC's US partner CBS News.
He was brought into court in a wheelchair, escorted by two US Marshals. Markle was wearing black trousers and a black t-shirt.
No plea was taken during the hearing, and an arraignment date in California will be determined in due course, a joint statement from the DoJ and the US Attorney's Office Central California said.
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex have not commented on Markle's arrest.

Markle was arrested after the FBI, acting on warrants, searched storage units in LA registered to him which he had rented since 2008, with the last payment being made in October this year, the DoJ said.
Inside the units the FBI says agents seized about 78 items, including film negatives, slides and books that they allege contained child sex abuse material.
FBI director Kash Patel said authorities "moved quickly" when arresting Markle.
"Mr Markle allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions," Patel said.

He added that the FBI would "use every single resource at our disposal to protect innocent kids – any predator who targets children will have zero safe haven in this country or anywhere they try to hide".
Witnesses "positively identified" Markle in two of the images believed to contain child sex abuse material.
In those images, the man pictured "appears to be in the age range of 30s to 40s", which suggests the alleged abuse dates back decades as Markle is currently 82 years old.
Last month, police in the Philippines obtained a warrant to examine devices allegedly removed from Markle's former home in the country.
Four boxes of material, including computers, phones, hard drives and old video tapes, were handed to officers by Meghan's half brother Thomas Markle Jr.

Markle Sr moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes, and lived in Cebu until May. He was then reportedly living in a Florida rehabilitation centre learning to walk again after having his leg amputated.
In October, London's Metropolitan Police confirmed that it had received a letter in 2019 making a "number of claims" relating to Markle Sr.

The Met said information contained in the letter, which related to allegations against Meghan's father outside the UK, was passed on to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, but it did not share it with other law enforcement agencies.
The force has since voluntarily referred itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IPOC) over its handling of the letter.

In a statement released in October after the allegations against Markle Sr emerged, the Duchess of Sussex said: "I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed."
Meghan has been estranged from her father since 2018. The BBC understands she broke contact with him last year.

articles.title: Strait of Hormuz could reopen as part of Qatari plan for Iran nuclear inspections
articles.summary:
Trump still considering new assault on Iran nuclear sites – though threats less credible after Vance remarks

Qatar, the lead mediator in the US-Iran conflict, is seeking to persuade Tehran…

blocks.text: Qatar, the lead mediator in the US-Iran conflict, is seeking to persuade Tehran to allow UN nuclear weapons inspectors to visit Iran’s bombed nuclear sites, including those housing the country’s stockpile of highly enriched uranium.
Iran would not be required to make any commitment that the stockpile would be removed from the country, with other options on the table, including reducing the uranium content by down-blending it.
Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad al-Thani, the emir of Qatar, spoke to Donald Trump about the proposal, the emir’s office said on Friday without revealing the call’s contents.
The state news agency said the emir “emphasised the importance of continuing dialogue and embracing diplomacy as a means of resolving disputes, preventing further escalation in the region”.

Trump is still considering whether to mount a further assault on Iranian nuclear sites, though the credibility of his threats is weaker inside Iran after his vice-president, JD Vance, said the war itself, and not just its cost to American consumers, was critical to the collapse of the Republican vote in the US midterms.

Under the Qatar proposal, the US would immediately lift the naval blockade on Iran in the strait of Hormuz and release a portion of the $8bn (£6bn) of its frozen assets. In return, Iran would agree to visits by International Atomic Energy Agency inspectors to its bombed nuclear facilities, based on a previous abandoned agreement that had been reached in Cairo in September 2025.
Iran would open the strait of Hormuz on the second day, via a route it has already negotiated with Oman that they would jointly lodge with the International Maritime Organisation (IMO).

Iran has multiple other preconditions for opening the strait including ending the war in Lebanon, a withdrawal of US forces from the Iranian coastline, a commitment to lift some economic sanctions, and agreement to pay war reparations. The sequencing of these commitments has been at the heart of the mediation.
In the memorandum of understanding, a $300bn reconstruction and development fund was to be set up to help Iran recover economically, but it was never clear exactly how this proposal was to be funded.

Iran, in a triumphalist mood after Trump’s election wipeout, has been wary of allowing the UN nuclear inspectors back into the country, claiming it had lost faith in Rafael Grossi, the head of the inspectorate.

blocks.caption: A billboard bearing the message ‘we will kill Trump’ in Tehran. Photograph: Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Tehran claims Grossi betrayed his duty to uphold the nuclear non-proliferation treaty, by failing to criticise the US for bombing Iran’s nuclear sites. It fears that material gathered by the inspectors would be handed over as targeting data to the Americans and Israelis.

In the parallel talks on opening the strait, Oman’s foreign minister, Badr Albusaidi, spoke again to Iran about the future of the strait administration including the agreed route, the extent to which the agreement is temporary and the need to register the proposal with the IMO, either as a bilateral agreement or a joint regional proposal.
Oman has a long-term proposal for the administration of the strait compliant with the law of the sea in that shipping companies would be charged only for services, and not tolls.

Amir Hayat Moqaddam, the deputy chair of the Iranian parliament’s national security and foreign policy committee, told the Iranian Students’ News Agency (ISNA) on Tuesday that ships from four countries – China, India, Qatar and Iraq – were allowed to pass through the strategic waterway.

The exemptions served mutual interests, he said, adding that Iran charged Indian and Chinese vessels transit fees while allowing Qatari ships to pass free of charge. Medicine was received from India, while China provided political support.

It is reported that of the 10.23m barrels a day of Gulf crude that passed through the strait in October, about 42% went to China and 13% to India, said Muyu Xu, a senior crude oil analyst at the analytics firm Kpler.

The navy of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said two “violating” oil tankers attempting to pass through an unauthorised route in the eastern sector of the strait of Hormuz had collided with mines and caught fire.
The IRGC said the two tankers had turned off their navigation and identification systems and that the attempted crossing was with the support of US military forces.

articles.title: Pope in 'pretty good health' as he starts Latin America tour
articles.summary: Pope Leo travels to Uruguay just three weeks after having surgery for lung cancer.

blocks.text: Pope Leo XIV has told reporters travelling with him to Latin America he is "in pretty good health", in his first comments on his condition since having surgery for lung cancer.
The Pope has arrived in Uruguay, the first stop of a 12-day tour which he is undertaking only three weeks after his operation.
The pontiff, 71, also said he was "very happy" to be able to make the trip which was thrown into doubt last month when doctors discovered a tumour during a routine scan.
The tour will cover Argentina and a much anticipated return to Peru, which the Vatican described as a "homecoming" as the Pope was based there for many years as a missionary, then a bishop.
"I must confess that, from the very first day, I never had any doubts; I was convinced that this journey had to go forward," the Pope told journalists on his plane to Uruguay.
"Thanks to the marvellous medical staff... I believe I am in quite good health," Pope Leo confirmed.
Last month's operation to remove a tumour was successful and his doctors say the cancer has not spread.
On Friday, he arrived in Monetevideo to a seafront lined with crowds shouting his name as his Popemobile passed.
In his first speech of the trip, the Pope said universal healthcare should be "accessible to everyone".
He told the crowd in Plaza Independencia the care he received made him think of the "many men and women who lack the means to obtain a timely diagnosis" or receive treatment.
He capped his day with a prayer at the Montevideo Cathedral.
Pope Leo will cover more than 20,000 miles on his sixth international tour.
On Sunday he will travel to Argentina, the homeland of his predecessor Pope Francis who did not return during his own papacy.
The Pope said his visit was about being near the people who were looking to the Church for a message of "hope".

articles.summary: Polls show no coalition is expected to secure a majority of seats, in one of the closest elections in recent history

blocks.text: Let the count begin

Six weeks of campaigning, politicking and debates is done. New Zealand has voted and over the next few hours we’ll find out the results of what has been cast as one of the tightest elections in recent memory.

For weeks, the polls have shown no clear path to government for any potential coalition, left or right. Seemingly unimpressed by National and Labour, polls have tracked voters turning to the smaller parties, such as the centrist Opportunity party.

Tonight could see Opportunity potentially end up as kingmaker, unless that pre-election support and hype has failed to translate into votes. Stay with us as we learn the answer to that big question and others, as we keep you across the counts and results as they come in. It’s going to be an exciting night!
Key events

items: 30m agoLet the count begin

blocks.text: Michelle Duff

As the first results of the night flashed up onto the big screen, Labour party volunteer Jasmine, 22, who works in the public service and didn’t want to use her last name, stopped talking mid-sentence.

A hush fell over the room as the first poll results show the main parties neck and neck . “That’s close,” she said, exhaling. “It’s great that Opportunity is over 5%, I’m happy about that. It’s just overwhelming; this is years of work, and that’s real numbers.” She’s been working for the party since she was 16.
Cheers are going up in the room as electorate results begin to come in. About 200 party supporters are expected here tonight.
Another update here with 8% of the vote counted.
National on 31.2%, Labour 28.4%, the Greens 12.9%, Act 11.2%, NZ First 9.6%, Opportunity 5.7% and Te Pāti Māori 0.4%.
On these numbers, we would have a right bloc coalition back in power. Long way to go.
Jamie Tahana has this from the Backbencher pub in Wellington:

At the Backbencher, a politics and puppet themed pub across the road from the Beehive, people are splitting their attention between the election coverage, the football, the cricket, and tonight’s rugby league.

Many people spoken to by the Guardian weren’t prepared to go bold with a prediction, nervous about the likely tight result. One man, Joel, told the Guardian Opportunity making parliament would “shake things up.”
Also here is NZ First local candidate and former Wellington mayor Andy Foster, and his team. Foster said he was nervous.
“Let’s get through tonight, but I’m feeling confident,” he told the Guardian. “The country needs NZ First and we still have a lot to do,” he said.
Some colour from voting stations around the country today.

blocks.caption: A dog sits outside a voting place on election day in Wellington.  Photograph: Charlotte Graham-McLay/AP
Electoral officials speak to voters inside a voting place at Kokiri Marae on the day of the general election in Lower Hutt.  Photograph: Hollie Adams/Reuters
People enter a voting place at St Anne’s Anglican church on the day of the general election in Wellington. Photograph: Hollie Adams/Reuters
Election workers prepare ballot papers for voters in Wellington. Photograph: Charlotte Graham-McLay/AP

blocks.text: The Labour party election night event has kicked off in the Upper Hutt Cosmopolitan Club, a popular suburban venue in the middle of Labour party leader Chris Hipkins’ Remutaka electorate, which he’s held since 2008.

As Te Awa Kairangi (the Hutt River) flows by a few sleepy streets away, the Cossie Club has begun to fill with party supporters and volunteers, many who are travelling to this small city in the Wellington region by bus. At first stride into this red-hued room, festooned with fairy lights and balloons, it’s difficult to know if you’ve walked into a political event or a 21st party.

Politicians expected here tonight include Ginny Anderson, Labour’s candidate for the Hutt South electorate; Barbara Edmonds, standing for Mana; and Ayesha Verrall, who is contesting Wellington North against incumbent Green party MP Tamatha Paul.
Hipkins (whose nickname is Chippy) said his family tradition is fish and chips on election night as the votes are counted, so he is expected here later.

blocks.caption: Eva Corlett

blocks.text: Eva Corlett
Seats to watch
Hutt South, Nelson, Banks Peninsula, Wigram, Whanganui and Kāpiti were either tight races between National and Labour last time around, or could change hands after boundaries were re-drawn.
Wairarapa, West Coast-Tasman and Hamilton East are historically National strongholds. If they flip red, that could be an early signal for good overall outcome for Labour.

The Tāmaki electorate has traditionally been held by National but was taken by the libertarian Act party in 2023. This year, the race between those parties’ candidates and newcomer Labour candidate Max Harris is tight – a Harris win would be a surprise upset for the right.

Meanwhile, Green candidate Kahurangi Carter is vying to claim Christchurch Central. If Greens co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick keeps Auckland Central and Tamatha Paul nabs Wellington North, New Zealand’s three largest city centre electorates will be represented by the Green party.

Maungakiekie could also be an indicator for the final results. Over the past two elections, the Maungakiekie electorate has proven to be an “extraordinary” bellwether seat, accurately reflecting the mood of the nation.
If six weeks of campaigning has left you cold, then sit back as Matilda Boseley spills the tea on the two Chrises, election vibes and the Luxon-Opportunity question.

blocks.caption: What’s up with the New Zealand election? – video

blocks.text: Seeing some numbers. So with just 1% of the vote counted, National are on 31%, Labour 29.8% and Opportunity party 5.7%, so they are above the threshold. There is obviously a long, long way to go tonight. The Greens are on 12.2%, Act 11% and New Zealand First 9.4%. Te Pāti Māori are on 0.3%.

So, what’s at stake for Luxon and National tonight? A lot. The party is facing the dire possibility of being the first one-term National-led government since it was founded in 1936. Remember, National has never led for less than three terms, ever. So this is a huge night for Luxon’s legacy and the National party, both past and present.

blocks.caption: Ahead of tonight, Christopher Luxon has long struggled in the preferred prime minister poll. Photograph: Phil Walter/Getty Images

blocks.text: Tonight, our New Zealand correspondent Eva Corlett is posted at National party’s main gathering at Viaduct Events Centre, in Auckland, awaiting the arrival of Christopher Luxon.

In Upper Hutt, north of Wellington, we’ll have updates from Michelle Duff who is mingling alongside the Labour faithful at the local Cosmopolitan Club. That’s happening in Chris Hipkins’ electorate, and he’ll show up there once the lay of the electoral land becomes clear.

In Wellington, Jamie Tahana is at the Backbenchers pub, which is a brief stroll from New Zealand’s Beehive. He’ll be checking the mood with keen voters who have pulled up a pew and are ready to watch the results start coming in.

articles.title: US midterm results may help unite Israeli coalition to unseat Netanyahu
articles.summary: Democrats’ sweep could urge Israel’s divided opposition to join forces and remove prime minister closely allied with Trump

blocks.text: The Democrats’ sweep of Congress may make it easier for Israel’s splintered opposition to overcome deep internal divisions and form a coalition government, by increasing the urgency of unseating Benjamin Netanyahu, who has associated himself so closely with Donald Trump’s Republicans.
But as Israel took stock of the results, there was also a sense that the elections marked a longer-term shift in US politics that will make the job of any new Israeli leader far more difficult.

The United States provides Israel with critical military and diplomatic support, so nurturing bipartisan ties was the cornerstone of foreign policy for decades. Netanyahu ripped up that commitment to throw his lot in with the Republicans in general and Trump in particular.
The opposition had always attacked his decision as ill-judged. By the end of the week, they were warning that it was positively dangerous.

“These people aren’t against Israel,” prominent opposition politician Yair Lapid said of incoming Democratic lawmakers, urging his country to rebuild bridges. “They’re mainly against Netanyahu – for them, anything connected to him is toxic.”
“The easiest thing is to scream that ‘America is lost,’ because if it’s lost, you don’t have to work. That’s just not true. Not at all.”
Lapid laid out a plan to “rebuild trust” in the US, but it perhaps did more to demonstrate the scale of the problem than reassure Israelis.
His proposal of a transatlantic charm offensive by officials of a prospective new government drew a swift and sharp rebuke from the New York congressman-elect Brad Lander.
Lander, a Democrat who is Jewish and describes himself as a liberal Zionist, was detained in the occupied West Bank last month while joining Palestinians trying to harvest olives.

“Minister Lapid: As someone who won a seat in Congress last night, and who cares about Israel: you’re not listening to what American voters – Jewish and non-Jewish – are saying,” Lander wrote in a direct response.
“We aren’t starving for a barnstorming tour. We’re hungry to see respect for international law and human rights.”

In his exchange with Lapid, Lander also highlighted the arrest of journalist Abed Abu Shehada, a Palestinian citizen of Israel, as an example of how Israel violates international law. He drew a direct link with the ICE “regime of detention without charges, based on secret evidence, designed to intimidate and chill speech” that he said was rejected by US voters.

Abu Shehada was reportedly taken from his home by 15 masked security officials in a night-time raid, without an arrest warrant. Interrogators have only questioned him about a podcast interview with a public figure, lawyers acting for Abu Shehada said.
On Friday, Lander and two other incoming Jewish members of Congress, Daniel Bliss and Scott Wiener, wrote to Israel’s ambassador to the US calling for the immediate release of Abu Shehada.

“Detaining a reporter for conducting an interview — the only issue that interrogators questioned him about — is a violation of international law,” Lander said when he published the letter. “It comes at a time when senior Israeli officials are trying to delegitimize the participation of Palestinian citizens in Israel’s recent elections.”
Nor do Israel’s problems end with angry Democrats. The wounded Republican establishment lost no time looking a few thousand miles away to find reasons for the collapse of its voter base.

Soon after the election results came in, the vice-president, JD Vance, put “our relationship with Israel” on a short list of reasons for voter fury, and on election day Trump made a last-ditch attempt to woo voters with a pledge to cut off $4bn (£3bn) in annual military aid to Israel.

The announcement caused panic in Israel’s defence establishment. “When the commander of the Israel air force hears something like that, he might slit his wrists,” one official told Channel 12 news. “Where are we going to come up with 15 billion shekels every year, and what does that mean for Israel’s future defence budget?”

Netanyahu only responded to Trump’s electioneering on Friday with an attempt to spin the cut as a joint decision reflecting Israel’s economic strength. It demonstrated a “move from aid to partnership”, his office said in a statement.

Netanyahu has long flaunted his relationship with Trump, his fluent English and experience in the US, presenting himself as the only man with the international standing to guarantee Israel’s security in a hostile world.
After Tuesday’s US election, he looks more like an agent of its destruction to many in Israel. “One thing is clear: we are losing America,” Ben Caspit wrote in Ma’ariv, a daily newspaper.

“This isn’t a process; it isn’t happening in stages; it is happening all at once. It is an avalanche. It is a reverberating collapse of the foundation of Israel’s national defence doctrine. This isn’t a decree of fate. It is a decree of Netanyahu.”

Some advocates for change inside Israel found cause for hope in the Democrats’ victory, if Israel’s opposition can turn their mandate for change into a new government. They won 67 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, but more than a quarter went to Palestinian citizens of Israel, and some of the Jewish Israeli opposition parties have ruled out sitting with them.

US administrations have for too long equated support for Israel with blind support for its government, said Nadav Tamir, a former senior Israeli diplomat in the US who is now executive director of J Street Israel.
That consensus is cracking, but the majority of lawmakers from both parties still see Israel as a key US ally in the Middle East, he wrote in the Times of Israel.

External pressure from those who support its security but see current policy as self-destructive might push the country towards necessary change, including a resolution of the Israel-Palestine conflict.

“Perhaps this will be the paradox of the new [US] Congress,” he wrote. “It will be less willing to define support for Israel as automatic alignment with every policy of its government, but precisely for that reason, it may offer Israel more meaningful support in breaking out of the cycle of wars and building a future of security and prosperity.”

articles.title: Paraguay's President Santiago Peña impeached and arrested
articles.summary: Santiago Peña was ousted due to a banking crisis which left millions of people unable to access their money.

blocks.text: Paraguay's President Santiago Peña has been impeached and placed under house arrest after the collapse of a digital bank with links to his private business interests.

Peña was arrested on Friday minutes after lawmakers, including from his own party, unanimously voted to remove him from office due to a widening crisis triggered by the collapse of Ueno Bank earlier this week.

He had offered to step down on Thursday. Rather than accept his resignation, senators impeached Peña and charged him with misconduct, meaning he has been stripped of the immunity usually granted to ex-presidents.
Peña, who until last year held shares in the company that owned the bank, has denied any wrongdoing.
The demise of the digital bank has left more than half of Paraguay's population without access to their savings after it was seized by Paraguay's central bank.
An estimated three million depositors remain unable to access their savings and pensions prompting widespread protests particularly in the capital, Asunción.

The impeachment charges that led to Peña's removal alleged he had conflicts of interest, manipulated regulatory oversight, diverted pension funds, and participated in an institutional cover-up involving the central bank.
Peña is due to be questioned on Saturday over allegations of breach of trust, influence peddling, and misappropriation of funds, prosecutor Silvia Margarita Gonzalez Vester said.
Peña's impeachment passed with 44 out of 45 senators voting in favour of it. One lawmaker was absent.
Afterwards, senate president Basilio Núñez said Peña was found guilty of "dereliction of duty".
Paraguay's Vice-President Pedro Alliana was then sworn in as interim President.
"Compatriots who are now going through a difficult time as a result of the financial collapse will be fully compensated," said Alliana, who will serve as President until 2028.

articles.title: US carries out another round of ‘minor’ strikes on Iran, Trump says
articles.summary:
The president’s announcement comes days after an earlier attack on Iran was made public, and as diplomatic efforts to end the conflict have accelerated

Donald Trump has said the US military…

blocks.text: Donald Trump has said the US military on Friday carried out a new round of limited strikes on Iran, targeting an air defence system, describing the action as “minor.”

Iranian state media reported the sound of two explosions in the Suza area of Qeshm Island, which is in the strait of Hormuz, the crucial waterway for oil shipments that has been disrupted since the beginning of the US war on Iran in February.
